lectures.name: Introduction to MSK Anatomy
lectures.title: Introduction to MSK anatomy
lectures.framing: The vocabulary the rest of the musculoskeletal (MSK) block is built on, and the approach every MSK complaint gets: which structure is the pain coming from, what is wrong with it, and are there red flags?
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Red flags? is the step you never skip. Degenerative = pain with activity, better with rest · inflammatory = pain at rest, morning stiffness, warm and swollen. Upper motor neuron = increased tone, brisk reflexes, Babinski positive · lower motor neuron = normal or low tone, reduced reflexes · MSK weakness has no objective sensory loss. Muscle and tendon hurt to contract AND to stretch; ligament hurts on passive movement. Concentric shortens, eccentric lengthens, isometric doesn't move. Hilton's law: the nerve to the muscle is the nerve to the joint. Joint pain comes from the capsule, ligaments and bone, not the cartilage.

blocks.html: 1. The general approach to an MSK complaint

• Step 1 · know the anatomy: consider every structure in the area as a possible pain generator, plus pain referred in from elsewhere
  • Step 2 · the clinical features of each structure (the history and exam below)
  • Step 3 · red flags? No → treat in the usual fashion · Yes → investigate the red flag
  • Anatomic localization (which structure) is not the differential diagnosis (what is wrong with it)
  • History: OLDCARS - onset, location, duration, character, aggravating or alleviating, associated features, radiation, severity · works for pain, sensory symptoms and weakness
  • Exam: the body part and the joint above and below (referred pain is real)

rows: Constitutional symptoms · history of cancer · site-specific
Fevers, chills · looks unwell · immunocompromised · IV drug use
Depends on the site: flank or writhing pain · aortic aneurysm · kidney stones · GI or genitourinary symptoms
Morning stiffness · rashes · marked joint swelling, redness
The 5 P's · skin discolouration · aortic aneurysm · claudication
Urinary retention, bowel incontinence · saddle anesthesia · frank weakness or sensory loss · claudication

blocks.html: • Some of these clues are specific to one condition - give the ones that fit, not the whole list
2. Which structure? Clues on history and exam

rows: Pain with use, weight-bearing, or touch even when still
Fracture: is the bone normal? (normal bone, real trauma vs weak bone: osteoporosis, tumour, infection) · tumour (+ systemic features) · avascular necrosis · infection (+ systemic features)
Pain around the joint, worse weight-bearing, may be swollen
Pain around the joint · instability, pain on PASSIVE movement
Sprain (hurts in any direction) → rupture (frank instability: subluxation, dislocation)
Pain with MOVEMENT · hurts to CONTRACT and to STRETCH
Strain (hurts to use) vs rupture (looks weak) · tendinosis (overuse, not -itis) · inflammation, infection · tumour (soft-tissue mass) · compartment syndrome
Compression or stretch from any cause (nearby arthritis, abscess, inflamed tendon, tumour, sleeping on the arm) · intrinsic nerve damage (infection, inflammation, tumour invasion)
Pain with activity, better with rest · gradual onset · ± stiffness through the day · ± locking or instability · may be weak · swelling only secondary
Pain at rest · morning stiffness · swelling, warmth, redness · ± rash · malaise · fever, weight loss (especially infection) · acute or subacute onset

blocks.html: 3. Weakness: pain, muscle, or nerve?

• Weakness is very common when pain is present, because it hurts to move: is it weakness, pain, or both?
  • Upper motor neurons live in the brain and spinal cord · the lower motor neuron starts at the anterior horn cell and runs out to the muscle

cols: Upper motor neuron (stroke, spinal cord injury)
rows: Acute (Achilles rupture) or chronic (rotator cuff degeneration)
Sensory loss in the same nerve's territory
Sensory loss in the matching territory
Only that muscle (others may look weak from pain)
Reflex lost only at the ruptured tendon
Normal or low tone · reduced reflexes · Babinski negative

blocks.html: • Three dropped feet: same weakness, three sites - tendon rupture (no sensory loss, tender dorsum) · common peroneal nerve (lateral leg numb, tender at the fibular head) · L5 root (lateral leg and dorsal foot numb, pain from the back down)
4. Managing a non-red-flag MSK diagnosis

• Education first: what it is, what to expect
  • ① Non-drug: relative rest, activity changes · RICE or POLICE (protection, optimal loading, ice, compression, elevation) · heat, cold, ultrasound, laser · acupuncture, yoga, massage · rehabilitation · gait aids · braces (orthoses)
  • ② Drugs: topical (anti-inflammatory) → injected (local steroid) → systemic (oral NSAID such as ibuprofen, acetaminophen)
  • ③ Interventional or surgical: only after the less invasive options fail
  • Then follow-up · contributing factors (mood, fatigue) · treat the activity and participation limits, not just the impairment
  • Red-flag conditions get their own treatment: cancer → surgery, chemotherapy, radiation · infection → antibiotics ± debridement · trauma → casting, surgery, rehab
5. Somatic nervous system

• Carried by all spinal nerves and some cranial nerves
    • general sensory fibres (afferent): pain, proprioception, temperature, pressure, touch from skin, muscle and joints → cell body in the dorsal root ganglion
    • general motor fibres (efferent): to skeletal muscle → cell body in the ventral grey horn
  • Reflex arc: sensory neuron → (± interneuron) → motor neuron in the cord, bypassing the brain
  • Who supplies what: dorsal rami → deep back muscles + skin of the back · ventral rami → the limbs and the rest of the trunk

blocks.alt: somatic nerve pathway reflex arc - sensory in, motor out - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Reflex arc: the sensory neuron enters through the dorsal root ganglion, the motor neuron leaves through the ventral root to the muscle

blocks.html: 6. Development: dermatomes and myotomes

• Paraxial mesoderm forms paired somites, each supplied by one spinal nerve · the dermomyotome splits into a dermatome (→ skin) and a myotome (→ muscle)
  • Myotomes fuse, so most muscles get more than one spinal segment (e.g. diaphragm C3-C5)
  • Neighbouring dermatomes overlap, so test the middle of a dermatome
  • Two skin maps: dermatome (one spinal nerve, e.g. C5) vs peripheral nerve territory (one named nerve, e.g. axillary nerve)
7. Muscle contractions and the kinetic chain

rows: Lifting a dumbbell in a curl

blocks.html:
• Open kinetic chain: the limb is free (biceps curl, bench press)
  • Closed kinetic chain: the limb is fixed (push-up, walking, squatting) · rotation of one link sets off a chain reaction, so biomechanics matter

blocks.cap: Isometric (no length change) vs isotonic concentric (shortening) and eccentric (lengthening)

blocks.html: 8. Joints

• Laws of joints
    • any muscle that crosses a joint acts on that joint
    • Hilton's law: the nerves supplying the muscles that move a joint also supply its sensation
  • Stability comes from 3 things: shape of the articulating surfaces · ligaments · muscles
  • Synovial joints are freely movable
    • hyaline cartilage and synovial membrane are poorly innervated · joint pain comes from the capsule, ligaments and bone
    • ligaments = thickenings of the fibrous capsule where it needs reinforcing

rows: Flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction (more range than condyloid)

blocks.cap: The six synovial joint types: plane, pivot, hinge, saddle, condyloid, ball-and-socket

blocks.html: 9. The skeleton and bony terms

• Anatomical position: standing upright, face, palms and toes forward · supine = face up · prone = face down
  • Axial skeleton: skull (only freely movable joint = temporomandibular) · vertebral column (bigger lower down; coccyx not weight-bearing) · sternum · 12 pairs of ribs (lowest 2 floating)
  • Appendicular skeleton: pectoral girdle (clavicle, scapula) → humerus → radius, ulna → carpals → metacarpals → phalanges (thumb 2, other digits 3) · pelvic girdle → femur → patella (a sesamoid bone) → tibia (weight-bearing), fibula → tarsals → metatarsals → phalanges
    • the sacroiliac joint barely moves · it hurts when it does (e.g. pregnancy)

rows: head (rounded end on a neck) · condyle (rounded distal end) · facet (small flat surface)
trochanter (femur only) > tuberosity > tubercle · process · protuberance · epicondyle (beside a condyle) · crest > line · spine
groove · notch (edge) · fossa (shallow basin) · sulcus (narrow crevice)
ramus (flat branch at an angle) · neck · sinus (air-filled cavity)

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Joint stability: shape of the articulating surfaces is the #1 factor, then ligaments, then muscles
  • Dermatome landmarks: T4 = nipple, T10 = umbilicus
  • MSK is the 2nd most common reason for physician visits and the 2nd most common self-reported chronic condition

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Back & Neck
lectures.title: Anatomy of the back and neck
lectures.framing: Every structure here is a possible pain generator in the mechanical back pain lecture. Learn what makes each region's vertebrae different, which ligament stops which movement, and which back muscles a strain hits.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Anterior longitudinal ligament resists hyperextension; the narrow posterior longitudinal ligament resists hyperflexion (which is why discs bulge out beside it). Cervical = transverse foramina + bifid spines · thoracic = costal facets + long downward spines · lumbar = big bodies. C1 nods "yes", C2 turns "no"; no disc between them. Trapezius = cranial nerve XI · deep back muscles = dorsal rami. Erector spinae → lifting strains · transversospinalis → rotation strains.

blocks.html: 1. The vertebral column

• Jobs: protect the spinal cord · carry body weight · posture and movement (flexion, extension, lateral flexion, rotation)
  • 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical · 12 thoracic · 5 lumbar · 5 sacral (fused into the sacrum) · 4 coccygeal (fused into the coccyx)
  • Curves absorb stress and protect the back

rows: Fetal period (flexed fetal position), kept for life
Early infancy, as the baby extends out of flexion
Kyphosis (thoracic): anterior vertebrae eroded or fractured, e.g. osteoporosis
Lordosis (lumbar): pelvis tilts forward · weak trunk muscles, pregnancy

blocks.html: • Scoliosis = an increased sideways curve with rotation of the vertebrae (weak back muscles, posture, congenital vertebral defects, unequal leg length)
2. A typical vertebra

• Body (front): carries weight, gets bigger going down
  • Arch (back) = pedicles (join arch to body) + laminae (close it behind)
    • vertebral foramen = the hole for the cord, between body and arch
    • spinous process (back) and transverse processes (sides) = muscle and ligament attachments
    • 4 articular processes → facet (zygapophyseal) joints = plane synovial joints between neighbours
  • The superior and inferior vertebral notches of neighbouring pedicles form the intervertebral foramen, where the spinal nerve exits
  • Joints between vertebrae: each vertebra joins the ones above and below at the disc (bodies) and the facet joints · except C1 (joins the skull) and L5 (joins the sacrum)
  • Rib joints (thoracic): the rib head meets the superior costal facet of its own vertebra, the inferior costal facet of the vertebra above, and the disc between · the rib tubercle meets the transverse process of its own vertebra (costotransverse joint)
  • Laminectomy = removing spinous processes and laminae to take pressure off the cord or roots (tumour, herniated disc, bony overgrowth)

blocks.cap: Typical vertebra from above and from the side: body, pedicles, laminae, processes, vertebral foramen and intervertebral foramen

blocks.html: 3. The intervertebral disc

• Between vertebral bodies: attaches neighbours, permits movement, absorbs shock
    • joined to the bodies at the end plate (cartilage fused to the disc + a thin layer of porous bone)
    • anulus fibrosus = outer rings of fibrocartilage · nucleus pulposus = inner gel, high water content
  • About 25% of the column's height · thickest in cervical and lumbar spine · no disc between C1 and C2
  • Herniation: most posterolateral herniations are at L4/L5 or L5/S1 and hit the root just below (the L4 disc hits L5)
4. Regional differences

rows: Large, especially C3-C7 (cervical enlargement of the cord)
Short, with transverse foramina (vertebral artery C6 up to C1; only the vein at C7)
Long, with facets for the rib tubercle
Long, slopes down over the next one
Superior facets up and back · inferior facets down and forward
Superior facets back and slightly out · inferior forward and slightly in
Superior facets back and in · inferior forward and out
Rotation, some lateral flexion · facet orientation blocks excessive flexion and extension
Flexion, extension, some side bending, limited rotation

blocks.html:
• Atypical cervical vertebrae
    • C1 (atlas): a ring - two lateral masses joined by an anterior arch (in place of a body) and a posterior arch (in place of laminae) · a groove for the vertebral artery on its upper surface · atlanto-occipital joints → "yes" nod (flexion, extension)
    • C2 (axis): the dens projects up from the C2 body and pivots against the back of C1's anterior arch → atlanto-axial pivot → "no" rotation
  • Sacrum: 5 fused vertebrae · carries body weight to the ilium through the sacroiliac joints · front (pelvic) surface smooth and concave, back rough and convex · paired sacral foramina for the sacral nerves · sacral hiatus = site of a caudal epidural
5. Ligaments

rows: Broad, strong band on the front of bodies and discs, occiput to sacrum
Narrow, inside the canal on the back of the bodies
Tips of the spinous processes, C7 to sacrum
Continues the supraspinous above C7: very strong band from the external occipital protuberance to the cervical spinous processes, out to the skin · fills the neck curve
Attachment for neck and upper back muscles

blocks.alt: vertebral column ligaments - ALL, PLL, flavum, supraspinous, interspinous, nuchae - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Ligaments of the vertebral column on a sagittal section, with the same ligaments on MRI

blocks.html: 6. Muscles of the back

rows: Elevates, depresses, retracts scapula · turns the glenoid up
Extends, adducts, medially rotates the humerus
Elevates scapula · turns the glenoid down
Retract scapula, turn the glenoid down, hold it to the chest wall
Deep (intrinsic) - posture and control of spinal movement
Erector spinae (iliocostalis lateral → longissimus → spinalis medial)
Both sides: extend spine and head, eccentrically control trunk flexion · one side: lateral flexion
Both: extend head and neck · one: lateral flexion + rotation
Rotation to the opposite side · stabilise · proprioception

blocks.html:
• Why they matter for back pain
    • erector spinae: strained lowering things to the floor (eccentric) or lifting them (concentric)
    • transversospinalis: rotates each segment, so over-rotation tears it - a frequent cause
  • Dorsal rami also become the skin nerves of the back and neck, which is why they pierce the superficial muscles
  • Dermatomes and myotomes by root: see the table in 03.1 - Anatomy of the Back & Spinal Cord

blocks.alt: back muscle layers - superficial, intermediate serratus posterior, deep - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Back muscles in three layers: superficial, intermediate (serratus posterior superior and inferior) and deep

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
lectures.title: Clinical approach to mechanical back and neck pain
lectures.framing: Most back and neck pain is "mechanical": axial pain that is worse with movement and better with rest. The work is to screen every patient for red flags and, with none, to treat conservatively without imaging, since an exact anatomical diagnosis is often unnecessary.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ No red flags and under 6 weeks → no imaging. Disc pain is worse with flexion; facet pain is worse with extension. Mechanical pain is worse with movement, better with rest. Herniation = worse with cough or sneeze, sudden after lifting, younger patient. Whiplash: keep moving, no collar. Muscle pain has no diagnostic test.

blocks.alt: mechanical back and neck pain overview.svg

blocks.html: Nerve-root pain, stenosis and the red-flag conditions themselves are on the non-mechanical chart; the vertebrae, ligaments and back muscles are in 02.1 - Anatomy of the Back & Neck.
1. The approach

• Possible pain generators: paraspinal muscle and soft tissue · intervertebral disc · facet (zygapophyseal) joint · nerves in the spine · sacroiliac joint
  • History: OLDCARS (onset, location, duration, character, alleviating or aggravating, radiation, severity) plus red flags
  • Exam: the spine itself · contributing lower-limb problems · a neurological exam · signs of red flags
    • palpable landmarks: C7 (vertebra prominens) · acromion · spine and medial border of the scapula · ribs 6-12 · iliac crest · sacrum
2. Red flags

rows: Progressive weakness or sensory change · saddle anesthesia · incontinence · erectile dysfunction · loss of hand dexterity · ataxic gait · abnormal reflexes
Morning stiffness · improves with exercise · pain in the 2nd half of the night · family history · rashes · eye symptoms
Young age · severe night pain, no relief with rest · weight loss · night sweats · history of cancer · associated signs (e.g. blood in the urine)
Fall or trauma · osteoporosis · previous fragility fracture
Neck pain with dizziness on neck movement, cranial nerve signs, drop attacks · limb pain with activity, with or without neck or back pain (claudication)

blocks.html: 3. Investigations: when (not) to image

• Most low back pain needs no imaging: soft tissue often doesn't show · it can't separate symptomatic from asymptomatic changes · it rarely changes management · but it is required to look for red flags
  • With red flags, add targeted tests: blood work and cultures (infection) · abdominal or other imaging (cancer) · angiography (vascular) · electromyography (nerve)
  • Who to image (Canadian Association of Radiologists)
    • no red flags and under 6 weeks → NO imaging
    • symptoms over 6 weeks despite good conservative care → an X-ray can be the starting point
    • imaging indicated → MRI is best · CT only if MRI is contraindicated or unavailable · X-ray otherwise only to look for red-flag conditions (fracture, malignancy)
    • suspected uncomplicated herniated disc or spinal stenosis → image only after a failed 4-6 week conservative trial
    • red-flag indications for MRI: suspected cancer · infection · cauda equina syndrome · severe or progressive neurological deficit · suspected compression fracture · urgent if an epidural abscess or hematoma is a worry

rows: Cheap, quick screen of alignment and fractures
Disease in many places · "hot" vs "cold" lesions
Dye injected into the thecal sac · only if MRI is contraindicated

blocks.html: 4. Mechanical pain: what it looks like

• Definition: axial pain that is worse with movement and relieved by rest
    • location: midline or just beside it, neck or back
    • onset: anywhere from acute to chronic · usually built up by degeneration, then "tweaked" by stairs or a bad bend
    • character: dull ache or sharp, stabbing
    • red flags: none · imaging often normal (disc degeneration shows up in many adults with no back pain)
5. Muscle pain and whiplash

• Three muscle problems: acute strain or spasm · repetitive strain (repetitive tasks, forceful exertion, vibration, compression, awkward postures) · myofascial trigger points (hyperirritable spots, tender when pressed, can refer pain)
  • No test diagnoses it: investigate only to rule other things out
  • Treatment: rule out red flags → reassure (excellent prognosis) → relative rest → ice or heat → topicals · a short course of oral anti-inflammatories → physiotherapy for postural support
  • Whiplash associated disorder: neck symptoms after an acceleration-deceleration injury (car crash)
    • muscles most often (strains, partial tears) · less often facets > anterior longitudinal ligament > bone > cord
    • under 5% still have severe symptoms at 2 years
    • more than pain, stiffness and reduced range → X-ray if fracture is a worry · MRI if neurological signs · otherwise keep moving, no collar, heat or ice, acetaminophen or NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, oral or topical), modest physiotherapy (aggressive programs can worsen it)
6. Spondylosis: the degenerative cascade

• Spondylosis = degenerative disc disease + facet arthropathy (degenerative disc disease, facet syndrome) with loss of disc height and thickened ligaments
  • The cascade: repeated axial loading → end-plate damage → tears in the anulus → nucleus pushes into the tears (internal disc disruption) → disc loses height → angles change, facets overloaded: synovial thickening, cartilage loss, osteophytes, lax capsule → slipping (degenerative spondylolisthesis) · thickened ligaments, bulging disc → lateral stenosis (roots in the foramina) and central canal stenosis

rows: Pain from the disc itself, not from it pressing on something · nucleus pushes out through radial or concentric tears in the anulus, but the anulus stays intact
Arthritis of the synovial facet joints
Localised, may be one-sided · refers: headache from the neck · lumbar rarely past the knee
Conservative: therapy, exercise · NSAIDs acutely, acetaminophen
Flexion-based therapy · NSAIDs acutely, acetaminophen · ? joint injection · medial branch block or ablation

blocks.alt: disc vs facet loading in flexion and extension - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Bending forward squeezes the disc; bending backward squeezes the facet joints
Referred pain maps from facet joints at each spinal level

blocks.html: 7. Disc herniation

• Disc herniation: disc material goes beyond the anulus (diffuse bulge → protrusion, broad-based = 25-50% of the circumference, or focal → extrusion → sequestration, which has lost contact with the parent disc)
    • causes both disc pain and compression of nerve structures
    • younger patients · sudden axial pain after lifting · worse with coughing or sneezing
    • lumbar discs herniate posterolaterally, away from the ligamentum flavum and towards the nerve roots

blocks.alt: disc bulge, protrusion, extrusion and sequestration - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: From normal disc to diffuse bulge, protrusion, extrusion and a free sequestered fragment

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Back & Spinal Cord
lectures.title: Anatomy of the back and spinal cord
lectures.framing: The spinal cord is shorter than the spine, and almost every clinical rule in the non-mechanical back pain lecture follows from that: where it ends, which root a disc hits, where a needle can go safely, and why lumbar and cervical stenosis behave differently.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The cord ends at L1-L2 (conus medullaris) but the dural sac runs to S2 - so a lumbar puncture or epidural goes in at L3/L4 or L4/L5, into the cauda equina, not the cord. C1-C7 exit above their vertebra, C8 below C7, everything after below. Epidural space and subarachnoid space are real; subdural is potential. Ventral root = motor, dorsal root = sensory. C7 = middle finger, triceps · L5 = big toe extension · S1 = lateral foot, Achilles.

blocks.html: 1. The spinal cord

• Part of the central nervous system, continuous with the medulla · a reflex centre and the pathway between body and brain
  • Runs from the foramen magnum to L1-L2 in adults
  • Not uniform in width
    • cervical enlargement (C4-T1 cord levels) → brachial plexus (upper limb)
    • lumbosacral enlargement (L1-S3 cord levels) → lumbar and sacral plexuses (lower limb)
  • The end of the cord
    • conus medullaris = the tapered tip, at L1-L2, just below the lumbar enlargement
    • filum terminale (internum) = a thread of pia from the tip to the coccyx, anchoring the cord
    • cauda equina ("horse's tail") = the lower lumbar, sacral and coccygeal roots running down past the cord's end to their own foramina
  • Why it is short: in the embryo the cord fills the whole canal, but the spine outgrows it, leaving the cord in the upper two-thirds of the canal

blocks.alt: spinal cord enlargements and 31 pairs of spinal nerves - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The cord ends at L1-L2; cervical enlargement for the brachial plexus, lumbar enlargement for the lumbosacral plexus; 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal nerves

blocks.html: 2. Spinal nerves and where they exit
• 31 pairs: 8 cervical · 12 thoracic · 5 lumbar · 5 sacral · 1 coccygeal

rows: Below C7 - 8 cervical nerves, only 7 cervical vertebrae
Below their own vertebra (under its pedicle)
Leave the cord high, travel down as the cauda equina, exit at their own foramen
The gap between cord segment and foramen grows going down

blocks.html:
• Making a spinal nerve
    • ventral (anterior) rootlets = motor (+ presynaptic autonomic fibres; cell bodies in the anterior horn) · dorsal (posterior) rootlets = sensory (cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion)
    • roots join in the intervertebral foramen as a mixed spinal nerve
    • it splits into a dorsal ramus (skin and deep muscles of the back) and a ventral ramus (limbs and the rest of the trunk)
  • L5 is the biggest lumbar nerve in the smallest lumbar foramen: the lower lumbar nerves are the most easily compressed
  • Review the inside of the cord in 04 - Introduction to the Nervous System
3. Meninges and spaces

rows: Real space outside the dura · fat + internal venous plexus
Tough outer layer · forms the dural sac down to S2 · anchored to the coccyx (filum terminale externum) · continuous with the cranial dura
Delicate, no blood vessels · held against the dura by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure
Real space with CSF and the cord's vessels · enlarges below the cord as the lumbar cistern (L2 to S2), holding the cauda equina
Directly on the cord, roots and vessels · denticulate ligaments anchor the cord in the dural sac · continues as the filum terminale

blocks.html: 4. Epidural vs spinal block and lumbar puncture

• Both done at L3/L4 or L4/L5 - below the end of the cord, so the floating cauda equina roots move away from the needle
  • Epidural: needle into the epidural space, around the dura · bathes the cauda equina roots after they leave the sac → numb below the level · widely used in labour
  • Spinal block / lumbar puncture: needle into the subarachnoid space · drug straight into CSF or CSF sampled from the lumbar cistern
    • patient on their side with the trunk flexed

blocks.cap: Epidural: needle stops in the epidural space; spinal block or lumbar puncture: needle enters the subarachnoid space and CSF

blocks.html: 5. Dermatomes, myotomes and root lesions

• Dermatome = the skin supplied by one spinal nerve root · myotome = the muscles supplied by one root
  • A root lesion gives sensory change in its dermatome, weakness in its myotome, and a reduced reflex
  • Neighbouring dermatomes overlap a lot · overlap is minimal only at the ventral axial line, where non-sequential segments sit side by side
  • Why the pattern is segmental: each somite keeps the nerve of its own segment, even when its muscle cells migrate down the limb
    • epimere → epaxial back muscles (splenius, erector spinae, transversospinalis) · dorsal ramus
    • hypomere → lateral and ventral trunk muscles and all limb muscles · ventral ramus
    • most myotomes fuse, so most muscles get more than one segment (several nerves to one trunk muscle, or several nerves joined in the brachial and lumbosacral plexuses)

blocks.alt: cauda equina, conus medullaris, and filum terminale.png
blocks.cap: The cord tapers to the conus medullaris at L1-L2; the filum terminale anchors it; the cauda equina roots run on below

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain
lectures.title: Clinical approach to non-mechanical back and neck pain
lectures.framing: Non-mechanical pain is either a squeezed nerve - at the side (radiculopathy) or in the centre (stenosis, cauda equina, myelopathy) - or "everything else" that the red flags find (inflammatory, fracture, visceral, infection, tumour). Without red flags, start the same conservative care as for mechanical pain.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Saddle anesthesia + urinary retention or fecal incontinence = cauda equina syndrome → urgent MRI and decompression within 48 hours. Lumbar stenosis squeezes roots (neurogenic claudication, eased by bending forward, no bladder change); cervical stenosis squeezes the cord (clumsy hands, upper motor neuron signs) → urgent consult. A disc hits the lower root: C4/5 → C5, L4/5 → L5. Radicular pain is eased by slackening the nerve. Inflammatory pain gets better with movement. Spondylosis degenerates, spondylolysis fractures, spondylolisthesis slips.

blocks.alt: non-mechanical back and neck pain overview.svg

blocks.html: The red-flag list and who to image for mechanical pain are on the mechanical chart; the cord, its exits and the dermatome table are in 03.1 - Anatomy of the Back & Spinal Cord. Reading the spine on X-ray is in 04 - Axial Spine Radiology.
1. Triage: which group is this?

• Take the history and exam, and exclude non-spinal causes: hip disease · visceral (pancreatitis, endometriosis, kidney stone) · vascular (aortic aneurysm, claudication) · systemic (e.g. endocarditis) · viral syndromes
  • Diagnostic triage (Traeger 2017, primary care)
    • serious spinal disease, under 1%: vertebral fracture · metastasis · spinal infection · axial spondyloarthropathy · cauda equina
    • radicular pain, radiculopathy, spinal stenosis, 5-10%
    • non-specific low back pain, 90-95%: acute or persistent
  • No red flags → advice and reassurance: good prognosis, no immediate imaging, consider non-drug treatment

rows: NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) · skeletal muscle relaxants · weak opioids
Exercise · psychological therapies · multidisciplinary care · physiotherapy

blocks.html: • Nerve compression can come from ANYTHING that takes up space: disc, spondylosis, abscess, tumour, bleed, a slipped vertebra (spondylolisthesis)
2. Radiculopathy: compression at the side

• Definition: a spinal nerve root compressed or malfunctioning in or around the neural foramen, from any cause
    • degenerative causes are by far the most common (disc herniation, spondylosis)
    • others: tumour (primary, metastasis, carcinomatous meningitis) · infection (abscess, tuberculosis) · sarcoidosis · diabetic neuropathy of the root · trauma · arteriovenous malformation
  • Presents as
    • onset acute or insidious, depending on the cause
    • limb > neck or back, in a dermatome
    • burning, tingling, electrical
    • eased by positions that slacken the nerve (arm overhead, legs curled)
    • weakness and reduced reflexes in a myotome · sensory change
  • Where: lumbar - under 1% non-degenerative, mostly the L5 and S1 roots · cervical - mostly C7 and C6, from cervical spondylosis
  • Which root does the disc hit? The lower one
    • cervical: nerves exit above their vertebra → C4/5 disc → C5 · a C6/7 disc → C7
    • lumbar: the upper root has already left; a paracentral disc hits the traversing root → L4/5 disc → L5 · a far-lateral L4/5 disc catches L4
  • Treatment
    • conservative first: education, excellent prognosis (most settle over months) · relative rest, ice or heat · topicals, oral anti-inflammatories, short course of opioids if severe · physiotherapy
    • image if red flags, or the deficit is severe or progressing (e.g. marked arm weakness) · electromyography tests the root
      • neck pain or arm pain from degeneration: MRI only with neurological signs or symptoms, or pain over 4 weeks of conservative care · CT only if MRI is contraindicated · X-ray not indicated (degenerative changes from early middle age, usually unrelated to symptoms)
    • next: epidural steroid injection → surgical decompression (refractory symptoms · progressive or severe deficit · tumour, large abscess, trauma)

blocks.alt: which nerve root a lumbar vs cervical disc herniation hits - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: A paracentral L4/5 disc hits L5 while a far-lateral one hits L4; a C6/7 disc hits C7

blocks.html: 3. Central stenosis: lumbar roots vs cervical cord
• The cord ends at ~L1 → lumbar central stenosis squeezes roots, cervical central stenosis squeezes the cord - so they look and are treated entirely differently

rows: Picture of an atraumatic spinal cord injury
Clumsy hands, wasted intrinsic hand muscles · arm tingling, distal worse · gait and balance problems · urinary incontinence (retention with overflow) · often a radiculopathy too
Neurogenic claudication: worse walking a distance · relieved by bending forward (grocery cart, walking uphill) and by sitting (more slowly than vascular claudication)
Upper motor neuron signs below the level
Mild to moderate claudication: none, or non-urgent MRI (especially a surgical candidate)
Flexion-based activity and physiotherapy are the mainstay
Urgent neurosurgical or spine consult for decompression

blocks.html: 4. Cauda equina syndrome

• The severe end of lumbar central stenosis: heavy compression, worst at the lowest roots
  • Red flags: weakness · saddle anesthesia · urinary retention · fecal incontinence
  • Urgent MRI · a neurosurgical emergency - outcomes much better if decompressed within 48 hours of onset
  • See cauda equina syndrome
5. "Everything else": the red flags

rows: Night pain in the 2nd half of the night
Sacroiliac joints · ask about eyes, rashes, family history, enthesopathy, other inflammatory joint pain

blocks.html:
• Inflammatory → seronegative spondyloarthropathies: ankylosing spondylitis · psoriatic arthritis · inflammatory bowel disease arthritis · reactive arthritis (more in the rheumatology lectures)
  • Fractures
    • osteoporotic compression fracture: elderly, on steroids · minor or no trauma · axial pain with radiation · treat the pain and the osteoporosis
    • spondylolysis: fracture of the pars interarticularis · young athletes who extend the back (gymnasts, football players, weightlifters) · may lead to spondylolisthesis

rows: Slip of one vertebra on the next (degenerative, or from a spondylolysis)

Cardiovascular: abdominal aortic aneurysm (pulsatile mass), vertebral artery insufficiency (dizziness, cranial nerve findings), atypical cardiac pain · GI: peptic ulcer, pancreatitis · genitourinary: pyelonephritis, kidney stones, gynecologic (endometriosis)
Bone tumour · epidural or intradural mass · drop metastases · referred (e.g. renal carcinoma)
Young age, severe night pain, weight loss, night sweats, cancer history, blood in the urine

blocks.html: • Any red flag → investigate it: plain films if worried about fracture · MRI if worried about neurological compromise, infection or neoplasm

lectures.name: Axial Spine Radiology
lectures.title: Axial spine radiology
lectures.framing: Read every spine film the same way, ABCS, and then ask of each finding: which view shows it best, what is the sign, and does it change what happens next? Fracture (stable or unstable), spondylolysis (the Scottie dog's collar) and scoliosis (the Cobb angle) are the three the objectives name; the normal variants are the things not to call disease.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A fracture that reaches the posterior elements is unstable. Spondylolysis = collar on the Scottie dog (oblique view); isthmic spondylolisthesis adds the forward slip (lateral). Cobb angle over 10° is scoliosis, over 50° is surgical. Lateral C-spine: four smooth lines, atlantodental interval under 3 mm, prevertebral tissue under 7 mm at C2 and 22 mm at C6. Perched facets → MRI and urgent neurosurgery. A limbus vertebra is not a fracture.

blocks.html: 1. The systematic approach: ABCS

• Alignment: cervical mild lordosis · thoracic kyphosis · lumbar lordosis, and each vertebra lined up with the next
  • Bones: follow the cortices · vertebral body height · pedicles and transverse processes
  • Cartilage and joints: cartilage is invisible, so read the disc spaces (calcification, bony bridging) and the facet joints
  • Soft tissues: prevertebral and paraspinal · then the whole image (lungs, heart shadow, kidney or gallstones, bowel, free air)
  • Start with alignment: a break in it tells you where to look · then the vertebrae, the disc spaces and the soft tissues in turn
  • Compare with previous imaging when you have it
2. Cervical spine

• Standard views: AP (anteroposterior) · lateral · right and left oblique · open-mouth (odontoid)
    • acute trauma, especially in a collar: no oblique views (don't move the neck) · most acute trauma gets CT instead, because plain films miss subtle fractures
    • flexion and extension views are not routine: only when subluxation or instability is suspected (the atlantodental interval can be measured on them)

rows: Count all seven: T1 meets the 1st rib, C7 above it · C1 is a ring, C2 has a body and the dens (the mandible may hide both, so they get the open-mouth view) · spinous processes in a straight line · facet joints parallel · uncinate processes at the sides (enlarge in osteoarthritis) · C7 transverse process over ~2-2.5 cm = cervical rib
Spinous processes off the midline or unevenly spaced → facet dislocation

C1-C7 and T1, counted down from C1-C2 or up from the prominent C7 spinous process (vertebra prominens) · 4 smooth lines: anterior vertebral · posterior vertebral · spinolaminar · spinous process · atlantodental interval under 3 mm adults, under 5 mm children · prevertebral soft tissue under 7 mm at C2, under 22 mm at C6 (or no wider than the vertebral body) · airway smooth and open: nasopharynx, oropharynx, laryngopharynx, trachea
Fractures, perched facets, spondylosis · prevertebral widening: retropharyngeal abscess, trauma, hematoma
The neural foramina open up (C2-C3 down to C6-C7, both sides), bordered above and below by the pedicles · spinous processes look foreshortened
The neural foramina and the facets
C1's lateral masses line up with C2 · joint spaces symmetric
Misalignment = injury or instability · dens fracture

blocks.html: 3. Thoracic spine

• Standard views: AP · lateral · swimmer's view (arm raised) for the upper thoracic spine hidden by soft tissue
    • added when an upper thoracic abnormality is suspected, or when the radiographer finds the standard views don't show it · it also shows the lower cervical spine, and T1 is the vertebra below the prominent C7 spinous process
  • AP: count from T1 (1st rib) to T12 (12th rib) · spinous processes teardrop-shaped over the bodies · endplates as sclerotic margins · pedicles oval with corticated margins · transverse processes and ribs · a mild curve can be positional when the patient is in pain, or come from osteoarthritis
  • Lateral: the normal kyphosis · bodies, endplates, disc spaces · pedicles look elongated and border the oval neural foramina · facet joints easiest to see in the mid to lower thoracic spine · the ribs curve behind
4. Lumbar spine and sacrum

• Standard views: AP and lateral · oblique only when requested, for the pars interarticularis · sacrum and sacroiliac joints on dedicated views if asked
  • AP: five lumbar vertebrae, L1 is the one below the 12th rib (4 or 6 lumbar-type vertebrae = transitional) · broader than thoracic, with more horizontal spinous and transverse processes · both pedicles visible on every level · sacroiliac joints and sacral foramina symmetric
  • Lateral: bodies, endplates, disc spaces, pedicles, foramina · the pars interarticularis (between the superior and inferior articular processes) - its defect is a cause of low back pain
  • Oblique: the Scottie dog - nose = transverse process · ear = superior articular facet · front leg = inferior articular facet · neck = pars interarticularis
  • Sacrum and sacroiliac joints: sacral ala = the sides of S1 (beside the first sacral foramina) · lateral masses beside the S2-S4 foramina · coccyx of 4 or 5 segments · the sacroiliac joint runs obliquely, so the AP shows only parts of it · a dedicated sacral film centres lower than the lumbar AP (which centres near the umbilicus)

blocks.cap: Oblique lumbar views: the Scottie dog outline, and a pars defect forming its collar

blocks.html: 5. Pathology

• Any bone, any body part: TIMS-C = Trauma and tumours · Infection, inflammatory (rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis), idiopathic · Metabolic and malignancy · Systemic disease (leukemia, lymphoma) and senile (osteoarthritis) · Congenital (look on an immature skeleton)
  • Trauma: hyperflexion, hyperextension, compression, burst and distraction injuries
    • Jefferson = C1 ring broken in several places · hangman's = both pars of C2 (traumatic slip of C2), unstable · extension teardrop = anteroinferior corner (C2), a hyperextension injury; rotation can injure the cord · flexion teardrop = front of the body, with cord, posterior column and interspinous ligament injury
    • hyperflexion: a torn interspinous ligament widens the gap between two spinous processes · simple wedge = anterosuperior corner only · unstable wedge also involves the posterior structures
    • dens fractures: type I tip · II base · III into the C2 body (detail not required)
    • Stability: anterior body only = more likely stable · involving the posterior elements = UNSTABLE
    • a fragment pushed back toward the canal, or any break in the posterior vertebral line, means the fracture reaches past the back of the body: unstable
    • perched facets (facets incongruent, one body slipped forward) → MRI + urgent neurosurgery · bilateral facet dislocation slips further than unilateral · on the AP, spinous processes crowded, uneven or off the midline point to it when there is no lateral
    • a widened disc space without a fracture (hyperextension, often in a spondylotic neck) may be a ligament injury → MRI · ligament injuries are easy to miss on X-ray
  • Cervical spondylosis (the commonest non-traumatic cervical finding): disc-space narrowing · marginal osteophytes · endplate sclerosis · straightened lordosis (can be muscle spasm) · the same signs as osteoarthritis anywhere
  • Retropharyngeal abscess: retropharyngeal soft tissue wider than the vertebral body at C5-C6 · airway pushed forward · air locules (anaerobic infection or an airway cause)
  • Spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis
    • pars defect on the oblique view = a collar on the Scottie dog's neck (collar sign)
    • pars defect + slip = isthmic spondylolisthesis (e.g. L4 on L5, measured in mm and graded, with a narrowed disc space) · no pars defect, older adult = degenerative
    • the pars defect often shows on the lateral; the oblique helps when it is subtle
  • Inflammatory (mostly seronegative): ankylosing spondylitis - ossified anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments, bony bridging across discs, fused facets → rigid spine, fractures next to mobile segments · sacroiliitis: erosions of the iliac and sacral subchondral plates with pseudo-widening, sclerosis mostly on the iliac side, ankylosis late · bone marrow edema (active inflammation) needs MRI
  • Tumour: an expansile lytic lesion replacing a pedicle (an aneurysmal bone cyst in the lecture) was obvious on the AP and nearly invisible on the lateral - always read both views
  • Scoliosis: sideways curve ± rotation (pedicles shift)
    • Cobb angle: superior endplate of the top tilted vertebra and inferior endplate of the bottom one, angle between their perpendiculars · over 10° = scoliosis, under 10° normal · over 50° → consider surgery
    • the primary curve (e.g. right thoracic) brings a compensatory one below (left lumbar) · corrected with Harrington rods + transpedicular screws
  • Hardware: transpedicular screws through the pedicles, joined by posterior rods (scoliosis, spondylolisthesis) · vertebroplasty: cement in bodies with painful compression fractures, often in thin, osteopenic bone: relieves pain and slows progression, does not restore height

blocks.cap: Lateral X-ray: L1 compression fracture with loss of height compared with the normal T12 and L2 above and below

blocks.html: 6. Normal variants - not disease

• Cervical rib off C7 (bony ones show, fibrous ones don't; a complete one can pseudoarticulate with the 1st rib): can cause neck pain, and arm pain by pressing the neurovascular bundle
  • Transitional vertebrae: lumbarization or sacralization
  • Schmorl's nodes: depressions in the superior or inferior endplates, usually incidental (some studies link them to pain)
  • Limbus vertebra: a triangle of bone at the anterosuperior corner from an unfused ring apophysis - adolescents, often L4 - not a fracture
  • A curve under 10°

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Proximal Upper Extremity
lectures.title: Anatomy of the proximal upper extremity
lectures.framing: The bones and joints of the shoulder girdle and arm, learned for what goes wrong with them: which landmark breaks, which nerve runs beside it, and what holds each joint together. The muscles, nerves and vessels are next week; what to do about a separated, arthritic, unstable or frozen shoulder is on the SHOULDER BONES AND JOINTS chart.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Surgical neck fracture → axillary nerve · shaft fracture → radial nerve (it lies in the radial groove). The glenohumeral joint trades stability for range - held by the labrum, rotator cuff and ligaments, and dislocates anteroinferiorly. The coracoclavicular ligament, not the acromioclavicular, carries the AC joint: tear both and it dislocates. The coracoacromial arch stops upward displacement, and the cuff tendons run underneath it. Sternoclavicular joint: the clavicle fractures before the joint dislocates. Supraglenoid = biceps, infraglenoid = triceps.

blocks.html: 1. The pectoral girdle and its four joints

• Pectoral girdle = clavicle + scapula, with four joints
  • Scapulohumeral rhythm: full shoulder movement needs the scapula to reposition the glenoid as the arm moves, so the muscles work from a stable origin
  • Shoulder range of motion uses the glenohumeral joint plus the sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints and the scapula gliding on the chest wall

rows: The only joint linking the arm to the axial skeleton · dislocation is rare - the clavicle breaks first
Acromial end of the clavicle + acromion
Plane synovial, uniaxial · wedge-shaped articular disc

Acromioclavicular ligament: strengthens it superiorly · coracoclavicular ligament: the strong pair of bands to the coracoid that gives most of the stability and suspends the scapula and arm from the clavicle
AC ligament alone torn = subluxation · AC + coracoclavicular torn = dislocation (clavicle up, acromion prominent)
Deep surface of the scapula on the thoracic wall

blocks.alt: pectoral girdle bones and its four joints - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Clavicle, scapula and humerus with the sternoclavicular, acromioclavicular, scapulothoracic and glenohumeral joints, and the same bones outlined on an X-ray

blocks.html: 2. Clavicle and scapula

• Clavicle: S-shaped (medial half convex forward, lateral half concave forward) · enlarged triangular sternal end · flat acromial end
  • Scapula: triangular flat bone, essential for overhead movement

rows: Large projection for muscle and ligament attachments
Shallow socket for the humeral head
Long head of biceps · long head of triceps
Splits the back into the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae (homes of supraspinatus, infraspinatus)
Bridged by the transverse scapular ligament → a foramen for nerves and vessels

blocks.html: • On an AP shoulder X-ray (arm internally rotated) find: scapula · clavicle · coracoid process · glenoid fossa · acromion · humeral head · greater tubercle
3. Humerus and the elbow end

• Proximal humerus
    • head (meets the glenoid) · anatomical neck (separates the head from the tubercles)
    • greater (superolateral) and lesser (superoanterior) tubercles = insertions · between them the intertubercular (bicipital) groove for the long head of biceps
    • surgical neck = the narrowing below the head and tubercles, a common fracture site
    • deltoid tuberosity (mid-shaft) · radial (spiral) groove on the back of the shaft for the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
  • Distal humerus
    • medial epicondyle: common flexor origin · ulnar nerve runs behind it
    • lateral epicondyle: common extensor origin
    • capitulum (lateral) ↔ radial head · trochlea (medial) ↔ trochlear notch of the ulna
    • coronoid fossa takes the ulna's coronoid process in full flexion · olecranon fossa takes the olecranon in full extension
  • Proximal forearm
    • radius (lateral, shorter): head pivots in the annular ligament and meets the capitulum and the ulna's radial notch · neck (between head and tuberosity) · radial tuberosity (biceps)
    • ulna (medial, longer): olecranon (triceps) · coronoid process (brachialis) · trochlear notch · radial notch

rows: Surgical neck (low-energy fall onto the hand, elderly with osteoporosis)
Radial nerve ± deep brachial (profunda brachii) artery

blocks.cap: Proximal humerus: head, anatomical and surgical necks, greater and lesser tubercles, intertubercular groove, deltoid tuberosity and radial groove

blocks.html: 4. The glenohumeral joint

• Built for mobility: poor fit of a large head in a shallow glenoid · several bursae · lots of articular cartilage · lax capsule
  • Stabilisers
    • Glenoid labrum: fibrocartilage ring that deepens the socket and improves the fit
    • rotator cuff tendons: supraspinatus · infraspinatus · teres minor · subscapularis
    • ligaments

rows: Thickenings of the front of the capsule
Base of the coracoid → front of the greater tubercle
Acromion → coracoid = with the bones beneath, the coracoacromial arch
Roof that stops the head moving up · so strong the humerus or clavicle breaks first
Holds the biceps tendon in its groove

blocks.html:
• The rotator cuff tendons pass under the arch; the gap narrows in full abduction
  • Subacromial (subdeltoid) bursa between the acromion and the cuff · axillary recess: a loose pouch of the inferior capsule that allows the range
  • Blood supply: anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries · suprascapular artery
  • Nerves (Hilton's law): suprascapular · axillary · lateral and medial pectoral · musculocutaneous · upper and lower subscapular · thoracodorsal · radial
  • Clinically
    • dislocation is usually anterior and inferior - the arch blocks upward escape and the capsule is weakest in front and below → axillary nerve at risk · treatment usually immobilisation, then rotator cuff strengthening
    • impingement: the supraspinatus tendon is pinched in the subacromial space → tendonitis · overuse stretches the static stabilisers → mild instability → the cuff tires → secondary impingement (see the ROTATOR CUFF DISEASE chart)

blocks.cap: Coronal section of the shoulder: labrum, axillary recess, long head of biceps tendon, supraspinatus and subdeltoid bursa

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the bones and joints of the shoulder
lectures.framing: Two questions sort most of this lecture: is it the acromioclavicular (AC) joint or the glenohumeral joint, and is passive range of motion lost as well as active? Separation, arthritis, instability and frozen shoulder each answer them differently. Rotator cuff disease is on the ROTATOR CUFF DISEASE chart, biceps tendinopathy in 03.2 - Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Arm, and the ligaments behind each problem on the anatomy chart in 05.1 - Anatomy of the Proximal Upper Extremity.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Passive range of motion splits deep shoulder pain: lost in noninflammatory arthritis (cuff strong, asymmetric joint space) and frozen shoulder (X-ray normal), kept in inflammatory arthritis (cuff weak, symmetric joint space, erosions). AC separation: types I-III nonoperative, IV-V surgery. Traumatic instability is unidirectional and "torn loose" (reduce, then labral repair if young or recurrent); atraumatic is multidirectional and "born loose" (rehab first). Frozen shoulder: 20% of diabetics, global loss of active and passive motion, normal X-ray.

blocks.html: 1. AC joint problems

• Common, and easy to sort out: acute injury = AC instability ("separation") · gradual onset = AC osteoarthritis (wear and tear)
  • AC joint separation
    • a fall or blow onto the tip of the shoulder (the lecture's cyclist going over the handlebars)
    • graded I to V by increasing displacement
    • treatment: types I-III: education, sling, analgesics, local therapy (ice) and early exercises · types IV-V: surgery
  • AC joint osteoarthritis
    • treatment: education · activity modification · local treatment (ice, injections) · analgesics · surgery
2. Glenohumeral arthritis
• Progressive pain, reduced motion and loss of function · two clinical patterns, told apart by passive range and cuff strength

rows: Active reduced · passive often greater than active
Asymmetric joint space · osteophytes · cysts · subchondral sclerosis

blocks.html:
• Treatment: nonoperative first (education · activity modification · medications · physiotherapy exercise program) · then operative (debridement or replacement)
    • debridement: reserved for young patients · not curative, relieves "catching"
    • replacement: anatomic or reverse · 85% good or excellent · 90% survive 10 years · joint replacement is effective · complications: infection, loosening, instability, fracture, progressive rotator cuff disease

blocks.cap: X-rays of a normal shoulder, an anatomic (standard) replacement and a reverse replacement

blocks.html: 3. Instability

• Shoulder instability = the inability to keep the humeral head centred in the glenoid · a continuum: reduced → subluxated → dislocated
  • Anatomic factors: ligaments and labrum matter most · then bones (a shallow glenoid: the golf ball on a tee) · rotator cuff and muscle forces · nerves
    • ligaments can be torn or stretched · the labrum adds surface area and depth and acts as a bumper
    • ligament laxity gives multidirectional instability (? connective tissue disorder, ? poor motor control)
  • Name it by onset (traumatic or atraumatic), direction (anterior, posterior, inferior, combined) and degree (subluxation or dislocation)

rows: Reduce: safety first (monitors) · analgesia · manipulate to correct the deformity · re-examine neurovascular status · post-reduction X-ray · surgery often: young or recurrent dislocators → labral (capsule-labral) repair, 85% success
Rehab (physiotherapy, muscle control) first · surgery uncommon: inferior capsular shift (open or arthroscopic), 70% success

blocks.alt: glenohumeral joint reduced subluxated dislocated - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Degree of instability: reduced (head centred on the glenoid), subluxated (partly off), dislocated (fully off)

blocks.html: 4. Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)

• Shoulder stiffness has three kinds of cause: intra-articular (arthritis, post-traumatic joint deformity) · extra-articular (capsular, muscular, heterotopic bone) · combined
  • Adhesive capsulitis = spontaneous, global restriction of active AND passive motion with no known intrinsic shoulder disorder
    • 2% of adults · 20% of people with diabetes · onset in the 40s-50s · pathophysiology unknown
    • associations: diabetes · most often idiopathic · cervical disc, thyroid and cardiac disease
  • Stages: freezing (inflammatory) → frozen → thawing
  • Diagnosis: arthritis and post-traumatic deformity are the differential, but the X-rays are normal and there was no trauma
  • Treatment
    • education · pain management · usually self-limited
    • physiotherapy is controversial: no quality studies show a significant effect
    • intra-articular steroid: better than physiotherapy, no difference at 1 year · hydrodistension (hydroplasty, "brisement" from the French briser, to break: liquid injected under pressure)
    • surgery (manipulation or arthroscopic capsulectomy): faster return of motion, same as everything else at 2 years

weeks.label: Week 8 - Brachial Plexus, Rotator Cuff & the Distal Upper Limb

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Brachial Plexus
lectures.title: Anatomy of the brachial plexus
lectures.framing: Five roots (C5-T1) regroup into five terminal nerves. The question the lecture turns on: from the muscles and skin that are lost, which part of the plexus is injured? Learn which roots feed each branch, and where along the plexus each branch leaves.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Superior trunk = C5 + C6, middle = C7, inferior = C8 + T1 - and the posterior cord takes all three posterior divisions, so the radial nerve, like the median, carries every root (C5-T1). The roots are ventral rami. Divisions give off no branches. Long thoracic nerve → serratus anterior → winged scapula. Axillary nerve (C5, C6): deltoid + teres minor. Ulnar nerve = C8, T1, from the medial cord. The median and ulnar nerves pass through the arm but supply nothing there.

blocks.html: 1. The five segments

• The brachial plexus = the ventral rami of C5-T1 (the cervical enlargement of the spinal cord) · starts in the neck, ends in the axilla as the terminal branches · brachial = arm, plexus = braid
  • In order: roots → trunks → divisions → cords → branches ("Really Thirsty? Drink Cold Beer")
  • The plexus "roots" are ventral rami, not the dorsal and ventral roots of a spinal nerve · each is already a mixed nerve (motor + sensory)
  • Drawing it: "3 Wise (Y) Men (M) go bowling. One got a strike (X); the other got a spare (\\)" - three Y's at the roots, the M of the terminal branches, the X where the superior and middle trunks' divisions cross, the \ where the inferior trunk's posterior division joins the posterior cord

blocks.cap: The whole plexus: roots C5-T1, superior, middle and inferior trunks, anterior and posterior divisions, lateral, posterior and medial cords, and the five terminal branches with their roots

blocks.html: 2. Trunks, divisions and cords

• Trunks: superior = C5 + C6 · middle = C7 alone · inferior = C8 + T1 · only the superior trunk gives off a nerve (suprascapular); the middle and inferior trunks give off none
  • Divisions: each trunk splits into an anterior (A) and a posterior (P) division (6 in all)
    • no nerves branch off the divisions
    • anterior divisions → nerves to the flexor (front) compartments · posterior divisions → nerves to the extensor (back) compartments
  • Cords, named by where they sit around the axillary artery

rows: Anterior divisions of the superior + middle trunks
Anterior division of the inferior trunk, carrying on alone

blocks.html: 3. Branches before the terminal five

rows: Pierces the middle scalene, then runs back to the rhomboids
Runs above and medial to pectoralis minor
Pierces pectoralis minor on its way to pectoralis major
Medial cutaneous nerve of the arm
Skin of the medial arm and axilla · upper forearm
Medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm
Skin of the medial and anterior forearm
Also called the middle subscapular nerve

blocks.html: • The nerve to the subclavius also comes off at trunk level (not examinable)
4. The five terminal branches

• The lateral and medial cords make an "M": musculocutaneous (lateral) · median (one root from each cord) · ulnar (medial) · the posterior cord ends as the axillary and the radial nerves
  • Root count: "3 Musketeers Assassinate: 5 Mice, 5 Rats and 2 Unicorns" - musculocutaneous 3 · median 5 · radial 5 · ulnar 2 · axillary C5, C6

rows: All of the anterior arm: pierces coracobrachialis, then runs between biceps and brachialis
Lateral forearm (ends as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm)
Most forearm flexors + five hand muscles · nothing in the arm
Extensors of the back of the arm and forearm

blocks.html:
• The lateral cord sends a lateral root and the medial cord a medial root; the two join to form the median nerve
  • Each nerve's course through the arm (median crossing the brachial artery, ulnar piercing the medial septum, radial in the radial groove) and the skin it supplies are on the neurovascular chart
  • Which fracture threatens which nerve (surgical neck → axillary, shaft → radial) is on the chart in 05.1 - Anatomy of the Proximal Upper Extremity

blocks.alt: terminal branches of the brachial plexus.png
blocks.cap: The "M" of terminal branches: musculocutaneous (C5-7), median (C5-T1) and ulnar (C8, T1) in front; axillary (C5, 6) and radial (C5-T1) from the posterior cord

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Muscles of the Shoulder
lectures.title: Anatomy of the muscles of the shoulder
lectures.framing: Three groups of muscles move the shoulder: the pectoral muscles in front, the deltoid and teres major, and the four rotator cuff muscles that hold the humeral head in its socket. For each one, know where it attaches, which nerve supplies it and what it does. The superficial back muscles this lecture reviews (trapezius, latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, levator scapulae) are on the chart in 02.1 - Anatomy of the Back & Neck; the axillary artery is in 04 - Neurovascular Supply of the Proximal Upper Extremity.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Supraspinatus starts abduction (the first 15°) and the deltoid's middle head carries it on. Infraspinatus and teres minor rotate laterally; subscapularis alone rotates medially and alone inserts on the lesser tubercle. Long thoracic nerve → serratus anterior → winged scapula. Axillary nerve = deltoid + teres minor. Teres major adducts and is not in the cuff. Pectoralis minor pulls the scapula down and forward; serratus anterior protracts it.

blocks.html: 1. Pectoral region

rows: Medial clavicle · sternum · upper 6 ribs and their costal cartilages
Lateral lip of the intertubercular groove
Adducts, flexes and medially rotates the humerus
Stabilises the scapula by drawing it inferiorly and anteriorly against the chest wall

blocks.html: • Long thoracic nerve lesion → winged scapula: serratus anterior can no longer hold the medial border of the scapula against the chest wall when the patient pushes with the arm
2. Deltoid and teres major

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Shoulder
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the muscles of the shoulder
lectures.framing: Rotator cuff disease is the most common shoulder disorder: stage it by how far the tendon has gone, and treat it nonoperatively unless pain persists, the shoulder is weak, or it followed an acute injury. The other painful shoulders (AC joint separation and arthritis, glenohumeral arthritis, instability, frozen shoulder) are on the SHOULDER BONES AND JOINTS chart in 05.2 - Clinical Approach to Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity; the cuff muscles themselves are in 02.1 - Anatomy of the Muscles of the Shoulder; biceps tendinopathy is in 03.2 - Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Arm.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Rotator cuff disease: active motion is less than passive, unlike frozen shoulder and noninflammatory arthritis where passive motion is lost too. Usually intrinsic (vascularity, tension overload, degeneration); acromion shape is the extrinsic factor. Stage I inflamed → physiotherapy or subacromial decompression · II partial → consider repair · III full → repair · arthropathy (head rides up to the acromion) → reverse replacement. Surgery only for persistent pain, weakness or an acute tear.

blocks.html: 1. Rotator cuff disease

• Rotator cuff disease: the most common shoulder disorder · prevalence rises with age · onset in the 40s · progressive
  • The cuff's two jobs: shoulder stabilisation and arm motion · four muscles: supraspinatus · infraspinatus · teres minor · subscapularis
2. Why the tendon fails

• Intrinsic (the usual cause): vascularity · tension overload · tendon degeneration
  • Extrinsic: acromion morphology - the subacromial space volume
  • or a combination
3. Presentation and examination

• Symptoms: restricted motion · pain · weakness
  • Move: active motion << passive motion (in frozen shoulder and noninflammatory arthritis passive motion is lost too)
  • Impingement signs: Neer · Hawkins · painful arc
  • Strength tests: supraspinatus · infraspinatus · subscapularis
4. Stages and treatment

rows: Massive defect · humerus migrates superiorly and abuts the acromion · arthritis results

blocks.html:
• Treatment, first for every stage: education · activity modification · pain management (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) · physiotherapy (muscle reconditioning) · injections - nonsurgical in the majority
  • Surgery when: pain persists · weakness · following an acute injury - "the best surgeons know when NOT to operate"

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Muscles of the Arm
lectures.title: Anatomy of the muscles of the arm
lectures.framing: The arm (shoulder to elbow) is two compartments, each with one job and one nerve: the front flexes the shoulder and elbow and supinates; the back extends them. The detail worth knowing is which joints each muscle crosses, because that decides what it can move.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The biceps is a strong supinator; brachialis, not biceps, is the primary flexor of the forearm. Musculocutaneous = everything in front; radial = triceps behind. Biceps long head starts on the supraglenoid tubercle, triceps long head on the infraglenoid tubercle - both cross the shoulder. Coracobrachialis crosses only the shoulder; brachialis only the elbow. The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis.

blocks.html: 1. Two compartments
• Deep to the skin, the brachial fascia wraps the arm · the medial and lateral intermuscular septa run from it to the humerus and split the arm into front and back

rows: Flex the shoulder · flex the elbow · supinate the forearm

blocks.cap: Cross-section of the arm: biceps and brachialis in front (musculocutaneous nerve), the three heads of triceps behind (radial nerve), split by the medial and lateral intermuscular septa

blocks.html: 2. Anterior compartment

rows: Long head: supraglenoid tubercle, then through the intertubercular groove · short head: coracoid process
Strong supinator · flexes the elbow · weak shoulder flexor · resists shoulder dislocation
Middle ⅓ of the medial humerus

Primary flexor of the forearm (more than the biceps)

• Biceps is the most superficial · coracobrachialis and brachialis lie deep to it
  • The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis, then runs between biceps and brachialis
3. Posterior compartment

rows: Proximal ⅓ of the posterior humerus
Distal ⅓ of the posterior humerus
