• All three heads insert on the olecranon of the ulna
  • Actions: primary elbow extensor · the long head also extends the shoulder and resists shoulder dislocation
  • Nerve: radial, which runs in the radial groove (its course is on the NEUROVASCULAR chart)

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Arm
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the muscles of the arm
lectures.framing: Anterior shoulder pain: is it the long head of the biceps tendon, or something next to it? The tendon shares its space with the rotator cuff and its origin with the labrum, so the anatomy explains why it gets into trouble and the examination does most of the diagnosing. (The other shoulder conditions in the objectives are on the shoulder chart.)
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Tenderness in the intertubercular groove, with pain on shoulder and elbow flexion with the forearm supinated, points to the long head of biceps; weakness plus a visible retracted-muscle defect means it has torn. The exam is the most useful test - ultrasound if unclear, MR arthrogram if you suspect a SLAP lesion. The tendon is hypovascular, and most cases settle with active physiotherapy.

blocks.html: 1. Proximal biceps tendinopathy

• Proximal biceps tendinopathy = a common cause of shoulder pain
  • "Tendinopathy", not "tendinitis": a spectrum from overuse and degeneration (tendinosis) to acute inflammation to a partial or complete tear
  • Who (it can affect anyone)
    • younger: athletes, especially overhead throwing · inflammatory conditions
    • older: overuse and degeneration (very common)
2. Why the long head is vulnerable: location, location, location

• Lives right next to the rotator cuff tendons → shares their trouble
  • Weaves through the tight intertubercular groove → susceptible to impingement
  • Starts on the supraglenoid tubercle AND the superior glenoid labrum → labral problems = biceps problems
  • The proximal tendon is relatively hypovascular → heals poorly

blocks.cap: The long head of biceps tendon runs over the humeral head beside the rotator cuff tendon and attaches at the top of the glenoid

blocks.html: 3. History and exam

• History: acute (tear or inflammation) or chronic (degenerative, overuse) onset · anterior shoulder pain
  • Physical exam
    • tender over the tendon in the intertubercular groove
    • pain worse with shoulder flexion and elbow flexion, particularly with the forearm supinated
    • a frank tear → weakness and a visible defect as the muscle retracts (the "Popeye" deformity)
4. Differential and investigations

• Clinical examination is often the most helpful
  • Differential diagnosis
    • neighbouring tendon or bursa: rotator cuff tendinopathy · subacromial bursitis
    • joint: labral tear (SLAP lesion) · shoulder or acromioclavicular (AC) joint arthritis
    • referred: cervical radiculopathy · facet joint (facetogenic) pain · a visceral cause presenting as shoulder pain
    • a C8 radiculopathy gives pain or tingling in the hand, so it sits low on the list (C4 or C5 can give shoulder pain)
  • Investigations
    • ultrasound if unclear: assesses the rotator cuff tendons and the subacromial bursa at the same time
    • MR arthrogram if you suspect a SLAP lesion
5. Management

• Education: prognosis depends on the injury · the vast majority are chronic and improve with conservative management
  • Non-drug: physiotherapy is the mainstay - modalities may help acute pain, but active therapy is necessary · relative rest from overhead activity
  • Drugs: analgesia as needed
  • Intervention: surgery can be considered for refractory cases

lectures.name: Neurovascular Supply of the Proximal Upper Extremity
lectures.title: Neurovascular supply of the proximal upper extremity
lectures.framing: Follow the main artery from the neck to the elbow, then the nerves that run beside it. The clinical payoff is which nerve or vessel sits where a fracture can reach it and which nerve supplies which patch of skin.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The radial nerve and profunda brachii lie together in the radial groove, so a mid-shaft humerus fracture threatens both; the brachial artery hugs the medial shaft and is at risk too. Median and ulnar nerves supply nothing in the arm. Axillary → brachial at the lower border of teres major; brachial → radial + ulnar in the cubital fossa. Median cubital vein = blood draws. Biceps reflex = C5, C6.

blocks.html: 1. Arteries

• Subclavian artery: from the brachiocephalic trunk on the right, straight off the aortic arch on the left · two branches join the anastomosis around the scapula
    • dorsal scapular → upper superficial back muscles
    • suprascapular (often off the thyrocervical trunk) → back of the shoulder · runs with the suprascapular nerve, above the superior transverse scapular ligament
  • Axillary artery: from the lateral border of the 1st rib to the lower border of teres major · 3 parts, set by pectoralis minor in front of it
    • the brachial plexus cords are named for where they sit around it (see the brachial plexus chart)

rows: Rib 1 to the top edge of pectoralis minor
Superior thoracic → upper chest wall (for interest only)
Thoracoacromial → acromial, clavicular, deltoid, pectoral branches · lateral thoracic → lateral chest wall, pectoral region, breast; runs with the long thoracic nerve (for interest only)
Lower edge of pectoralis minor to the lower edge of teres major

Subscapular → thoracodorsal (superficial back) + circumflex scapular (round the scapula's lateral border) · anterior and posterior circumflex humeral → round the surgical neck; the posterior one runs with the axillary nerve

blocks.html:
• Brachial artery: runs medial to biceps, in front of coracobrachialis and brachialis · ends in the cubital fossa as the radial (lateral) and ulnar (medial) arteries
    • Profunda brachii (deep brachial) → the posterior compartment, in the radial groove · becomes the radial collateral artery at the elbow
    • superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries → the network around the elbow
    • used to measure blood pressure (cuff round the arm, stethoscope over the artery in the cubital fossa)
    • lies against the medial humeral shaft → injured by mid-shaft or supracondylar fractures
2. Veins

• Deep veins: paired, travel with the major arteries
  • Superficial veins
    • cephalic vein: up the anterolateral forearm and arm, through the deltopectoral triangle → the end of the axillary vein
    • basilic vein: up the medial forearm and lower arm → joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein
    • median cubital vein: crosses the cubital fossa between them → the usual vein for blood draws and IV access
3. Nerves of the arm

rows: Lateral cord · pierces coracobrachialis, then between biceps and brachialis · ends as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm
Medial + lateral cords · lateral to the brachial artery, crossing to its medial side mid-arm · deep to the bicipital aponeurosis in the cubital fossa
Medial cord · medial in the anterior compartment, then pierces the medial intermuscular septum mid-arm into the posterior compartment
Posterior cord · in the radial (spiral) groove with the profunda brachii · pierces the lateral septum, then between brachialis and brachioradialis
Triceps (posterior compartment) · skin of the back of the arm and forearm

blocks.html:
• Radial nerve + profunda brachii share the radial groove → both at risk in a mid-shaft humerus fracture
  • The ulnar nerve can be hard to pick out: the medial cutaneous nerves of the arm and forearm (both medial cord) run beside it
  • The biceps (bicipital myotatic) reflex tests C5 and C6
4. Skin of the arm and forearm

rows: Medial cutaneous nerve of the arm
Posterior cutaneous nerves of the arm and forearm
Medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm
Lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm

blocks.html: • Dermatome test points: C5 lateral upper arm · C6 thumb · C7 middle finger · C8 little finger · T1 medial arm above the elbow

lectures.name: Osteology of the Distal Upper Extremity
lectures.title: Osteology of the distal upper extremity
lectures.framing: From the elbow to the fingertips: which bump fits into which socket, and what each joint lets you do. The landmarks matter because they are what you name on a plain X-ray and where the tendons and nerves attach. (What goes wrong at the elbow is on the elbow chart.)
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Scaphoid = the most fractured carpal bone; lunate = the most dislocated, and it can press on the median nerve in the carpal tunnel. Capitulum ↔ radial head, trochlea ↔ trochlear notch. Carrying angle over 15° = valgus, under 5° = varus. Proximal and distal radioulnar joints are pivots; the middle one is a syndesmosis. The ulnar collateral ligament's anterior band is the strongest. Distal humerus fracture → median nerve; medial epicondyle fracture → ulnar nerve.

blocks.html: 1. Bones of the elbow and forearm

rows: Radial nerve + profunda brachii artery run along it
Common flexor origin · ulnar nerve runs behind it
Meets the trochlear notch of the ulna
Take the coronoid process in full flexion · the olecranon in full extension
Meets the capitulum and the radial notch of the ulna · pivots inside the anular ligament
Hold the trochlea · the radial head

blocks.html: • Fractures and the nerve at risk: surgical neck (low-energy fall onto the hand, elderly with osteoporosis) → axillary nerve · transverse shaft (direct blow) → radial nerve ± deep brachial artery · distal humerus → median nerve · medial epicondyle → ulnar nerve

blocks.cap: Elbow from the front and back: capitulum meets the radial head, trochlea sits in the trochlear notch, with the epicondyles, coronoid and olecranon fossae

blocks.html: 2. Elbow joint

• Elbow = a synovial hinge (uniaxial: flexion and extension only) with two articulations
    • humeroulnar (trochlea + trochlear notch) · humeroradial (capitulum + radial head)
  • Capsule weak in front and behind, reinforced at the sides by the collateral ligaments · muscles strengthen it front and back
    • radial collateral ligament: lateral epicondyle → head of the radius, where it blends into the anular ligament
    • ulnar collateral ligament: medial epicondyle → coronoid process and olecranon · 3 bands: anterior (cord-like, strongest) · posterior (fan-like, weakest) · oblique (deepens the socket for the trochlea)
  • Bursae ease movement: the subcutaneous olecranon bursa (between the skin and the olecranon, lets the skin glide) · the biceps bursa
  • Blood supply: superior and inferior ulnar collateral · anterior and posterior ulnar recurrent · radial collateral branch of the deep artery of the arm · recurrent radial
  • Posterior dislocation = the most common elbow dislocation · torn capsule, ruptured collateral ligaments, bone damage · ulnar nerve at risk behind the medial epicondyle
  • Carrying angle (look for symmetry): over 15° = cubitus valgus · under 5° = cubitus varus

blocks.cap: Medial elbow: the ulnar collateral ligament with its anterior, posterior and oblique bands, and the anular ligament round the radial head

blocks.html: 3. Radioulnar joints (pronation and supination)

rows: Synovial pivot · inside the elbow capsule, sharing its synovial membrane
Radial head + radial notch of the ulna
Anular ligament, which lets the head rotate

blocks.html:
• Proximal joint: the radial head rotates inside the anular ligament → supination and pronation
  • Nursemaid's elbow = subluxation of the proximal radioulnar joint · preschool child, after a pull on the hand or forearm · painful because the well-innervated anular ligament or capsule is pinched
4. Wrist and hand

• Carpals, lateral → medial, proximal row first: "Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle"
    • proximal row: scaphoid · lunate · triquetrum · pisiform
    • distal row: trapezium · trapezoid · capitate · hamate (with a hook)
  • Scaphoid = the most commonly fractured carpal bone
  • Lunate = the most commonly dislocated (still uncommon) · can compress the median nerve in the carpal tunnel
  • Pisiform + hook of the hamate form the ulnar canal
  • Metacarpals: 5, each with a base, shaft and head · phalanges: thumb 2 (no middle phalanx), other digits 3 (proximal largest, distal smallest) · the thumb has 2 sesamoid bones
  • Joints: carpometacarpal (CMC) · metacarpophalangeal (MCP) · interphalangeal (IP)
  • Digits: 1-5 from thumb to small finger · clinically thumb, index, long, ring, small

blocks.cap: Carpal bones from the front: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform in the proximal row; trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate with its hook in the distal row

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to the Elbow
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the elbow
lectures.framing: Elbow pain is sorted two ways: by where it hurts (front, inside, outside, back) and by which structure is at fault (bone, ligament or joint · muscle or tendon · something else). Overlay the anatomy, look for the pattern, rule out the red flags, and remember a fracture can sit anywhere. (The bones and ligaments themselves are on the osteology chart.)
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A young child who will not use an arm after it was pulled has a radial head subluxation: reduce it by pronation and extension, no cast, and image only to rule out a fracture. An elbow dislocation after a FOOSH is a red flag: check the ulnar nerve and watch for compartment syndrome. A red olecranon swelling with systemic signs is infected: aspirate and give antibiotics. Medial pain with no end point on valgus stress in a pitcher = ulnar collateral ligament.

blocks.html: 1. The approach

• History: look for patterns · OLDCARS · acute (traumatic, inflammatory) vs chronic (degenerative, overuse) · overlay the anatomy: which structures are medial, which lateral
  • Physical exam: look (swollen? deformed?) · feel (where is it tender? hot?) · move (is range of motion restricted?) · specific tests for specific structures · don't forget the nerves
  • Management approach: which investigations (if any) will help · no red flags → apply your pattern · then educate → non-drug → drug → interventional · your patient is a person
2. The differential

rows: Ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) sprain or tear

blocks.html: • Fracture can be anywhere · joint and ligament problems cost range of motion, stability and pain
3. Arthritis of the elbow

• Types: degenerative (osteoarthritis) · inflammatory (rheumatoid arthritis, gout, psoriatic arthritis; more in the rheumatology lectures) · post-traumatic (earlier osteoarthritis, possibly in a different pattern)
  • Osteoarthritis presents as: a degenerative history, gradual onset · achy, sore pain with flares · mechanical symptoms: stiffness, loss of range of motion, locking · bony changes
  • X-ray: loss of joint space · osteophytes · subchondral sclerosis or cysts
  • Treatment
    • education: a grumbling, long-term course with no cure
    • non-drug: ice · physiotherapy to keep range of motion · occupational therapy to keep function
    • drugs: topical anti-inflammatories · oral acetaminophen or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs; mind the side effects) · steroid injection
    • surgery only for an intolerable end stage: debridement or arthroplasty (joint replacement)

blocks.cap: Lateral X-ray of an osteoarthritic elbow: narrowed joint space with bony spurs

blocks.html: 4. Dislocations: two joints, two different patients

rows: Proximal radioulnar: the anular ligament is thinner and weaker distally in children, letting the radial head slip
Fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH) · posterior is the most common
Child, rare after age 5 · girls and the left arm more often · a pull (longitudinal traction) along the arm
Capsule and ligament rupture · skin breaks · nerve injury, especially the ulnar nerve · compartment syndrome
Acute pain · refuses to use the arm, holds it flexed against the body
Imaging only to rule out something else (a fracture)
Closed reduction + splint at 90° · may fail if soft tissue is interposed or it will not stay reduced → open reduction internal fixation (ORIF)
Closed reduction by pronation and extension · no cast or orthosis

blocks.cap: Elbow dislocations by direction: posterior (the most common), anterior, lateral, medial and divergent

blocks.html: 5. Ulnar collateral ligament injury

• The UCL stabilises the medial elbow · injured by chronic, repetitive overuse (baseball pitchers)
  • Presents as: a pop over the medial elbow if it tears suddenly · pain on palpation of the medial elbow · no end point on valgus stress, excessive motion
  • Investigations: probably needs an exam by sports medicine or orthopaedics · MRI may help
  • Treatment
    • education: ligaments heal slowly, if at all, depending on the tear
    • non-drug: ice · physiotherapy to strengthen the dynamic elbow stabilisers, proprioceptive work · an orthosis for extra stability
    • drugs: topical anti-inflammatories · oral acetaminophen or NSAIDs
    • reconstruction (Tommy John surgery) only if needed for functional goals: a tendon graft (palmaris longus, semitendinosus, others), then years of physiotherapy
6. Olecranon bursitis

• A bursa (over 150 in the body) is a thin, fluid-filled sac between bone and soft tissue that lets tissue glide; irritated, it fills with fluid → pain, tenderness, swelling when superficial
  • The most common superficial bursitis
  • Causes: a single hard blow (fall on the elbow) · sustained or repeated pressure (leaning on the elbow; develops over months) · infection through a skin break, seen or not
  • Tell them apart: the history helps, and they look different
    • "not scary": often no investigations · X-ray if there was trauma · ultrasound or MRI if it does not behave normally
    • "bad" = infected: erythema and systemic signs → aspirate and choose antibiotics (± incision and drainage)
    • gout or an inflammatory arthropathy can swell the whole elbow and be mistaken for bursitis → treat the cause
  • Treatment (red flags ruled out): benign and often self-limiting once the cause is removed · ice, rest, compression, elevation · modify the activity, pad the elbow · topical anti-inflammatories, NSAIDs · bursectomy if infected or chronic

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity
lectures.title: Anatomy of the muscles of the distal upper extremity
lectures.framing: The forearm is two compartments with two nerves and two epicondyles: the front flexes and pronates, runs on the median nerve and starts at the medial epicondyle; the back extends and supinates, runs on the radial nerve and starts at the lateral epicondyle. The exceptions are what gets examined.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Flexor carpi ulnaris and the half of flexor digitorum profundus to the ring and little fingers are the 1½ anterior forearm muscles on the ulnar nerve; every other anterior muscle is median, and every posterior muscle is radial. Flexor digitorum profundus is the only muscle that bends the fingertip. Brachioradialis sits in the back but flexes the elbow. Side-to-side wrist movement pairs a flexor with an extensor. Mallet finger = splint; a complete avulsion fracture = surgery.

• Radius laterally, ulna medially, joined by the interosseous membrane · the anterior intermuscular septum runs from the radius to the antebrachial fascia (the forearm's deep fascia)
    • bones + membrane + septum split the forearm into two compartments

• The three thumb muscles are the "outcropping" muscles: they surface between the extensors on their way to the thumb
  • Anconeus sits in the slide table above the two layers: lateral epicondyle to the olecranon · weak elbow extension, steadies the elbow
  • Extensor expansion: a flat, triangular hood of tendon over the back of each finger; extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, extensor indicis, the lumbricals and the interossei all insert into it
  • Under the extensor retinaculum the tendons run in 6 bony-fibrous tunnels, each in a synovial sheath that cuts friction
4. Moving the wrist takes both compartments

rows: Flexor carpi radialis + extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis
Flexor carpi ulnaris + extensor carpi ulnaris

blocks.html: 5. Clinical notes on the anatomy slides

• Anatomical snuffbox: the hollow at the base of the thumb when it is fully extended
    • borders: abductor pollicis longus + extensor pollicis brevis in front, extensor pollicis longus behind
    • floor: scaphoid and trapezium · the radial artery lies in the floor, where its pulse can be felt
  • Ganglion (synovial) cyst: clear, mucinous fluid, usually on the back of the wrist, connected to the extensor tendons' synovial sheaths
    • treatment: nothing, or drainage or excision · the old "Bible bump"
  • Mallet finger: a jammed finger bends the tip suddenly and the extensor tendon partly tears off the base of the distal phalanx
    • cannot straighten the fingertip (DIP) joint
    • rest, ice, compression, elevation (RICE) and splinting · a complete avulsion fracture needs surgery to pin the bone back
  • Golfer's elbow (common flexor origin) and tennis elbow (common extensor origin) are on the Clinical Approach chart, 06.2 - Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the muscles of the distal upper extremity
lectures.framing: Tendon problems around the elbow are sorted by where the pain sits and whether the tendon has ruptured. Most are a slow, degenerative tendinosis rather than an inflamed tendinitis, which is why the treatment is education, activity change and eccentric physiotherapy rather than anti-inflammatories alone.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Most elbow tendon pain is tendinosis: collagen degeneration without inflammation, treated with education, activity change and eccentric physiotherapy twice daily for 12 weeks rather than anti-inflammatories alone. Tennis elbow = extensor carpi radialis brevis, pain just distal to the lateral epicondyle, worse gripping and supinating. Golfer's elbow = common flexor origin, pain on resisted wrist flexion and pronation. A distal biceps rupture (pop, bruise, changed contour, poor supination) needs orthopaedics urgently; a proximal one usually does not.

blocks.html: 1. Approach to a muscle or tendon problem

• History: look for patterns · onset, location, duration, character, aggravating and relieving factors (OLDCARS) · acute (traumatic, inflammatory) vs chronic (degenerative, overuse) · overlay the anatomy (which structures are medial, which lateral)
  • Physical: look (swollen? deformed?) · feel (where is it tender? hot?) · move (is range of motion restricted?) · specific tests for specific structures · don't forget the nerves
  • Management: which investigations (if any) will help? · if no red flags, apply your pattern · educate · non-pharmacologic · pharmacologic · interventional · remember the patient is a person
  • Muscle and tendon problems affect elbow pain and elbow strength; the full elbow differential by structure and location is on 05.2 - Clinical Approach to the Elbow
2. Tendinitis vs tendinosis

rows: Degeneration of collagen, not the inflammatory cascade · immature, disorganised collagen and abnormal vessels under the microscope
Rheumatologic conditions · acute injury (tendon overloaded too much or too suddenly) · infection
Chronic overuse with too little recovery time
Reduce inflammation: rest, ice, compression, elevation (RICE) for acute injury · anti-inflammatories · treat the underlying condition
No inflammation to reduce: therapies that rebuild collagen · analgesics (may still include anti-inflammatories)
Faster, if the underlying problem is treated
Slow: "100+ days" to make new collagen

blocks.html: 3. Lateral epicondylosis (tennis elbow)

• What it is: a tendinopathy of extensor carpi radialis brevis mostly (or another muscle of the common extensor origin)
  • Who: common, 1-3% of people a year · 30s and 40s · occupational more than recreational
  • Presents as: pain just distal to the lateral epicondyle · classic "pain and weakness", especially gripping and supination
  • Exam
    • pain on palpation over the common extensor tendon
    • pain on resisted extension of the middle finger, ± wrist extension, ± supination
    • pain on passive stretch of the common extensor origin
  • Memory hook: TENnis = exTENsor · "tennis" has no L, so add one: Lateral
4. Medial epicondylosis (golfer's elbow)

• What it is: a tendinopathy at the common flexor origin
  • Presents as: pain at the common flexor origin
  • Exam: pain on resisted wrist flexion and pronation · pain on passive stretch
  • Memory hook: goLFEr = FLExor · "golf" already has its L, so Medial

blocks.alt: medial epicondylosis common flexor origin - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The common flexor origin at the medial epicondyle

blocks.html: 5. Biceps tendinopathy and rupture

rows: Insidious onset · pain on resistance · pain on stretch · the usual treatments
Trauma, or the end of long overuse · a "pop" heard or felt · pain (or none) · bruise · weakness · change in muscle contour
Not uncommon (especially in the elderly) · often degenerative · usually still functional: typically non-operative
Rare but consequential: poor supination, weak flexion · call orthopaedics urgently: a limited time window for repair

blocks.html: 6. Managing any tendinopathy

• Education: tell them what it is and what to expect · many improve quickly, some become quite chronic · address the offending movements and activities
  • Non-pharmacologic
    • modalities (ice), RICE
    • modify the offending activity: rest by time or by task · adjust ergonomics and biomechanics (positioning, less excess force)
    • orthoses and taping to support and realign forces · tennis elbow counterforce strap during the offending activity
    • physiotherapy: eccentric strengthening twice daily for 12 weeks (stimulates collagen production and strength)
    • massage, which may stimulate fibroblasts to make collagen
  • Pharmacologic: anti-inflammatories can be considered, but may not help much in chronic tendinOSIS (topical preferred)
  • Intervention or surgery: regenerative options such as platelet-rich plasma (PRP) are uncertain · surgical referral if refractory
  • Practice pointer: rather than "have you tried physio?", ask "show me what you've been doing in physio"

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html: • All three review points for this lecture are carried above (bolded): lateral epicondylitis (extensor carpi radialis brevis; 30s-40s, occupational; pain distal to the lateral epicondyle with gripping, supination, resisted extension and passive stretch), medial epicondylitis (common flexor origin; resisted flexion + pronation, passive stretch) and distal biceps rupture (rare, urgent orthopaedic referral, poor supination, weak flexion).

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity
lectures.title: Anatomy of the neurovascular supply of the distal upper extremity
lectures.framing: Know which nerve supplies which forearm muscle, where each nerve and artery runs and can be hurt, and which spinal root a movement or patch of skin tests. The cubital fossa is where most of it meets.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The median nerve and its anterior interosseous branch supply the whole anterior forearm except flexor carpi ulnaris and the ring-and-little-finger half of flexor digitorum profundus (ulnar); the radial nerve and its deep and posterior interosseous branches supply the whole posterior forearm. Cubital fossa, lateral to medial = biceps Tendon, brachial Artery, median Nerve. The ulnar nerve is exposed behind the medial epicondyle; the median nerve is pinched between the heads of pronator teres and in the carpal tunnel; the radial deep branch pierces supinator. Radial pulse = between flexor carpi radialis and abductor pollicis longus. C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger; C8 bends the fingers, T1 spreads and closes them.

blocks.html: 1. Arteries of the forearm
• The brachial artery divides into the radial artery (lateral) and the ulnar artery (medial)

rows: Lateral forearm, deep to brachioradialis · at the wrist it wraps laterally round onto the back, through the floor of the anatomical snuffbox
Recurrent radial → joins the radial collateral artery
Radial pulse: between the flexor carpi radialis and abductor pollicis longus tendons, and in the snuffbox
Medial forearm, deep to pronator teres · enters the wrist beside the pisiform

Anterior ulnar recurrent → inferior ulnar collateral · posterior ulnar recurrent → superior ulnar collateral · common interosseous → anterior interosseous (with the anterior interosseous nerve, on the front of the membrane) + posterior interosseous (into the posterior compartment, above the membrane)

blocks.html: • Collateral circulation round the elbow: the recurrent and collateral arteries join up, so if the brachial artery is blocked or clamped below the deep artery of the arm (profunda brachii), the distal limb still gets enough blood

blocks.alt: arteries and veins of the upper extremity.png
blocks.cap: Arteries and veins of the upper limb

blocks.html: 2. Veins of the forearm

• Superficial veins start in the dorsal venous network on the back of the hand
    • Cephalic laterally · basilic medially · the median cubital vein joins them across the front of the elbow
  • Deep veins are paired and run with the major arteries · perforating veins connect the superficial veins to the deep ones
3. Cubital fossa

• A shallow triangle on the front of the elbow: brachioradialis · pronator teres · a line through the medial and lateral epicondyles
  • Contents: biceps Tendon (most lateral, easy to feel) · brachial Artery (and veins) · median Nerve ("TAN", lateral to medial) · the radial nerve with its deep and superficial branches
  • Superficial: median cubital, cephalic and basilic veins · medial and lateral cutaneous nerves of the forearm
  • Clinically: the median cubital vein is where blood is drawn and IVs go in
  • Anatomical snuffbox (back of the hand, seen with the thumb fully extended): abductor pollicis longus + extensor pollicis brevis in front · extensor pollicis longus behind · floor = scaphoid + trapezium, with the radial artery (pulse) lying on it
    • Scaphoid fracture: the most commonly fractured wrist bone · small and hard to immobilise, so continued wrist movement often leaves a nonunion · a fragment cut off from its radial artery supply → avascular necrosis

blocks.cap: The cubital fossa and its contents

blocks.html: 4. Nerves of the forearm

rows: Through the cubital fossa, deep to the bicipital aponeurosis and median cubital vein, medial to the brachial artery · between the two heads of pronator teres · between the two finger flexors · deep to the flexor retinaculum

Main nerve: pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, flexor digitorum superficialis · anterior interosseous branch (leaves just below the cubital fossa): lateral flexor digitorum profundus, flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus
Cut in the cubital fossa · between the heads of pronator teres (pronator syndrome) · carpal tunnel
Behind the medial epicondyle · between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris · down between flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum profundus · through Guyon's canal
Flexor carpi ulnaris + the medial (ring and little finger) half of flexor digitorum profundus: the 1½ muscles the median nerve misses
Behind the medial epicondyle ("funny bone") · between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris · Guyon's canal
Into the cubital fossa between brachialis and brachioradialis, where it splits

Main nerve: brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus · deep branch (pierces supinator): supinator, extensor carpi radialis brevis, extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, extensor carpi ulnaris · posterior interosseous nerve: the 3 thumb muscles + extensor indicis · superficial branch: SENSORY only, back of the hand lateral to the 4th finger
Deep branch where it pierces supinator · superficial branch in the anatomical snuffbox (it crosses its roof)

blocks.html:
• Pronator syndrome: median nerve squeezed between the two heads of pronator teres · pain and tenderness at the top of the front of the forearm · hyperesthesia of the palm side of the lateral 3½ fingers and adjacent palm · usually muscle bulk from elbow overuse
  • "Funny bone": behind the medial epicondyle the ulnar nerve lies just under the skin, so a knock to the elbow sends tingling or pain down the forearm
  • Guyon's (ulnar) canal: pisiform, hook of the hamate and the ligament over them (pisohamate) · carries the ulnar nerve and artery
    • compression ("handlebar neuropathy": cycling with the wrists extended and pressure on the hook of the hamate) → reduced sensation in the medial 1½ fingers + weak intrinsic hand muscles · more in 01.2 - Clinical Approach to the Wrist and Hand - PART 2
  • What goes wrong at each site, and how it presents, is on 07.2 - Clinical Approach to the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity
5. Skin nerves of the arm and forearm

rows: Medial cutaneous nerve of the arm (medial cord)
Posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm (radial nerve)
Medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm (medial cord)
Lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm (musculocutaneous nerve)
Posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm (radial nerve)

blocks.html: • In the hand: superficial branch of the radial (back, lateral side) · dorsal branch of the ulnar and the ulnar nerve (medial side) · median nerve (palm, lateral side); the detail is in Wrist and Hand Part 2
6. Myotomes and dermatomes
• Myotome = the movements one spinal level powers, tested by strength · dermatome = a key patch of skin that tests a single spinal level

rows: Abduction of the arm · flexion of the forearm
Flexion of the forearm · extension of the wrist
Front of the tip of the thumb
Extension of the forearm · flexion of the wrist · extension of the fingers
Front of the tip of the middle finger
Front of the tip of the little finger

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the neurovascular supply of the distal upper extremity
lectures.framing: With tingling or numbness around the elbow, first ask whether there is true sensory loss: tingling can come from any tissue or be referred, but true sensory loss is neurogenic. Then map it to one nerve and one site; the one this lecture works through is the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow = medial elbow pain, numbness and tingling into the ring and little fingers and a positive Tinel sign at the elbow; treat it by educating (it is reversible), keeping pressure off the elbow and splinting against night-time hyperflexion, and go to EMG/NCS and surgery early only for significant or progressive weakness. True sensory loss is neurogenic; tingling alone can come from any tissue or be referred. The sensory loss of UNE is ulnar, sparing the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm, which is what separates it from a C8 problem. Pronator syndrome = median nerve between the heads of pronator teres: proximal anterior forearm pain plus the lateral 3½ fingers and palm.

blocks.html: 1. Abnormal sensation: nerve or not?

• Tingling or abnormal sensation can come from lots of things: nerve, muscle, tendon, ligament, joint
  • Don't forget referred pain: is it cardiac?
  • True sensory LOSS is neurogenic
  • Where the forearm nerves run and where each can be pinched is on 07.1 - Anatomy of the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity
2. Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow (UNE)

• Also called cubital tunnel syndrome · the ulnar nerve can also be compressed at the wrist, but that is less common (Wrist and Hand Part 2)
  • Causes of nerve irritation
    • direct trauma: hitting the "funny bone" · repeated pressure (leaning on a desk)
    • elbow flexion puts the nerve under tension (during sleep)
    • the nerve subluxing as the elbow flexes · ligament hypertrophy? · medial epicondylosis (bulk)?
  • Clinical features
    • pain at the medial elbow
    • numbness and tingling from the medial forearm into the ring and little fingers · the fingers "fall asleep"
    • positive Tinel sign at the entrapment site: light tapping over the nerve sends tingling ("pins and needles") into its distribution
    • check for sensory loss · check for motor deficits
  • Motor and sensory features
    • sensory: ulnar territory (the medial hand and the ring and little fingers, palm and back), which is NOT the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm and NOT C8
    • motor: may or may not be weak · if weak, the small muscles of the hand are usually most affected
3. Managing ulnar neuropathy at the elbow

• Rule out red flags: significant or progressive weakness may need more aggressive treatment at an earlier stage
  • Electromyography (EMG) / nerve conduction study (NCS): identifies the diagnosis and its severity · separates nerve irritation (neuritis) from nerve damage (neuropathy)
  • Education is critical: neuritis is totally reversible, and so is mild neuropathy
  • Non-pharmacologic: avoid external pressure (don't lean on it; ergonomics) · avoid hyperflexion of the elbow: a towel splint or elbow pad overnight
  • Pharmacologic: not much
  • Intervention / surgery: ulnar neurolysis or ulnar nerve transposition

blocks.cap: The ulnar nerve's sites at risk

blocks.html: 4. Pronator syndrome

• What it is: the median nerve compressed between the two heads of pronator teres, usually from muscle bulk built by elbow overuse
  • Presents as: pain and tenderness at the top of the front of the forearm · hyperesthesia over the palm side of the lateral 3½ fingers and the adjacent palm

blocks.cap: The median nerve's sites at risk

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Carried above (bolded): ulnar neuropathy (cubital tunnel): pain at the medial elbow, positive Tinel at the elbow, the nerve subluxes with flexion, causes including leaning, direct trauma and sustained flexion in sleep; management: reversible, towel splint against night-time hyperflexion, neurolysis or transposition.
  • The review's sensory flag is settled from this year's slides: the symptoms run from the medial forearm into the ring and little fingers, while the sensory loss on exam is ulnar territory, not the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm and not C8.

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Wrist and Hand - PART 1
lectures.title: Anatomy of the wrist and hand, part 1
lectures.framing: Part 1 builds the hand from the joints up: what each joint allows, the fascial bands that hold the tendons down and roof the carpal tunnel, the four muscle compartments with their nerves, and the two arterial arches. The nerves of the hand and the carpal tunnel's clinical problems are Part 2; the wrist fractures are on the Clinical Approach chart.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The flexor retinaculum roofs the carpal tunnel, which carries 9 tendons (4 superficialis, 4 profundus, flexor pollicis longus) plus the median nerve; the ulnar nerve and artery pass on top of it. The thumb's CMC joint is a saddle, which is what lets the thumb oppose. Thenar muscles = recurrent branch of the median; hypothenar, adductor pollicis, interossei and the medial two lumbricals = ulnar. PAD and DAB: palmar interossei adduct, dorsal interossei abduct. Superficial arch = mostly ulnar; deep arch = mostly radial.

blocks.html: 1. Joints of the hand
• IP and MCP joints are held by a joint capsule plus medial and lateral collateral ligaments; all the hand's joints have a capsule and extensive ligament support

blocks.cap: Fascia of the wrist: palmar carpal ligament, palmar aponeurosis, flexor retinaculum and carpal tunnel

blocks.html: 2. Fascia of the wrist and hand

• Palmar carpal ligament: a thickening of the forearm (antebrachial) fascia, continuous with the extensor retinaculum · superficial and proximal to the flexor retinaculum
  • Palmar aponeurosis: where palmaris longus inserts · thick longitudinal fibres from the flexor retinaculum to the medial four fingers, blending with their fibrous tendon sheaths · its septa divide the palm into compartments
    • Dupuytren's contracture: unexplained progressive shortening, thickening and fibrosis of the aponeurosis that draws the fingers into permanent flexion · the diseased fascia must be surgically excised to open the palm
  • Flexor retinaculum: deep to the palmar carpal ligament · the roof of the carpal tunnel · spans scaphoid and trapezium to pisiform and hook of the hamate

cols: Deep to the flexor retinaculum (in the carpal tunnel)
rows: 4 flexor digitorum superficialis tendons · 4 flexor digitorum profundus tendons · flexor pollicis longus · the median nerve
Ulnar nerve and artery · palmar (cutaneous) branch of the median nerve · palmaris longus tendon (if present)

blocks.html:
• Fibrous digital sheaths: bony-fibrous canals binding the long flexor tendons to the phalanges · they act as pulleys and stop "bowstringing"
  • Synovial sheaths: fluid-filled sleeves that lubricate the tendons and cut friction
    • an infected finger sheath (tenosynovitis) makes the finger swollen and painful to move · usually it stays in that finger, but it can spread to the common flexor sheath and the forearm
3. Compartments and intrinsic muscles of the hand

rows: Abductor pollicis brevis · flexor pollicis brevis · opponens pollicis
Recurrent branch of the median nerve (deep head of flexor pollicis brevis: deep branch of the ulnar)
Abducts, flexes and opposes the thumb (at its CMC joint)
Abductor digiti minimi · flexor digiti minimi brevis · opponens digiti minimi
Abducts, flexes and opposes the little finger
The long flexor tendons · lumbricals (4, from the profundus tendons)
Lumbricals: lateral two median · medial two ulnar
Lumbricals flex the knuckle (MCP) and extend the finger joints (IP)
Adductor pollicis (not a thenar muscle) · palmar interossei (3) · dorsal interossei (4)
Adductor pollicis adducts the thumb · Palmar ADduct (PAD) toward the middle finger · Dorsal ABduct (DAB) away from it · both help the lumbricals

blocks.html:
• Bedside tests: adductor pollicis = hold a sheet of paper between thumb and index finger as it is tugged away · dorsal interossei = spread the fingers against resistance · palmar interossei = grip paper between two fingers
  • Extrinsic recap: flexor digitorum superficialis splits at the middle phalanx and profundus passes through it · flexor pollicis longus runs between two sesamoid bones

blocks.alt: compartments of the hand cross-section - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: The palm in cross-section: hypothenar, central, thenar, and the deeper adductor and interosseous compartment

blocks.html: 4. Arterial supply of the hand

rows: Ulnar artery, which enters on top of the flexor retinaculum through Guyon's canal
Superficial palmar branch of the radial artery
Common palmar digital → proper palmar digital arteries
Radial artery, which crosses the snuffbox and dives between the two heads of the 1st dorsal interosseous
Deep branch of the ulnar artery (through the hypothenar compartment)
Across the metacarpals, just past their bases

blocks.html: • The radial artery also gives the princeps pollicis (thumb) and radialis indicis (lateral side of the index finger) arteries

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to the Wrist and Hand - PART 1
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the wrist and hand, part 1
lectures.framing: Two fractures from a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH): the distal radius, judged on X-ray by three questions (crooked? short? smooth?) and reduced if it is not, and the scaphoid, which can hide on the first X-ray and loses its blood supply if missed. Treatment is dictated by age and activity level and by how displaced the fracture is. The chart also carries part 2, the numb hand (carpal tunnel syndrome and ulnar neuropathy at the wrist).
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Snuffbox swelling and tenderness after a FOOSH with a normal X-ray is treated as a scaphoid fracture and imaged with CT or MRI: its blood flows retrograde, so a missed fracture can end in nonunion or osteonecrosis. Distal radius X-ray: crooked (normal ~12° palmar tilt), short (ulnar variance; compare sides), smooth (a step over 1 mm → arthrosis). Closed reduction = analgesia, traction, increase the deformity to unlock it, correct, 3-point mould; surgery if reduction is inadequate. Scaphoid: undisplaced or distal → cast; displaced or proximal → surgery.

blocks.html: 1. Joints of the hand
• IP joints: hinge · MCP joints: condyloid · CMC joints: plane (fingers 2-5) and saddle (thumb, allowing opposition) · the anatomy is on 08.1 - Anatomy of the Wrist and Hand - PART 1
2. Distal radius fracture

• Very common injury · FOOSH · localized pain · poor function if the anatomy is not restored
  • Three X-ray questions

rows: The articular angle on the lateral view
About 12° of palmar tilt (the lecture's fracture: 20° dorsal)
Distal radio-ulnar joint motion is altered · forearm rotation becomes restricted
Ulnar variance: greater than neutral = the radius is short · compare with the other side
A step over 1 mm → post-traumatic arthrosis: radiocarpal arthritis with pain and stiffness, treated by fusion

blocks.html:
• Treatment principles
    • ① age dependent: treatment is forgiving at the extremes of age
    • ② closed reduction
    • ③ surgical reduction if the reduction is inadequate (still crooked or not smooth): open reduction internal fixation (ORIF) or external fixation
    • ④ rehabilitate
  • Closed reduction, step by step
    • adequate analgesia: hematoma block (1% lidocaine into the fracture hematoma) · regional anaesthesia · conscious sedation
    • traction · then increase the deformity, which unlocks the fragments · then correct the deformity
    • 3-point mould + cast · well moulded does not mean tight

rows: Lightweight yet strong · waterproof options · more radiolucent

blocks.html: • Padding: cotton (cheap, under plaster or fibreglass) or synthetic (waterproof)

blocks.cap: Volar (palmar) tilt on the lateral wrist X-ray

blocks.html: 3. Scaphoid fracture

• The most common carpal bone fracture · young people · usually heals uneventfully, but sometimes difficult to diagnose, and delayed diagnosis brings complications
  • Unique blood supply: retrograde flow (it enters distally and flows back) → nonunion and osteonecrosis
  • Clinical exam: swelling and localized tenderness (the snuffbox)
  • Imaging: be SUSPICIOUS · an X-ray is usually sufficient, but if the X-rays are normal, treat it as fractured and get CT or MRI
  • Treatment: undisplaced or distal pole → cast until union · displaced or proximal pole → surgery (volar approach)
  • Complications: nonunion · osteonecrosis · late arthrosis
  • The lecture's cases: a scaphoid tubercle fracture · a 25-year-old man whose CT showed the fracture, casted and healed on CT at 8 weeks · a displaced proximal-pole fracture, fixed operatively
4. Soft tissues of the hand
• The fascia, compartments, intrinsic muscles, digital sheaths and arterial arches in this deck are charted on 08.1 - Anatomy of the Wrist and Hand - PART 1

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Carried above (bolded): distal radius fracture (FOOSH): X-ray for angulation, length against the ulna (compare the other side) and joint surface; an uneven joint surface → radiocarpal arthritis → fusion · forgiving at the extremes of age · closed reduction: traction → increase the deformity → correct → cast; ORIF or external fixation if alignment fails · scaphoid: FOOSH, young; X-ray can be normal → treat as fractured, then CT/MRI; retrograde blood supply → nonunion, osteonecrosis · undisplaced/distal → cast; displaced/proximal → surgery.
  • Not carried: the review's casting rules ("weekly x-ray") are not on this year's slides; its ganglion cyst and mallet finger point is taught in 06.1 - Anatomy of the Muscles of the Distal Upper Extremity this year and is charted there.

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Wrist and Hand - PART 2
lectures.title: Anatomy of the wrist and hand, part 2
lectures.framing: Part 2 is the hand's nerves: which nerve feels which skin, which nerve runs which small muscle, and what the hand looks like when one of them is cut. Part 1 covered the joints, the soft tissues and the blood supply. The syndromes themselves (carpal tunnel, ulnar neuropathy at the wrist) are on the CLINICAL APPROACH PART 2 chart.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Median nerve = LOAF (lumbricals 1-2, opponens pollicis, abductor and flexor pollicis brevis) and the palm side of the lateral 3½ fingers; the deep ulnar branch runs every other intrinsic muscle. The palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the carpal tunnel, so carpal tunnel compression spares the central palm. Opponens pollicis has no backup: lose the median, lose opposition. Nine tendons + the median nerve in the tunnel; the ulnar nerve and artery go through Guyon's canal instead. Proximal ulnar = claw hand with radial deviation; Guyon's canal = claw without it; proximal median = hand of benediction.

blocks.html: 1. Nerves of the hand
• The palm is shared by the median (thumb side) and the ulnar (little-finger side) · the radial takes the back of the hand on the thumb side

rows: Runs a superficial course just past the tunnel
Thenar muscles: opponens pollicis · abductor pollicis brevis · flexor pollicis brevis (superficial head)
Through the carpal tunnel, deep to the flexor retinaculum
Palm side of the lateral 3½ fingers + the backs of their tips and nail beds
Leaves above the wrist, over the flexor retinaculum
Medial half of the back of the hand + the backs of the medial 1½ fingers
Every other intrinsic muscle: hypothenar (opponens, abductor and flexor digiti minimi) · lumbricals 3 and 4 · all interossei · adductor pollicis · deep head of flexor pollicis brevis
Metacarpal bones, and position sense from the joints

blocks.alt: sensory territories of the hand - median ulnar radial - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Skin territories of the hand: median (purple) over the palm of the thumb and 2½ fingers and their fingertips behind, ulnar (blue) over the little finger and half the ring finger on both sides, radial (red) over the back of the hand

blocks.html: 2. Testing the small muscles

• Median nerve = "LOAF": Lumbricals 1-2 · Opponens pollicis · Abductor pollicis brevis · Flexor pollicis brevis (superficial head) · the deep ulnar branch does everything else
  • Adductor pollicis (deep ulnar): squeeze a piece of paper between thumb and index finger while you tug it
  • Dorsal interossei spread digits 2-3 apart against resistance · palmar interossei hold a sheet of paper between two fingers
  • Opponens pollicis has no backup from outside the hand → lose the median and opposition is lost
  • Long flexors (review): flexor digitorum profundus is the only muscle that bends the fingertip (DIP) joint · flexor digitorum superficialis splits onto the middle phalanx · flexor pollicis longus runs between 2 sesamoid bones to the thumb tip
3. Carpal tunnel and Guyon's canal
• Carpal tunnel: an osseofibrous tunnel · floor = carpal bones (hamate, capitate, trapezoid, trapezium) · roof = flexor retinaculum (scaphoid and trapezium → pisiform and hook of hamate)

cols: <mark class="lo">Inside the tunnel (deep to the retinaculum)</mark>
rows: Median nerve + 9 tendons: flexor pollicis longus (1) · flexor digitorum superficialis (4) · flexor digitorum profundus (4)
Ulnar nerve and artery · palmar cutaneous branch of the median · palmaris longus · flexor carpi radialis · flexor carpi ulnaris · palmar carpal ligament

blocks.html:
• The tendons run in synovial sheaths; the median nerve is the most sensitive structure in the tunnel, so swelling there squeezes it first
  • The palmar cutaneous branch skips the tunnel, so carpal tunnel compression spares the central palm
  • Guyon's canal (ulnar canal): carpals + an overlying ligament, between the pisiform and the hook of the hamate · carries the ulnar nerve and ulnar artery

blocks.cap: Carpal tunnel in cross-section: the median nerve under the flexor retinaculum beside the superficialis, profundus and flexor pollicis longus tendons

blocks.html: 4. What each nerve lesion looks like

rows: Carpal tunnel (most common) · wrist cuts (the nerve is shallow) · a small cut over the thenar eminence severs the recurrent branch alone
Thenar muscles + lumbricals 1-2 · skin of the thumb and 2½ fingers
Thenar wasting · cannot oppose the thumb · clumsy index and middle fingers
Also superficialis + profundus to fingers 2-3, and lumbricals 1-2
"Hand of benediction" when trying to make a fist
Behind the medial epicondyle (most common) · between the 2 heads of flexor carpi ulnaris
Interossei, medial lumbricals, hypothenar, adductor pollicis · wrist flexion weak, hand pulled to the thumb side
"Claw hand": knuckles (MCP) overextended, cannot bend fingers 4-5 at the tip or straighten the finger joints
Medial 1½ fingers' skin · intrinsic hand muscles
Fingers 4-5 may claw, but finger flexion is kept and the hand is not pulled sideways

blocks.html: • The recurrent branch is at risk from a superficial cut on the lateral palm: it must be repaired or the thenar muscles waste
