lectures.name: Clinical Approach to the Wrist and Hand - PART 2
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the wrist and hand, part 2
lectures.framing: For a numb, tingling hand, ask which fingers. Thumb to half the ring finger is the median nerve, usually squeezed in the carpal tunnel; the little finger and half the ring finger is the ulnar nerve, squeezed in Guyon's canal. Each has a nerve-root mimic in the neck (C6 and C8), and electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction studies tell them apart. The nerve anatomy and the lesion-level hand signs are on the ANATOMY PART 2 chart; hand infections are on the MSK INFECTIONS chart. The chart also carries part 1, the distal radius and scaphoid fractures.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Carpal tunnel syndrome = numbness and tingling in the median territory, worse at night and with the wrist bent, with normal median function above the wrist; EMG and nerve conduction studies separate it from C6 radiculopathy, and treatment runs education → night orthosis → steroid injection → carpal tunnel release. Medial 1½ fingers + weak intrinsics = ulnar nerve; at the wrist think handlebars, and rule out C8 and the elbow. Both are reversible if caught early.

blocks.html: 1. Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS)

• Definition: compression of the median nerve at the wrist, in the carpal tunnel · the "bread and butter" peripheral nerve diagnosis
  • The tunnel: floor = carpal bones · roof = transverse carpal ligament (flexor retinaculum) · contents = tendons of flexor pollicis longus, flexor digitorum profundus and superficialis + the median nerve · the ulnar nerve and artery and palmaris longus run superficial to it
  • Causes
    • extrinsic (less space): fracture · flexor tenosynovitis (the finger flexor tendons share the space) · ganglia · inflammation (rheumatologic conditions) · pregnancy (edema) · acromegaly
    • intrinsic (a more susceptible nerve): diabetes · amyloidosis · alcohol
    • and, very commonly, idiopathic
  • Presents as
    • numbness and tingling in the median nerve territory, often predominantly at night
    • worse with the wrist flexed or extended (driving, holding a phone)
    • potentially thumb weakness (abductor pollicis brevis)
    • median function above the carpal tunnel is normal: the median-supplied forearm muscles are spared · maybe Tinel's and Phalen's signs
  • Differential: C6 radiculopathy is the main one · tendinopathy · thumb-base (carpometacarpal) arthritis
  • Investigations: electromyography (EMG) and nerve conduction studies: nerve vs muscle or bone · CTS vs C6 · how severe the nerve damage is
  • Treatment, in order
    • education: a common problem · hand position · reversible if discovered early
    • non-drug: a rigid wrist-hand orthosis worn overnight only · avoid aggravating positions and vibrating tools
    • drug: corticosteroid injection of the carpal tunnel
    • surgery: carpal tunnel release
2. Ulnar neuropathy at the wrist (Guyon's canal syndrome)

• Definition: the ulnar nerve compressed in Guyon's canal (carpals + an overlying ligament, carrying the ulnar nerve and artery) · the nerve's other site at risk is behind the medial epicondyle at the elbow
  • Causes (extrinsic, less space): fracture · ganglia · inflammation (rheumatologic conditions) · compression: "handlebar neuropathy"
  • Presents as: reduced feeling (hypoesthesia) in the medial 1½ digits · weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles
  • Differential: C8 radiculopathy is the main one · ulnar nerve at the elbow · tendinopathy
  • Investigations: EMG and nerve conduction studies: nerve vs muscle or bone · elbow vs wrist vs C8 · severity
  • Treatment: education (hand position and pressure; reversible if discovered early) → relieve the pressure (specialized gloves, change the handlebars) → Guyon's release

lectures.name: Upper Extremity Radiology
lectures.title: Upper extremity radiology
lectures.framing: Read every film the same way, then use the one line or landmark each joint gives you. Skeleton mature or not → bone (cortex, medulla, density) → alignment → joints → soft tissues. At the shoulder the Y-view sets the direction of a dislocation, at the elbow the fat pads and two lines find a hidden fracture, and at the wrist the three Gilula arcs check the carpal alignment.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A visible posterior fat pad is always abnormal: supracondylar fracture in a child, radial head or neck fracture in an adult. The Y-view decides anterior (subcoracoid) vs posterior dislocation. The anterior humeral line and the radiocapitellar line both aim at the centre of the capitellum. Osteoarthritis = joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, marginal osteophytes. Three smooth Gilula arcs = carpal alignment kept, even when a bone is fractured.

blocks.html: 1. The systematic read

• Skeletal maturity first: a visible, unfused physis (growth plate) = immature · fused, no visible plate = mature
    • long bone: epiphysis (end, with a growth centre) · physis (lucent line in children) · metaphysis · diaphysis (shaft) · cortex (dense outer layer) · medullary cavity
  • Then: bone integrity (cortex, medulla, density, generalized bone disease) → alignment (fracture, dislocation) → joints (inflammation, narrowing, degeneration) → muscles and soft tissues (can be abnormal when the bones look normal)
  • Bone pathology: "TIMS-C" = Trauma, tumours · Infection, inflammatory (rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis), idiopathic · Metabolic, malignancy · Systemic (leukemia, lymphoma), senile (osteoarthritis) · Congenital (mostly an immature skeleton)
  • Osteoarthritis = 3 findings: joint space narrowing (cartilage is radiolucent, so lost cartilage narrows the gap) · subchondral sclerosis (denser, not stronger) · marginal osteophytes · graded mild, moderate or severe on the combination
2. Shoulder

• Standard series (trauma, osteoarthritis): AP (front-to-back) · Y-view · Grashey · special views (instability, a suspected dislocation) are not covered · the lecture also reads the axillary view
    • AP: the anatomical neck (head-neck junction) and surgical neck (just below the articular surface) are reference lines, not visible structures · the labrum is fibrocartilage, so it does not show
    • axillary: beam through the armpit · the coracoid and the lesser tuberosity are both anterior, which orients the film · the acromion + distal clavicle form the acromioclavicular (AC) joint · an os acromiale (unfused ossification centre) is not a fracture · the anatomical and surgical necks don't show here, so find the lesser tuberosity (and roughly where the greater one is) · some overlap is normal, but the joint space should not look widened
    • Y-view: coracoid (anterior limb) · scapular spine + acromion (posterior limb) · scapular body (vertical limb) · the humeral head should sit centred over the glenoid
  • Dislocation: anterior = humeral head subcoracoid (under the coracoid) · posterior = farther from the coracoid · the Y-view tells them apart · subluxation = partial contact, dislocation = complete loss
  • Also seen: surgical neck fracture · osteoarthritis (the 3 findings)
3. Elbow

• AP and lateral views · orient the AP by the medial epicondyle (bigger) and the ulna (medial)
    • medial to lateral on the distal humerus: medial epicondyle · trochlea · capitellum (articulates with the radial head) · lateral epicondyle
    • sublime tubercle on the medial proximal ulna = the ulnar collateral ligament attachment, a post-trauma landmark
    • lateral, in order: humeral shaft (capitellum and trochlea overlap here; the capitellum sits next to the radius, so tell them apart on the AP) → proximal ulna: olecranon, trochlear notch, coronoid process, all prone to fracture → radial head, neck, shaft and radial tuberosity (biceps tendon) → fat pads → soft tissues, including the olecranon bursa (swells with inflammation or bleeding after trauma)
  • Fat pads (lateral view): the anterior fat pad is normal · a visible posterior fat pad is ALWAYS abnormal (fracture or effusion)

rows: Posterior fat pad seen (± anterior humeral line off the capitellum's centre)
Supracondylar fracture of the distal humerus

blocks.html:
• Anterior humeral line (along the anterior humeral cortex, lateral view) should pass through the centre of the capitellum (slight variation is fine) · the lateral is the best view for alignment, especially in children · passing through its anterior part + a posterior fat pad in a child → supracondylar fracture
  • Radiocapitellar line (along the radial shaft) must hit the centre of the capitellum on every view · if it misses → radial head dislocation or another alignment problem
  • Also seen: osteoarthritis with intra-articular bony bodies · a soft-tissue mass with normal bones (a lipoma, confirmed on CT or MRI): always look at the soft tissues
4. Wrist

• AP and lateral views
    • AP: distal radius and ulna at the distal radioulnar joint · radial and ulnar styloids · the radiocarpal joint · the TFCC (triangular fibrocartilage complex) is radiolucent, so calcification there hints at a TFCC problem
    • carpal bones, radial to ulnar: proximal row scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform · distal row trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate · never reverse the order
    • lateral: Lister's tubercle (dorsal radius, check it for fracture) · scaphoid and pisiform in front, triquetrum behind, trapezoid hidden behind the trapezium · carpal bones overlap, so the AP is essential for fractures
  • Arcs of Gilula: 1 = proximal surfaces of the proximal row · 2 = distal surfaces of the proximal row · 3 = proximal surfaces of the distal row · any break, step-off or widening → carpal injury
  • Fractures can keep the arcs intact: scaphoid (proximal pole) + triquetrum · distal radius + ulnar styloid base · look for cortical disruption or a lucent line in each bone
  • Also seen: an expanded distal radius with a large lytic lesion and thin cortex reaching the joint surface = giant cell tumour of bone

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Hip Joint
lectures.title: Anatomy of the hip joint
lectures.framing: The hip is the shoulder's opposite: it sacrifices some mobility for stability, and is the most stable joint in the body. The lecture builds it from the bones (pelvis, femur, and the tibia and fibula below), then the capsule and ligaments that hold it, then the arteries whose failure explains why a femoral neck fracture is so dangerous. The fracture itself (presentation, workup, surgery) is on the HIP FRACTURE chart.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The medial circumflex femoral artery carries most of the femoral head's blood, so a femoral neck fracture risks avascular necrosis; the artery of the ligament of the head is minor and often inadequate. Hip = stability over mobility (bony fit, ligaments, muscles); shoulder = mobility over stability. The iliofemoral (Y) ligament is the strongest in the body and limits extension; the pubofemoral limits abduction. The labrum deepens the socket; the ligament of the head adds no strength. Iliac crest = L4; ischial tuberosity = sitting bone and hamstring origin. Posterior dislocation = short, medially rotated leg and a sciatic nerve at risk.

blocks.html: 1. The pelvis (hip bone)
• Three bones - ilium, ischium, pubis - which all meet in the acetabulum, the socket for the femoral head

rows: Top of the crest = L4 level (lumbar puncture landmark) · back part is the origin of gluteus maximus
Anterior end of the iliac crest
Posterior end of the iliac crest
Curved lines on the outer ilium · bound the attachments of gluteus medius and minimus
Forms the top edge of the greater sciatic notch
The sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments make it the greater sciatic foramen: pelvis → gluteal region
Attachment of the sacrospinous ligament · the lesser sciatic notch lies between it and the tuberosity (→ lesser sciatic foramen: gluteal region → perineum)
Takes your weight when sitting · origin of the hamstrings
Front bony point · the inguinal ligament attaches
Superior fuses with the ilium and ischium at the acetabulum · inferior joins the ischial ramus to form the lower edge of the obturator foramen
Covered by the obturator membrane · passage for the obturator nerves and vessels
Joins the ilium · attachment of the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments and gluteal muscles

blocks.cap: The hip bone from the side and from inside: ilium (purple), pubis (orange) and ischium (green) meeting at the acetabulum, with the iliac spines, sciatic notches, ischial tuberosity and obturator foramen

blocks.html: 2. Femur, tibia and fibula

• Femur: the largest bone in the body · carries weight from the hip to the tibia
    • head (into the acetabulum) · neck (head to shaft) · greater trochanter (large, superolateral) · lesser trochanter (smaller, inferior and posteromedial) · intertrochanteric line (front) and crest (back) · trochanteric fossa (between the neck and the greater trochanter) · gluteal tuberosity and linea aspera (back of the shaft) · medial and lateral condyles (knee), separated behind by the intercondylar fossa
  • Tibia: the major weight-bearing bone of the leg · condyles form the tibial plateau · tibial tuberosity = where the patellar ligament inserts
  • Fibula: its head articulates with the tibia · no weight-bearing function
3. The hip joint: built for stability

• Type: ball-and-socket synovial joint, multiaxial · the acetabulum takes the femoral head, which is covered in hyaline cartilage
  • The most stable joint in the body, because of
    • congruency of fit (static, bony) - more than 50% of the femoral head sits in the acetabulum
    • stout ligaments (static) - including the strongest in the body
    • surrounding muscles (dynamic support)
• Versus the shoulder: the hip sacrifices some mobility for stability; the glenohumeral joint sacrifices stability for mobility

rows: Attaches to the intertrochanteric line in front, but not to the back of the femur · its inferior fibres wind round the neck and "screw" the head into the socket in extension and medial rotation
Strongest ligament in the body · front and top · limits extension
Fibrocartilage from the acetabular rim that deepens the socket · the transverse acetabular ligament bridges its gap at the acetabular notch
Ligament of the head of the femur
Runs from the head into the acetabulum · adds no significant strength · carries the artery of the ligament of the head

blocks.cap: The hip's capsular ligaments from the front (iliofemoral, pubofemoral) and from behind (ischiofemoral), with the zona orbicularis round the femoral neck

blocks.html: 4. Blood supply of the femoral head

rows: The most significant supply to the head and neck (via retinacular arteries)
With the medial, the majority of the blood supply
Artery of the ligament of the head
Runs inside the ligament · only minor blood flow

blocks.html:
• Collateral circulation: the inferior gluteal artery joins the medial and lateral circumflex arteries, so the lower limb still gets blood if the proximal femoral artery is occluded
  • A femoral neck fracture can disrupt the circumflex supply → only the ligament artery is left, and it is frequently inadequate → avascular necrosis of the femoral head, likely needing a total hip replacement · especially common in women over 60 with osteoporosis
5. Dislocation

• Congenital: a malformed acetabulum and/or femur at birth → less congruent, less stable joint
  • Acquired is uncommon, given the hip's strength · posterior dislocation in a car crash (force along the femur's long axis) → limb shorter and medially rotated · ⚠ the sciatic nerve lies close and can be stretched or compressed

blocks.cap: Arteries of the femoral head: the deep femoral artery giving the medial and lateral circumflex arteries round the neck, and the artery of the ligament of the head

blocks.html: 6. Osteoarthritis of the hip

• Common with ageing · changes in the articular cartilage, the bone under it, the synovium and the soft tissues around · thickened subchondral bone plate · osteophytes · deformed bone shape
  • Conservative treatment rarely works long term, so severe osteoarthritis → hip replacement (the clinical side is on the HIP PAIN chart)

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to the Hip Joint
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the hip joint: hip fracture
lectures.framing: The lecture is one condition worked in order: is this a hip fracture, is the patient stable, why did they fall (and why did the bone break), what is the plan, and what happens after surgery. "Hip fracture" means a proximal femur fracture, and the fracture's level on the X-ray picks the operation. The hip's bones, ligaments and blood supply are on the HIP JOINT ANATOMY chart; osteoarthritis, labral tears and the tendon problems are on the HIP PAIN chart.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Hip fracture = an older person after a fall with groin pain and a short, externally rotated, abducted leg; suspect it even when the pain or the fall was small, X-ray the AP pelvis and hip, and CT if the X-ray is clear. Then ask why they fell (bloods, troponin, ECG, chest X-ray) and why the bone broke (tumour, osteoporosis). Surgery within 24-48 hours: displaced neck → arthroplasty; intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric → intramedullary nail. Afterwards: early mobilization, heparin for 14-30 days, falls and fracture prevention.

blocks.html: 1. Is this a hip fracture?

• Who: the risk factors are whatever raises the risk of falls (previous falls · weakness: peripheral vascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, stroke · polypharmacy: sedatives, diuretics, psychotropics, antiarrhythmics · poor nutrition · poor eyesight · the environment) plus whatever raises the risk of osteoporosis
    • the lecture's bone mineral density (BMD) testing list: everyone 65 and over · 50-64 with a fragility fracture, long-term glucocorticoids, a parental hip fracture, a vertebral fracture or osteopenia on X-ray, heavy alcohol, smoking, weight under 60 kg or loss of over 10% since age 25, rheumatoid arthritis · under 50 with a fragility fracture, long-term glucocorticoids, hypogonadism or menopause before 45, malabsorption, primary hyperparathyroidism
  • History: sudden groin or lateral upper-thigh pain after a fall · sharp or deep ache · may radiate to the knee or leg · worse with movement and weight bearing, eased by staying still · ⚠ high suspicion in an older person even if the pain or the trauma was minimal
  • Exam: look: leg shortened, externally rotated and abducted · cannot bear weight · feel: tender over the hip · move: painful range, log roll, straight leg raise
  • Investigations: X-ray: AP pelvis and hip · negative but suspicion still high → CT
  • Types: femoral neck (subcapital) · intertrochanteric · subtrochanteric

blocks.cap: Types of hip fracture along the proximal femur: subcapital and transcervical neck fractures, intertrochanteric, subtrochanteric, and greater or lesser trochanter fractures

blocks.html: 2. Stable? Then why?

• Stable? airway, breathing, circulation (especially a young patient after high-velocity trauma) · pelvic fracture? · check distal pulses and nerve function, especially the sciatic nerve
  • Why did they fall? recent illness (nutrition, dehydration) · syncope or presyncope · cardiac symptoms → complete blood count, electrolytes, troponin · ECG (atrial fibrillation?) · chest X-ray (pneumonia)
  • Why did it break? a pathologic fracture (less trauma than it should take, e.g. a bone tumour)? · a fragility fracture automatically qualifies as osteoporosis → start the osteoporosis workup
3. Plan and after

• Surgery for the vast majority, within 24-48 hours (standard of care): quicker return to weight bearing, fewer complications of immobility
    • femoral neck, displaced → arthroplasty (hemi = femoral head · total = head + acetabulum), required to preserve the head's blood supply
    • femoral neck, non-displaced → maybe non-operative (only if very non-displaced in a poor surgical candidate) · maybe screws across the fracture · arthroplasty, the surgeon's choice
    • intertrochanteric and subtrochanteric → intramedullary nail (essentially all surgical)
  • After surgery: complications all come from immobility · venous thromboembolism → low-molecular-weight heparin for 14-30 days · pneumonia (a common cause of death) · muscle atrophy · infection (urinary) · delirium · bedsores
  • Early mobilization with interdisciplinary rehab · falls prevention (comorbidities, environment, occupational therapy and physiotherapy, gait aids) · fracture prevention (vitamin D, calcium, secondary osteoporosis workup, antiresorptive)

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html: • 147 hip fractures per 100,000 people aged 40 and over · women are 2× more likely to fracture a hip; men are 1.3× more likely to die afterwards, and about 25% die of any cause within a year

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Gluteal Region & Thigh
lectures.title: Anatomy of the gluteal region and thigh
lectures.framing: Two organising ideas carry the whole lecture. In the buttock, piriformis is the landmark: only the superior gluteal vessels and nerve leave the pelvis above it, everything else below. In the thigh, three compartments each have one job and one nerve - front: femoral, inside: obturator, back: sciatic.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Piriformis is the landmark: only the superior gluteal nerve and vessels leave above it; the sciatic, inferior gluteal and pudendal nerves leave below, and an injured superior gluteal nerve (hip replacement) gives the Trendelenburg sign. The pelvis drops on the unsupported side, so a right hip drop on right swing = a weak LEFT gluteus medius. Front = femoral, inner = obturator, back = sciatic - except the hamstring part of adductor magnus (tibial) and the short head of biceps (common fibular). NAVEL from lateral to medial; the femoral nerve sits outside the sheath. Injections go in the upper outer quadrant, away from the sciatic nerve. The saphenous nerve is at risk when the great saphenous vein is harvested.

blocks.html: 1. Passageways out of the pelvis
• The sacrotuberous (sacrum → ischial tuberosity) and sacrospinous (sacrum → ischial spine) ligaments turn the sciatic notches into two foramina

rows: Superior gluteal artery, vein and nerve
Inferior gluteal vessels and nerve · sciatic nerve · posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh · nerves to quadratus femoris and to obturator internus · pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels
Pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels, turning back in to reach the perineum

blocks.html: 2. Muscles of the buttock

rows: Extends the hip · helps you stand up from sitting
Abduct and medially rotate the thigh · stabilize gait
Flexes the hip · tenses the iliotibial band
Lateral rotators (deep to gluteus maximus): piriformis · superior gemellus · obturator internus · inferior gemellus · quadratus femoris
Laterally rotate the hip · stabilize the femoral head in the acetabulum · piriformis also abducts

blocks.html:
• Trendelenburg sign: gluteus medius and minimus contract on the standing leg as soon as the other foot leaves the floor, to stop the pelvis tipping to the unsupported side
    • superior gluteal nerve injured (e.g. hip replacement) → the pelvis drops on the unsupported side, so the weak gluteus medius is on the opposite (standing) side
    • the swinging leg is then too long, so the patient leans away from the unsupported side to clear the foot = gluteus medius gait
  • Intramuscular injections go in the superolateral (upper outer) quadrant, away from the sciatic nerve (index finger on the ASIS, fingers spread back along the iliac crest; inject between index and middle finger)

blocks.cap: Nerves of the buttock: the superior gluteal nerve leaving above piriformis; the inferior gluteal, sciatic, posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh and pudendal nerves leaving below it

blocks.html: 3. The thigh's three compartments

rows: Iliopsoas (also anterior rami L1-L3) · sartorius (flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the hip, flexes the knee) · quadriceps
Adductor longus, brevis, magnus · gracilis (also flexes the knee)

blocks.html:
• Exceptions to "one nerve per compartment"
    • adductor magnus: adductor part (obturator; adducts and flexes) + hamstring part (tibial; adducts and extends)
    • short head of biceps femoris = common fibular (peroneal) division; the other hamstrings = tibial division
    • pectineus is the other medial-compartment exception
  • Quadriceps: the powerful knee extensor · one tendon to the tibial tuberosity, with the patella inside · rectus femoris (from the AIIS) also flexes the hip · the patellar tendon reflex tests the femoral nerve and L3-L4
  • Pes anserinus ("goose's foot", SGT): sartorius + gracilis + semitendinosus insert together on the medial upper tibia
  • Injuries
    • hamstring strain: active contraction + passive stretch · extreme pain and hematoma · forced hip flexion with the knee straight can avulse the ischial tuberosity (the lecture's hurdler: a pop in the back of the lead thigh, then extensive bleeding over the back of the thigh, avulsion on X-ray)
    • groin pull: the adductors, same mechanism · bruising and pain · conservative: RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation) and NSAIDs
    • teenagers: the growth plate is weaker than the tendon → a powerful hip flexion can avulse the ASIS
4. Popliteal fossa

• Diamond behind the knee: biceps femoris (upper outer) · semimembranosus and semitendinosus (upper inner) · lateral and medial heads of gastrocnemius (below)
  • Contents: tibial and common fibular nerves · popliteal artery and vein (the femoral vessels after the adductor hiatus) · end of the small saphenous vein · popliteal lymph nodes · fat · from deep to superficial: artery → vein → nerve (AVN)
  • Popliteal aneurysm: the most common peripheral aneurysm · at risk of embolization, thrombosis and rupture · 80% have no symptoms · think of it with a pulsatile mass in the popliteal fossa (the lecture's case: an 85-year-old with a swollen, painless leg) · a rupture not treated quickly can cost the foot and leg

blocks.cap: Popliteal fossa: bounded by biceps femoris, semimembranosus, semitendinosus and the gastrocnemius heads, holding the tibial and common fibular nerves and the popliteal artery and vein

blocks.html: 5. Arteries, veins and lymph

rows: Joins the circumflex arteries round the hip
External iliac, under the inguinal ligament
Anterior thigh · becomes the popliteal after the adductor hiatus
Superficial in the femoral triangle, so easily injured · the femoral pulse

Perforating branches (usually 3-4) pierce adductor magnus to the posterior thigh and supply all three compartments · medial circumflex (most of the femoral head and neck) · lateral circumflex (lateral thigh: ascending branch to the femoral neck, transverse round the femur, descending to the knee)
Cruciate anastomosis (medial + lateral circumflex, inferior gluteal, 1st perforating): the leg survives a femoral artery ligation
Dorsal venous arch of the foot
Up the medial leg and thigh, with the saphenous nerve → saphenous opening → femoral vein
Harvested for coronary bypass; the saphenous nerve beside it is at risk
Deep vein of the thigh → external iliac vein

blocks.html:
• Collateral circulation: around the hip = inferior gluteal + medial and lateral circumflex + perforating branch · around the knee = the descending branch of the lateral circumflex (genicular anastomosis)
  • The posterior compartment has no artery of its own (inferior gluteal, medial circumflex, perforating, popliteal) · the medial compartment gets perforating branches + the obturator artery
  • Lymph: superficial inguinal nodes take the thigh, medial leg, perineum and abdominal wall below the umbilicus → deep inguinal → external iliac nodes · superficial veins and lymph run superficial to the fascia lata
6. Nerves of the thigh

rows: Above piriformis, between gluteus medius and minimus
Gluteus medius, minimus, tensor fasciae latae
Below piriformis, deep to the long head of biceps femoris
Largest nerve in the body = tibial + common fibular nerves in one sheath · hamstrings
Posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh
Below piriformis, deep to gluteus maximus
Skin of the lower buttock, back of the thigh, popliteal fossa
Out the greater foramen, back in through the lesser
Under the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral vessels
Anterior thigh muscles and anterior thigh skin
Skin of the anteromedial knee, leg and foot
Under the inguinal ligament beside the ASIS
Down medial to psoas major, through the obturator foramen · anterior and posterior divisions straddle adductor brevis
Medial thigh muscles (not the hamstring part of magnus) · some medial thigh skin

blocks.html: • Sciatic nerve injury ("sciatica"): pain or numbness from the buttock radiating down the leg · causes: herniated disc · hip surgery · piriformis syndrome · intragluteal injection
7. Femoral triangle

• Borders: inguinal ligament · sartorius · adductor longus
  • Contents, lateral to medial - "NAVEL": Nerve (femoral) · Artery · Vein · Empty space (femoral canal) · Lymphatics · the great saphenous vein ends here
    • the femoral sheath encloses the artery, vein and canal - not the nerve · the canal's entrance is the femoral ring: a loop of small bowel through it = femoral hernia (a groin bulge below the inguinal ligament that grows with straining, such as sit-ups)
  • Adductor canal (sartorius, vastus medialis, adductor longus) carries the femoral vessels to the adductor hiatus, where they pass behind the knee and become the popliteal vessels

blocks.cap: Femoral triangle under the inguinal ligament between sartorius and adductor longus: femoral nerve, artery, vein, the empty femoral canal and deep inguinal nodes from outer to inner, inside the femoral sheath

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to Hip Pain
lectures.title: Clinical approach to hip pain
lectures.framing: First ask where the patient means by "hip". True (intra-articular) hip pain is usually anterior, in the groin; patients often point to the lateral buttock, and sometimes to the buttock itself, and each place has its own short list. The hip fracture is on the HIP FRACTURE chart.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Point first: groin = inside the joint (OA, labral tear, avascular necrosis), lateral = the greater trochanter, buttock = piriformis. Hip OA is a clinical diagnosis: groin pain, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, internal rotation lost first; an X-ray confirms it, no MRI needed. Can't put socks on → hip OA; tender trochanter, can't lie on that side, socks fine → GTPS. Clicking and locking → labral tear; MR arthrogram is the study of choice. Buttock pain worse sitting, ± sciatica → piriformis syndrome.

blocks.html: 1. Anterior hip and groin pain: usually inside the joint

• Differential: arthritis (osteoarthritis, rheumatoid, septic) · labral tear · avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) · iliopsoas tendinopathy
  • Hip osteoarthritis (OA): degenerative, often age-related "wear and tear" · primary (idiopathic, elderly) or secondary (post-traumatic, younger)
    • presents as: anterior hip or groin pain, the "C" sign · gradual or sudden onset · worse with prolonged activity · night pain · morning stiffness under 30 min, and stiffness after prolonged sitting · crepitus, locking or sticking · decreased range of motion (getting in and out of a car, bending) · antalgic gait
    • exam: leg length discrepancy? · internal rotation is reduced first · FABER (flexion, abduction, external rotation) · Stinchfield · FADIR (flexion, adduction, internal rotation)
    • investigations: a clinical diagnosis · X-ray confirms it (and can monitor progression), but X-ray changes do not always match symptoms · CT or MRI generally not needed (secondary causes, surgical planning)
      • start with an X-ray: MRI adds nothing to the diagnosis and has a long wait · CT shows bone well but gives much more radiation · ultrasound is poor for a deep joint like the hip
    • treatment: non-drug first (education, exercise and physiotherapy, functional supports, weight management, tai chi, a cane) · drugs (oral NSAIDs, Tylenol, duloxetine) · image-guided intra-articular injection (steroid, hyaluronic acid or platelet-rich plasma) · hip replacement: hemiarthroplasty (femoral head and neck replaced, acetabulum spared) · total (head, neck and acetabulum) · resurfacing (head and acetabulum, neck spared)
  • Labral tear: all ages, commonly active females · vague groin pain with clicking, catching, snapping, locking · FABER and FADIR positive · X-ray only to exclude other pathology · MR arthrogram is the imaging study of choice · general hip pain treatment → arthroscopic labral debridement or repair
  • Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis): disrupted blood flow to bone, commonly the femoral head · causes: trauma · steroids (oral or intramuscular) · alcohol · lupus · sickle cell disease · radiation
2. Lateral hip pain

• Greater trochanter bursitis: a very common cause of lateral hip pain · chronic friction of the iliotibial band over the greater trochanter irritates the bursa · female > male
    • a clinical diagnosis: pain over the greater trochanter with point tenderness (highly sensitive) · worse with weight bearing · can't lie on that side · ± radiates into the buttock or down the thigh to the knee · no swelling, redness or skin changes
    • imaging not often needed · ask about a recent increase in activity · positive Ober's test
    • treatment: physio (stretch the iliotibial band, strengthen the hip abductors) · PRICE (protection, rest, ice, compression, elevation) · NSAIDs · corticosteroid injection
  • Greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS): bursitis is only half the story: overuse and chronic tendinopathy of gluteus medius and minimus (which insert on the greater trochanter), with flares of bursitis and/or tendinitis
    • similar presentation, but more chronic and recalcitrant · single leg stance test · insidious, or a sudden flare after unaccustomed exercise, a fall, prolonged weight bearing or sporting overuse
    • imaging: X-ray, ?ultrasound, ?MRI · treatment: physio (stretch the iliotibial band, strengthen the hip abductors) · load management · weight management · NSAIDs, injections · weak-evidence adjuncts (shock-wave therapy, ultrasound) · ?surgery
  • Can you put your socks on? Hip OA can present laterally and is easily confused with GTPS. Seated sock-putting needs hip flexion and external rotation (basically FABER), so it is hard in hip OA and fine in GTPS (standing on one leg to do it hurts in GTPS)

blocks.html: 3. Posterior hip (buttock) pain

• Piriformis syndrome: a muscle strain and/or tendinopathy with buttock pain · may impinge the sciatic nerve → radicular symptoms down the leg
    • causes: trauma to the buttock · prolonged sitting (sedentary jobs) · anatomic anomalies · ?piriformis hypertrophy
    • worse getting out of bed, with prolonged sitting and with hip movements · tender over piriformis · Pace (resisted abduction and external rotation) · Beatty (side-lying, hold the flexed knee off the table) · FAIR (flexion, adduction, internal rotation) · Freiberg (forceful internal rotation of the extended thigh)
    • electromyography (EMG) only if the nerve is involved · treatment: physio (stretch piriformis, range of motion, deep massage) · NSAIDs · ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injection · ?surgery
  • Snapping hip syndrome: very common · can be deep (inside the joint), anterior, lateral or posterior · if it isn't painful, don't worry about it; if it is, treat the structures in that area (muscle: stretch and strengthen · bone: strengthen, ?inject, ?surgery · ligament: strengthen, ?inject)

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Knee - PART 1
lectures.title: Anatomy of the knee, part 1
lectures.framing: The knee's bones barely fit together, so it is held by soft tissue: muscles (above all the quadriceps femoris) give most of the stability, and four cardinal ligaments plus two menisci add passive support. Knowing which structure resists which movement is what lets you name the injury on the acute knee injury chart.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Valgus stresses the MCL (which drags the medial meniscus with it); varus stresses the LCL (which has no meniscus attached). ACL: weaker, taut in extension, stops the tibia sliding forward, tested by Lachman. PCL: strongest, taut in flexion, stops the tibia sliding back. Dashboard injury = PCL; MCL injuries outnumber LCL injuries. The fibula is not in the knee joint. Peripheral meniscal tears heal; central ones don't. Skyline view = patellofemoral joint; tunnel view = loose bodies. Popliteus unlocks the knee.

blocks.html: 1. Osteology and the knee on X-ray

• patella = a sesamoid bone inside the quadriceps tendon
  • Femoral condyles (lateral, medial) sit on the tibial condyles (together the tibial plateau) · medial and lateral femoral epicondyles above them
  • Tibial tuberosity = anterior bump where the patellar ligament inserts
  • Intercondylar eminence of the tibia = attachment area for the cruciate ligaments and menisci · intercondylar fossa (notch) of the femur behind it
  • The fibula is NOT part of the knee joint - it does not touch the femur
  • Plain radiograph views

blocks.html: 2. The knee joint

• Hinge synovial joint, with some gliding and rotation about the long axis
  • 3 articulations: lateral femoral + lateral tibial condyle · medial femoral + medial tibial condyle · femur + patella
  • Largest joint in the body, with the largest capsule and an extensive synovial membrane
  • Capsule reinforcement

• Cruciates are named for where they attach on the tibia
  • Crossed-fingers trick: cross your fingers over the same-side knee - the middle finger is the ACL, the index finger the PCL
  • The MCL holds the medial meniscus, so damage to one puts the other at risk
  • How each one is injured
    • MCL injuries are more common than LCL injuries: a valgus force on an extended knee, or excessive twisting of the flexed knee · LCL: a strong varus force on the medial side of the knee
    • ACL: a forceful blow to the thigh with the foot fixed drives the tibia forward · or rotation plus valgus on a flexed knee → the unhappy triad (ACL + MCL + medial meniscus)
    • PCL: the "dashboard" injury - something strikes the front of the tibia with the knee flexed and forces the tibia back · the patellar ligament may avulse from the tibial tuberosity

blocks.html: 4. The menisci

• C-shaped fibrocartilage wedges, thick at the rim and thin in the middle: deepen and stabilize the joint and absorb shock
  • Blood supply: the periphery is richly vascularized, the centre is avascular (fed by synovial fluid) → peripheral tears can heal, central ones cannot

rows: Firmly fixed to the tibial collateral ligament, so little movement
Freely movable (popliteus pulls it back in flexion)
Torn more often (with the MCL, in the valgus-twist "unhappy triad")

blocks.html: 5. Locking and unlocking: the screw-home mechanism

• Locking: in the final 15-20° of extension the shapes of the condyles and menisci make the femur rotate medially on the tibia → the ligaments tighten maximally → the knee is stable for "quiet standing" with little muscle work
  • Unlocking: popliteus rotates the femur laterally (~5°) to start flexion, and pulls the lateral meniscus back out of the way

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to the Knee - PART 1
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the knee, part 1
lectures.framing: An acute knee injury is named from three things: the mechanism, how fast it swelled, and which test is positive. A pivot with a pop and immediate swelling is the ACL; a blow to the front of the flexed tibia is the PCL; a valgus or varus collision is a collateral; a twist on a planted foot with delayed swelling and locking is a meniscus.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Pop + immediate swelling (hemarthrosis) after a pivot = ACL; the other ligament injuries swell little, and a meniscal tear swells late. Lachman, anterior drawer and pivot shift for the ACL; posterior drawer, sag sign and reverse Lachman for the PCL. Dashboard knee = PCL. Valgus → MCL (± medial meniscus, ± ACL = unhappy triad); varus → LCL (look for a PCL injury). Locking or catching = meniscus. Red-zone tears are repaired, white-zone tears resected.

blocks.html: The structures themselves (where each ligament runs, why the medial meniscus is fixed, the red and white zones) are on the knee anatomy part 1 chart; knee pain without an injury, and the swelling timeline, are on the part 2 chart.

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Knee - PART 2
lectures.title: Anatomy of the knee, part 2
lectures.framing: The patella always wants to slide laterally, and the knee spends structures stopping it. The angle of the femur (the Q-angle) pulls it out; the vastus medialis and a buttress of bone on the femur hold it in. Around it sit the bursae that become knee bursitis, and the nerves and arteries that cross the joint.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The Q-angle makes the quadriceps pull the patella laterally; vastus medialis and the bony buttress on the lateral femur hold it in. Wider Q-angle in females → more lateral subluxation and patellofemoral pain. Genu valgum raises the Q-angle and loads the lateral condyles; genu varum lowers it and loads the medial. Housemaid's knee = prepatellar; clergyman's knee = superficial infrapatellar.

blocks.html: 1. The extensor mechanism and patellar stability

• Quadriceps femoris → quadriceps tendon → patella → patellar ligament → tibial tuberosity
    • the patella sits inside this tendon (a sesamoid bone), so the quadriceps are its main stabilizer
  • The pull is not straight: because of the Q-angle the quadriceps pull the patella superolaterally, while the patellar tendon pulls straight down
    • the resultant force tends to sublux the patella laterally during knee extension
  • Two things resist the lateral pull
    • ① vastus medialis pulls the patella medially
    • ② an extra buttress of bone on the lateral patellar surface of the femur (seen on a skyline X-ray)
    • abnormal bony shape of the patella or distal femur predisposes to patellar dislocation

blocks.alt: patellar forces and lateral pull from the Q-angle - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Quadriceps (Q) and patellar tendon (P) pulls add up to a lateral resultant (R); vastus medialis pulls back medially

blocks.html: 2. The Q-angle and knee alignment

• Q-angle = angle between a line from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the patella and a line from the patella to the tibial tuberosity
  • A normal Q-angle spreads weight evenly between the medial and lateral femoral and tibial condyles
  • Wider in females (wider hips) → more lateral pull → more lateral patellar subluxation and patellofemoral pain syndrome

blocks.html: 3. Bursae around the knee
• Fluid sacs that stop tendons and skin rubbing on bone; irritation from chronic friction = bursitis

blocks.html: 4. Nerves and blood supply

• Nerves (Hilton's law: a joint is supplied by the nerves to the muscles that act on it): femoral and sciatic nerves · articular branches of the obturator and saphenous nerves
  • Arteries: the genicular anastomosis - superior and inferior, medial and lateral genicular branches of the popliteal artery · collateral flow from the descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery
  • Popliteus: adds little posterior stability, but unlocks the knee (laterally rotates the femur to start flexion from full extension) and pulls the lateral meniscus back during flexion

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to the Knee - PART 2
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the knee, part 2
lectures.framing: Part 2 is the knee pain that builds up rather than happens: after any trauma, how fast it swelled sorts the injury; without trauma, where it hurts and whether there is a lump tells the overuse and swelling problems apart. Then the four injections, compared on onset, how long they last, cost and evidence.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Anterior knee pain worse after activity and prolonged sitting, with no swelling, in a young woman = patellofemoral pain syndrome: a clinical diagnosis, treated with physiotherapy to balance vastus medialis. Swelling within 6 hours of trauma = ACL tear, fracture or patellar dislocation. Lateral knee ache while running downhill (less with sprinting) = iliotibial band. A swelling behind the knee: ultrasound it, and don't miss a DVT or aneurysm; 6 weeks of conservative care unless vessels or nerves are compromised. Steroid: fast, cheap, short. Hyaluronic acid: long-lasting, expensive.

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Leg
lectures.title: Anatomy of the leg
lectures.framing: The leg is four sealed compartments, each with one job and one nerve: anterior dorsiflexes (deep fibular), lateral everts (superficial fibular), and both posterior compartments plantarflex (tibial). Learn that grid and nerve injuries, compartment syndrome and foot drop follow from it.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Anterior = dorsiflexion = deep fibular; lateral = eversion = superficial fibular; both posterior = plantarflexion = tibial. Common fibular nerve at the neck of the fibula → foot drop with a numb dorsum; deep fibular alone → numb first web space only. Tibialis anterior and tibialis posterior both invert. Tarsal tunnel: Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry. Standing calf raise = gastrocnemius; seated = soleus. The fibula breaks just above the lateral malleolus in extreme inversion.

blocks.html: 1. Bones of the leg and foot

• tibia: the major weight-bearing bone · shaft just under the skin (the "shin", so its periosteum bruises easily) · medial and lateral condyles (tibial plateau), tibial tuberosity, soleal line (soleus origin) · medial malleolus distally
  • fibula: posterolateral · no weight-bearing role (so it is the bone of choice for grafts) · head near the knee · lateral malleolus distally, which holds the talus in place with the medial malleolus
  • Fractures
    • tibia: at its narrowest point, between the middle and distal thirds, which also has the poorest blood supply · a broken tibia often takes the fibula with it (the interosseous membrane joins them)
    • fibula: just above the lateral malleolus, from the talus pushing it in extreme inversion
    • metatarsals: a heavy object dropped on the foot · "dancer's fracture" when a dancer loses balance onto the metatarsals
  • Foot: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, phalanges · the lecture's checks ask for the leg and foot bones on plain X-rays
  • Movements: dorsiflexion and plantarflexion happen at the ankle · inversion and eversion at the foot

blocks.html: 2. Fascia and compartments

• Crural fascia wraps the leg · the tibia, fibula, interosseous membrane and the intermuscular septa divide it into 4 compartments: anterior, lateral, superficial posterior, deep posterior (a transverse septum splits the posterior two)
  • Retinacula stop the tendons bowstringing at the ankle: superior and inferior extensor retinacula (anterior compartment) · superior and inferior fibular retinacula (lateral compartment) · flexor retinaculum roofs the tarsal tunnel (deep posterior)
  • Compartment syndrome: the fascia does not stretch, so pus or swelling from strenuous exercise raises the pressure → nerves and arteries in that compartment are squeezed · relieved by fasciotomy · shin splints = a mild anterior compartment syndrome (microtrauma where tibialis anterior attaches)

  • Entrapment: superficial fibular (stretched by repeated ankle sprains) → pain and tingling of the anterolateral leg and dorsum · deep fibular (overused anterior compartment, or tight ski boots or cleats over the inferior extensor retinaculum) → dorsal foot pain into the first web space

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Ankle and Foot
lectures.title: Anatomy of the ankle and foot
lectures.framing: The foot is built to hold its arches up and stay stable on uneven ground. Know which way the ankle is weakest (plantarflexed), which ligament gives first (the anterior talofibular), and which tendons and ligaments hold each arch up - sprains, flat feet and pulses all follow from it. The leg's compartments, the tarsal tunnel and the bones on X-ray are on the leg chart.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ The ankle is most stable in dorsiflexion and least stable in plantarflexion, so the plantarflexed, inverted ankle tears the anterior talofibular ligament first. The deltoid ligament is thick and strong and stabilizes eversion. Inversion and eversion happen at the subtalar joint, not the ankle. The talus head and spring ligament are the keystone of the medial arch; tibialis anterior, tibialis posterior and fibularis longus hold the arches - lose tibialis posterior and the foot goes flat. Posterior tibial pulse between the medial malleolus and the Achilles, foot inverted; always compare both sides. Deep fibular = the first web space; medial plantar = medial 3½ toes.

blocks.html: 1. Dorsum and sole of the foot

• Extensor retinacula = thickened fascia over the anterior compartment tendons · stop them bowstringing when the ankle dorsiflexes
    • superior: tibia to fibula · inferior: Y-shaped, stem from the calcaneus
  • Flexor retinaculum holds the deep posterior tendons as they pass behind the medial malleolus
  • Tendons on the dorsum: tibialis anterior (broad attachment on the medial foot) · extensor digitorum longus (splits into 4, works with extensor digitorum brevis) · extensor hallucis longus (to the big toe, works with extensor hallucis brevis)
  • Plantar fascia: continuous with the deep fascia of the leg · thick central part = plantar aponeurosis
    • protects the sole · supports the longitudinal arches · holds everything together
  • Intrinsic muscles of the sole: like the palm of the hand, but they work as a group to support stance and keep the arches up, most active at toe-off
    • 4 layers: ① abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor digiti minimi · ② quadratus plantae, lumbricals · ③ flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis · ④ plantar (3) and dorsal (4) interossei
    • or by compartment: medial (abductor hallucis, flexor hallucis brevis) · intermediate (flexor digitorum brevis, quadratus plantae, lumbricals, adductor hallucis) · lateral (flexor and abductor digiti minimi) · interosseous (= the 4th layer)
  • Long tendons in the sole: tibialis posterior · flexor digitorum longus · flexor hallucis longus, which runs under the sustentaculum tali
2. Ankle (talocrural) joint

• Hinge synovial joint: distal tibia and fibula grip the top (trochlea) of the talus · the lateral malleolus reaches ~2 cm lower than the medial
    • dorsiflexion: tibialis anterior, fibularis tertius, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus · plantarflexion: gastrocnemius and soleus through the Achilles tendon
  • Stability depends on position: the trochlea is wider in front
    • dorsiflexion = highest congruency, most stable ("digging in your heels")
    • plantarflexion = lowest congruency, least stable → some wobble allowed, and most injuries happen plantarflexed
  • Capsule thin front and back, reinforced at the sides by the collateral ligaments
3. Ankle ligaments

rows: ATFL = the most vulnerable, torn in inversion sprains · sprains are more often lateral because the ankle tends to invert
4 bands: anterior and posterior tibiotalar · tibiocalcaneal · tibionavicular
Severe inversion or eversion can avulse bone instead
Sustentaculum tali → navicular, below the deltoid
Holds up the head of the talus: with it, the "keystone" of the medial arch
Stretched or torn → talar head drops between calcaneus and navicular, medial arch flattens, forefoot abducts and everts

blocks.alt: lateral collateral ligaments of the ankle.png
blocks.cap: Lateral collateral ligaments: anterior talofibular, calcaneofibular and posterior talofibular
Medial side: the deltoid ligament from the medial malleolus, with the spring ligament below it

blocks.html: 4. Joints of the foot

• Subtalar (talocalcaneal) joint: plane synovial joint, talus on calcaneus · held by interosseous talocalcaneal ligaments
    • where the bulk of inversion and eversion happens · inverters: tibialis anterior and posterior · everters: fibularis longus and brevis (whose main job is to resist inversion injury)
    • falling hard on the heel → calcaneal fracture, often in pieces and disabling because it disrupts this joint
  • Transverse tarsal joint: two joints working as one · talonavicular (ball and socket) · calcaneocuboid (plane)
  • Plantar ligaments that hold the arch: spring · long plantar (calcaneus → cuboid and metatarsal bases, making a tunnel for the fibularis longus tendon) · short plantar (calcaneus → cuboid)
5. Arches of the foot

blocks.lead: Weight goes tibia → talus → back to the calcaneus and forward to the metatarsal heads; the arches flatten and spring back between those points.
rows: Calcaneus · talus (the keystone) · navicular · three cuneiforms · three metatarsals
Tibialis anterior · tibialis posterior · fibularis longus · foot ligaments (spring) · plantar aponeurosis
Lateral longitudinal - much flatter, rests on the ground
Transverse - medial to lateral across the midfoot
Cuboid · cuneiforms · metatarsal bases · the two longitudinal arches are its pillars
Tibialis anterior · tibialis posterior · fibularis longus

blocks.html:
• Flat foot (pes planus): often from damage to tibialis posterior → the talus drops inferiorly and medially and the medial arch flattens · usually no symptoms · if painful: shoes with orthotics (arch support) and foot exercises
  • Weight: each foot takes half the body weight, half of that through the calcaneus and half through the metatarsal heads · high heels or a lost arch support load the metatarsal heads

blocks.cap: Transverse, medial longitudinal and lateral longitudinal arches, with the talus as the keystone

blocks.html: 6. Arteries and veins of the foot

rows: Dorsum · lateral tarsal and arcuate branches · deep plantar artery dives between metatarsals 1 and 2 to the sole
Lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon · diminished or absent = vascular insufficiency from arterial disease
Through the tarsal tunnel → medial and lateral plantar arteries
Between the medial malleolus and the Achilles tendon · invert the foot to relax the flexor retinaculum

blocks.html:
• Deep plantar arch = the lateral plantar artery arching medially, completed by the deep plantar artery from dorsalis pedis → plantar metatarsal → digital arteries · the medial plantar artery contributes and supplies the medial sole and big toe
    • a puncture wound of the sole bleeds from both ends (rich anastomoses) and is hard to tie off
  • Take both pulses on both sides at once: look for symmetry
  • Five P's of acute arterial occlusion: pain · pallor · paresthesia · paralysis · pulselessness
  • Veins: plantar network → dorsal venous network → great and small saphenous veins · lymph follows the veins, deep vessels to the popliteal nodes
7. Nerves of the foot

rows: The dorsum, except the first web space

blocks.html:
• Dorsal foot dermatomes (the lecture's figure): L4 medial · L5 middle · S1 lateral edge
  • The deep fibular nerve reaches the dorsum alongside the dorsalis pedis artery

lectures.name: Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot
lectures.title: Clinical approach to the ankle and foot
lectures.framing: Two questions run the lecture: after a twisted ankle, does this patient need an X-ray (the Ottawa rules); and for a sore foot without injury, where exactly does it hurt? Almost every one of these gets better slowly with education, footwear and physiotherapy - surgery is the exception.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Ottawa rules: X-ray the ankle only for bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to bear weight immediately and in the emergency department; X-ray the foot only for tenderness at the navicular or base of the 5th metatarsal, or the same weight-bearing test. Lateral sprain = plantarflexion + inversion, ATFL first; treat with early mobilization. Plantar fasciitis = anteromedial heel pain on the first morning steps; Achilles tendinopathy = posterior heel, worse with passive dorsiflexion. Tibialis posterior dysfunction: medial ankle pain, then a flexible then rigid flat foot ("too many toes"). Morton's neuroma burns, sits between the 3rd and 4th metatarsals, and never weakens.

blocks.html: The ligaments, arches and pulses themselves are on the ankle and foot anatomy chart.
1. Ankle sprain

• "Sprain" = a ligament injury, from a partial to a full tear of any or all three lateral ligaments · dislocation when all three are fully torn
  • Lateral sprain - up to 85%
    • mechanism: foot plantarflexed and inverted at the "twist" (landing from a jump, stepping in a hole)
    • order of injury: anterior talofibular (ATFL) > calcaneofibular (CFL) > posterior talofibular (PTFL)
  • Medial sprain: similar, but the deltoid ligament (foot caught on turf during a kick)
  • Exam: swelling · bruising (ecchymosis) · pain on palpation over the ligament(s) · anterior drawer test (ATFL)
  • Treatment
    • education: most improve · how to avoid recurrence
    • rest, ice, compression, elevation (RICE) · brief immobilization only if needed · early mobilization · strengthening and proprioception · bracing or taping has pros and cons
    • NSAIDs or analgesics as needed
    • ligament reconstruction only for ongoing instability despite conservative care
2. Who needs an X-ray: the Ottawa foot and ankle rules

rows: Bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the lateral malleolus (back 6 cm) · or of the medial malleolus · cannot bear weight (4 steps) both immediately and in the emergency department
Bone tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal · or the navicular · cannot bear weight both immediately and in the emergency department

blocks.cap: Ottawa foot and ankle rules: malleolar zone (back 6 cm of each malleolus) and midfoot zone (navicular, base of the 5th metatarsal), plus inability to bear weight

blocks.html: • When a sprain isn't just a sprain (reading and managing the fracture is on the FRACTURE charts): unimalleolar (may be non-operative, decided by the stability of the talus) · bimalleolar (usually forceful eversion, both malleoli, usually surgical) · trimalleolar (unstable, surgical) · Maisonneuve (forceful external rotation, interosseous ligament torn, with a medial malleolus avulsion or deltoid rupture and an ATFL injury; usually surgical)
3. Overuse problems: where does it hurt?

rows: Posterior heel, just above or right at the calcaneal insertion · runners, especially after a rise in training

Education: a long, slow improvement · activity changes · footwear that does not press on the tendon · heel wedge used cautiously · physio: stretching, eccentric strengthening, friction massage, shock-wave therapy · topical or oral NSAIDs, ?topical nitrites · intervention or surgery rare
Active people in their 30s-40s (and older, as people stay active)
Surgical repair vs casting or an air-cast boot: surgery may re-rupture slightly less, but brings infection, wound problems, scarring and sural nerve injury · involve the patient in the decision
Anteromedial calcaneus, on the first morning steps and with ongoing activity · age 40-60, F > M

Chronic insertional inflammation of an overworked fascia · tender · worse with passive dorsiflexion · often a tight Achilles (less dorsiflexion) · an overuse injury (running, aerobics), often with improper footwear · pain also rises with extension of the big toe

Education: long, slow improvement · cushioned heel pad · heel lift (careful long-term) · shoes with arch support · weight loss · physio: stretch the fascia, strengthen tibialis posterior and the intrinsics · night splints · oral NSAIDs (rarely by injection) · surgical release very, very rarely

Tendon hypovascular distal to the medial malleolus · risks: trauma, steroid use, inflammatory arthritis, obesity, diabetes · a spectrum: mild → significant weakness → flexible flat foot → rigid flat foot · "too many toes" sign

Education on risk factors · RICE · physiotherapy (strengthen tibialis posterior and the other arch stabilizers) · orthosis (foot or ankle-foot; corrective or accommodative) · NSAIDs if needed · surgery by severity
Medial first metatarsophalangeal joint · tops of the toes in a tight shoe box
Footwear (why more common in women) · metatarsus varus · secondary toe deformities · the big toe is out of position for toe-off, so the other toes work harder
Treat early and often to avoid surgery · positioning only if flexible · wider toe box · nothing much pharmacologic (?topical NSAID) · surgical correction or realignment
Usually between the 3rd and 4th metatarsals · middle-aged, F > M

Perineural fibrosis of a common digital nerve · burning dysesthesia · provoked and relieved mechanically (high heels, narrow toe box) · squeeze or palpation reproduces it · possibly sensory findings, no motor
Education, so they own the fix · lower heels, wider and taller toe box · metatarsal pad in an orthosis · neuropathic pain agents · steroid injection · excision

blocks.html: 4. The diabetic foot

• Microvascular disease starves the skin and healing tissue · neuropathy: cannot feel the feet (shoes too small, cold without boots, banged and unnoticed), less sweat · motor loss: intrinsic atrophy, changed arches · Charcot (neuropathic) joint
  • Diabetic foot ulcer: a major complication, in 15% of people with diabetes · multifactorial (insensate, poorly perfused foot) · needs specialized treatment · debridement or amputation may be needed
    • prevention is key: monofilament sensation test · appropriate socks and shoes · daily foot checks with a mirror
    • how an ulcer forms (the lecture's diagram): motor neuropathy → foot deformity → abnormal mechanics · sensory neuropathy → lost protective sensation · autonomic neuropathy → less sweating, dry skin · all three → callus → repeated minor trauma → bleeding under the callus → ulcer, with peripheral artery disease adding to it

lectures.name: Lower Extremity Radiology
lectures.title: Lower extremity radiology
lectures.framing: Each joint has a standard pair of views plus an extra one for a specific question, and the lecture uses each joint to show one classic finding: osteoarthritis at the hip and knee, and fractures graded by where they sit at the ankle.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Weber type is set by the fibular fracture's level against the syndesmosis: A below (usually stable, boot), B at (depends on the medial side), C above (unstable, surgery). The mortise view is the one that shows the syndesmosis. Order an AP pelvis with a hip X-ray to compare sides. Osteoarthritis looks the same at every joint: lost joint space, osteophytes, subchondral cysts and sclerosis. Three malleoli broken = a dislocated ankle.

rows: AP pelvis alongside, to compare the two sides
Tunnel, skyline or standing views, depending on the differential
Mortise view: shows the tibiofibular syndesmosis, which overlaps on the AP

• Views: AP hip · AP pelvis (checks for asymmetry between sides) · cross-table lateral
  • Osteoarthritis - the same four signs at every joint
    • loss of joint space · osteophytes · subchondral cysts · subchondral sclerosis
  • Hip fracture: named by where on the proximal femur it breaks - femoral neck · greater trochanter · intertrochanteric · subtrochanteric

blocks.html: 2. Knee

• Views: AP and lateral are standard · add a tunnel, skyline or standing view when the differential needs it
  • Osteoarthritis: the same four signs - lost joint space, osteophytes, subchondral cysts, subchondral sclerosis
3. Ankle views

• AP · lateral · mortise
  • Mortise view = the one that opens up the tibiofibular syndesmosis (on the AP the tibia and fibula overlap there)
4. Ankle fractures
• Lateral malleolus fracture: graded by the Weber classification - the level of the fibular break relative to the tibiofibular syndesmosis

rows: Usually stable if the medial malleolus is intact
Walking boot and crutches for 6 weeks, weight-bear as tolerated
Variable - depends on the medial malleolus and deltoid ligament
Surgery (open reduction and internal fixation) if unstable
Unstable · often with a bimalleolar fracture or deltoid injury

blocks.html:
• Medial malleolus fracture (sources differ on the mechanism: this note says forced inversion, the ankle sprain note says forced eversion - check the slides)
    • chip fracture = an avulsion: the deltoid ligament pulls off a flake of bone as it ruptures
    • transverse · vertical
    • comminuted = several pieces, usually high-energy trauma
  • Bimalleolar: lateral and medial malleolus
  • Trimalleolar: both malleoli + the back of the distal tibia → no stable bony link between leg and foot, so the ankle dislocates
