lectures.name: Nerve Injury
lectures.title: Nerve injury
lectures.framing: Every nerve injury asks four questions: is it a nerve injury? where is it? how bad is it? what now? The pattern of numbness and weakness says where (root or named nerve); the layer that was cut says how bad, and that predicts recovery. Electrodiagnostic studies confirm both.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Neurapraxia (myelin only, compression) recovers in weeks; axonotmesis (axon cut, epineurium intact) regrows on its own at 1 mm a day (1 inch a month); neurotmesis (epineurium cut) cannot recover spontaneously. Radiculopathy = dermatome with fuzzy borders, myotome weakness and radiating neck or back pain; mononeuropathy = sharp-bordered patch and weakness confined to one nerve's muscles. Numb thumb: lateral forearm numbness or weak biceps → C6; weak abductor pollicis brevis → carpal tunnel. Nerve conduction size reflects the axon, speed reflects myelin. An axonal injury cannot be called axonotmesis or neurotmesis until you see whether it recovers.

blocks.html: 1. The peripheral nerve

• Somatic peripheral nervous system: sensory (afferent) fibres carry signals from skin, muscle and joints to the central nervous system · motor (efferent) fibres carry them out to skeletal muscle
  • Wrappings, inside out: endoneurium around each axon (a protective tube) · perineurium around each fascicle (holds a bundle of axons) · epineurium around the whole nerve (holds a bundle of fascicles)
  • One nerve = many axons, not a single wire · the layered wrappings keep it working, and which layers are torn decides how well it heals
  • Myelin lets the signal jump node to node, so it is faster and insulated
2. How bad: the Seddon classification

rows: Myelin only → conduction slowed or blocked (the signal cannot reach the target at all)
Temporary: resolves within weeks (6-12) once the cause is removed
Axon, with varying damage to its supporting tissues (endoneurial tube, perineurium) and fascicles deranged
Epineurium - a tube to keep regrowing fibres in line
Spontaneous but SLOW: 1 mm a day = 1 inch a month
No spontaneous recovery - no track for the axons to follow

blocks.alt: types of peripheral nerve injury (Seddon Classification).png
blocks.cap: Seddon classification: neurapraxia (myelin damaged), axonotmesis (axon cut, epineurium intact), neurotmesis (axon and epineurium cut)

blocks.html: • After an axon injury: Wallerian degeneration of the axon beyond the injury (cytoskeleton breaks down, membrane integrity is lost, macrophages clear the debris) → Schwann cells multiply, release cytokines and growth factors and clear debris too, the cell body releases trophic factors, the axon regrows - much better with an endoneurial tube to follow, very poorly with no epineurium to guide it
3. Where: localizing the lesion

• Levels: motor neuronopathy (anterior horn cell) · radiculopathy (spinal root) · plexopathy (brachial or lumbosacral plexus) · mononeuropathy (one named nerve) · polyneuropathy (diffuse)
  • First make sure it is a nerve: weakness may be a tendon and numbness may be poor blood flow · true sensory loss is always neurogenic, but central or peripheral? · pain with or without weakness can be hard to sort out clinically
  • Dermatome: skin supplied by one spinal root · dermatomes overlap, so the edges are fuzzy · e.g. C6: lateral arm, forearm and thumb
  • Myotome: the muscles one spinal root supplies, whatever peripheral nerve carries the fibres · e.g. C6: deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps, brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus, latissimus dorsi, serratus anterior, pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis
  • One nerve carries several roots: the radial nerve's muscles run from C5 to T1 (brachioradialis C5-C6, triceps C7-C8, extensor indicis C8-T1) · root charts come from surgically seen roots matched to the muscles abnormal on electromyography (EMG)

rows: Spinal nerve root · compressed in the intervertebral foramen ("pinched nerve")
One named nerve · compressed at a common site (carpal tunnel)
Sudden or insidious · usually a clear time of onset
Depends on the mechanism: chronic compression = insidious (more common) · traumatic cut = sudden
Neck or back pain radiating down the arm or leg · aching or sharp, then electric, burning or zinging along the dermatome
Numbness, tingling, sometimes neuropathic burning or electric pain
Well-circumscribed area of that nerve · may radiate: complaints outside the territory, but usually no objective signs there
Only that nerve's muscles - not other muscles from the same root supplied by another nerve
Positions that stretch the root (neck extension) / taking tension off (arm overhead)
Pressing on the nerve (leaning on the elbow, driving, typing) / position and rest

blocks.cap: Sensory maps: C6, C7, C8 dermatomes (radiculopathy) vs radial, median and ulnar nerve territories (mononeuropathy)

blocks.html:
• "Numb thumb" (frequent tingling, less feeling over the thumb): the median nerve territory and the C6 dermatome overlap at the thumb, so test what they do not share
    • carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve): thumb sensation + motor to abductor pollicis brevis (a C8 root muscle)
    • C6 radiculopathy: C6 dermatome (lateral arm, forearm, thumb) + what C6 sends through the musculocutaneous nerve: lateral forearm sensation (lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm) and biceps power
  • Foot drop after trauma: dorsiflexion, toe extension and eversion 0/5, sharp-bordered numbness over the dorsum of the foot, reflexes intact → electromyography abnormal in peroneus longus, tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum brevis only, paraspinals normal → common peroneal axonopathy at the fibular head · if gluteus medius, semimembranosus, tibialis posterior and the L5 paraspinals are abnormal too (one root, several nerves) → L5 radiculopathy
4. What now: electrodiagnostic studies

blocks.lead: Electrodiagnostic studies (EDX) = nerve conduction studies (NCS) + electromyography (EMG), often just called "EMG" (electrodiagnostic studies).
rows: Stimulate the nerve, record further along
Size of the response = axon health · timing/speed = myelin health

At rest (denervated muscle is not quiet; denervation can be seen and heard) · on voluntary activation · exactly which muscle (e.g. ulnar vs median parts of flexor digitorum profundus, pronator quadratus)

blocks.html:
• EDX answers: is there a nerve problem? where is it? how severe, myelin or axon, is the nerve in continuity? the expected timeline (may need repeat studies)? or is it a muscle problem (myopathy)?
  • ⚠ Not for musculoskeletal pain (rotator cuff tear) or central nervous system disease (stroke)
  • Foot drop case: nerve conduction: no response from the superficial peroneal sensory or the peroneal motor study · EMG: lots of abnormal spontaneous activity, no voluntary motor units in the peroneal muscles → axonal injury · axonotmesis or neurotmesis is only decided by whether it recovers on its own
  • Many of these levels can be told apart at the bedside; EDX helps clarify the diagnosis and set the prognosis

lectures.name: Acute Monoarthritis
lectures.title: Acute monoarthritis
lectures.framing: A hot, red, swollen joint is infected until the fluid says otherwise. Acute monoarthritis = one inflamed joint for less than 6 weeks (oligo = 2-3 joints, poly = 4 or more), and its differential is infection, infection, infection, gout, pseudogout (and, rarely, reactive or psoriatic arthritis). The three look alike at the bedside, so the needle, not the exam, decides.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Any red, hot, swollen joint gets aspirated for the 3 C's - cell count, culture with Gram stain, crystals - because septic arthritis is an emergency that gout and pseudogout imitate exactly. Gout = needle-shaped, negatively birefringent, big toe; pseudogout = rhomboid, intracellular, positively birefringent, knee of an older person with osteoarthritis. Septic arthritis = admit, urgent I&D, empiric IV cefazolin (or vancomycin + ceftriaxone), 4-6 weeks. Uric acid can be normal during an attack, and high uric acid alone is not gout. Never start allopurinol during an attack. Cell counts are inflammatory in all three: the Gram stain, culture and crystals decide.

blocks.html: 1. Approach: if the joint is red, aspirate it

• What it is: an intense inflammatory response to a foreign organism or substance in a joint · must rule out infection · crystals of uric acid or calcium pyrophosphate can do it too
  • Aspirate (joint aspiration) and send the 3 C's: cell count (a couple of hours) · culture and sensitivity with Gram stain (24-48 hours) · crystals (a couple of hours)
  • "To inject is human, to aspirate divine" - never inject a steroid before infection is excluded
  • Fluid in the three lecture cases: septic ankle 59 · gout 15 · pseudogout 18 (× 10⁹ cells/L as the slides print it, all inflammatory) · so the cell count does not separate them: Gram stain and culture find the infection (Gram-positive cocci in clusters); crystals tell gout from pseudogout (detailed fluid interpretation: 02 - Rheumatology Investigations)
2. Septic arthritis - a medical emergency

• Septic arthritis: without rapid detection and treatment → fulminant joint damage
  • Organisms: gram-positive cocci 80% - Staphylococcus 60%+, Streptococcus 20% · gram-negatives 15% (immunocompromised, elderly, neonates, intravenous (IV) drug users) · anaerobes (adults: S. aureus, including methicillin-resistant (MRSA), and group A, C, G streptococci)
  • How it gets in: through the blood from a remote site (#1) · direct inoculation (penetrating trauma, recent surgery) · spread from infected bone next door
  • Risk factors
    • systemic: immunosuppressed - diabetes, cancer, methotrexate, leflunomide, prednisone, anti-tumour necrosis factor (TNF) and other biologics · very young or old · alcohol excess, IV drugs · recent infection
    • local: prosthetic joint · recent joint surgery · existing joint disease (arthritis) · penetrating trauma · skin infection
  • Workup: aspirate (3 C's) · blood cultures · blood count, electrolytes, creatinine, C-reactive protein · ± imaging
  • Treatment: admit · urgent incision and drainage (I&D) - an infected joint is a closed space - repeated until the joint is clean · empiric IV antibiotics: cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours, or vancomycin 15 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours (MRSA risk) · 4-6 weeks in all
    • the lecture's case: sent urgently to the emergency department · orthopedic surgery consulted · to the operating room that evening · started on IV cefotaxime · analgesia and rest
3. Gout vs pseudogout

rows: Lower limb · 1st metatarsophalangeal joint (big toe) in 50%
Men 35-50 · women after menopause (estrogen helps excrete uric acid)
Impaired kidney function · diuretics (furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide) · alcohol · family history · male · with obesity, hypertension, diabetes, high lipids
Over a few hours, very intense · can't stand the bedsheets touching it · may have fever
Less intense, slower to peak · may have fever
Blood count (white cells, platelets may rise) · creatinine · uric acid (may be normal during an attack) · fasting glucose, lipids

Rest, ice, elevation · steroid injected into the joint · oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) or cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitor (COXIB): indomethacin 50 mg by mouth three times daily · colchicine 0.6 mg every 8 hours · prednisone 30 mg daily × 2 days, then down 5 mg every 2 days
Rest, ice, elevation, hydration · steroid injected into the joint · oral NSAID or COXIB: indomethacin 50 mg three times daily · the same prednisone taper (no colchicine on the lecture's list)

blocks.cap: Polarized microscopy: needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent urate crystals (gout) vs rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate crystals (pseudogout)

blocks.html: 4. Gout in more detail

• "The disease of kings": acute inflammatory arthritis from uric acid crystals deposited in the joint
  • Hyperuricemia: production > excretion · under-excretion is the commonest reason · ⚠ many people with high uric acid never get gout → hyperuricemia CANNOT diagnose gout, and isolated hyperuricemia is not treated
  • Uric acid rises with age: steadily in men · in women only after menopause
  • Order of treatment (the overflowing sink): mop up first = treat the attack · then lower the level = treat the hyperuricemia if needed
  • Triggers (SMARTS): Surgery · Mechanical injury · Alcohol · Recent illness · Travel or dehydration · Starting or stopping allopurinol
  • Diagnosis: aspirate and find urate crystals - the only proof
  • Diet: meat and seafood are bad · vegetables and low-fat dairy are good · less alcohol · good hydration
  • Recurrence: 60% in 1 year · 80% in 2 · 90% in 5 - one attack makes another likely
  • Allopurinol (blocks xanthine oxidase - "turning off the tap")
    • consider for: recurrent attacks affecting lifestyle · tophi (urate deposits in skin and bone) · risk from repeated acute treatment · a patient who accepts lifelong treatment
    • ⚠ never start it during an acute attack · cover the start with an NSAID or colchicine · aim for uric acid at the lower limit of the laboratory reference range
  • Chronic gout: hyperuricemia for years → uric acid deposits in skin and bone (tophi) → urate-lowering (hypouricemic) treatment is indicated
5. Pseudogout in more detail

• Pseudogout = the attack (acute arthritis from calcium pyrophosphate crystals) · chondrocalcinosis = calcium pyrophosphate seen in cartilage on X-ray (the lecture's knee film: a line in the joint cartilage)
  • Starts quickly and intensely, but less intense than gout and slower to peak · untreated, several days to a few weeks
  • Diagnosis: aspirate and find intracellular calcium pyrophosphate crystals

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Acute < 6 weeks, chronic > 6 weeks; the most common cause of an acute monoarthritis is infection, and an infectious monoarthritis is probably bacterial (viral is usually polyarticular)
  • Colchicine is also listed for pseudogout (the polyarthritis lecture lists it for both crystal arthritides; this lecture lists it for gout only)

lectures.name: MSK Infections
lectures.title: MSK infections
lectures.framing: First decide how deep the infection goes - skin, a closed space in the hand, a joint, or bone - because depth decides the treatment. Skin infections get antibiotics; pus in a closed space, a joint or dead bone needs drainage or debridement too: antibiotics alone will not save you.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Depth decides treatment: cellulitis (dorsal hand, irregular edge) gets antibiotics; a closed-space hand infection, an infected joint or dead bone needs drainage or debridement too - antibiotics alone will not save you. Kanavel's 4 signs = flexor tenosynovitis. Cat bite → Pasteurella; human bite → Eikenella. Several infected joints → think endocarditis. MRI is the most sensitive test for osteomyelitis; vertebral osteomyelitis = blood cultures + MRI spine, 6 weeks of IV vancomycin + ceftriaxone. A diabetic foot wound is not always infected, and a swab always grows something.

blocks.html: 1. An acutely swollen joint or soft tissue

• Musculoskeletal infections can sit in: joint · bone · tendon sheath (tenosynovitis) · bursa (bursitis) · muscle (pyomyositis, myositis) · skin and soft tissue (cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis)
  • Differential of an acute monoarthritis: infectious (bacterial, viral, mycobacterial, fungal) · crystal (gout, calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD)) · inflammatory (reactive arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoid) · trauma · blood (hemarthrosis) · malignant
  • History: onset · which joints · fever, rash · exposures (intravenous (IV) drug use, sexual contact, travel) · past medical and social history, past procedures · immune-compromising conditions, inflammatory joint disease (rheumatoid arthritis)
  • Exam: vital signs · effusion, redness, old scar, rash · warmth, a subtler effusion felt, compare with the other side · range of motion and function limited by pain · red flags for infection: fever, pain, a big loss of range of motion
  • Septic arthritis of one joint (also on the acute monoarthritis chart, 04 - Acute Monoarthritis)
    • How: blood-borne seeding or direct inoculation · risk: immune compromise, type 2 diabetes, alcohol, age over 80, IV drug use, rheumatoid arthritis · the joint is a "synovial Petri dish": inflammation → joint damage
    • Organisms: adults - S. aureus (methicillin-sensitive and methicillin-resistant (MRSA)) · streptococci (group A, also B, C, G) · rarely gram-negative bacilli · children - S. aureus, streptococci
    • Investigations: blood count, electrolytes, creatinine, C-reactive protein · blood cultures · joint aspirate (cell count, cut-offs over 20 000 and over 50 000 · microscopy for crystals · Gram stain) · ± imaging · keep the differential open: coagulopathy, HIV, travel
    • Treatment = surgery (incision and drainage) + antibiotics: joint decompression · irrigation (removes the organisms and the proteolytic and lysosomal enzymes) · debridement of dead soft tissue · goal: keep the synovium as an immune-competent natural barrier
    • Empiric: cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours vs vancomycin 15 mg/kg + ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours · course 2-4 weeks by the references, in practice S. aureus 4-6 weeks
    • Older patient, septic or gout? both may be febrile · septic: high white count, positive culture or Gram stain · gout: joint fluid 20 000-50 000, monosodium urate crystals on microscopy
2. Hand infections

blocks.lead: Hands are often injured and have closed compartments, joints, a nail fold, a pulp space and tendon sheaths: the key is telling cellulitis from a deep (closed-space) infection.
rows: Dorsal hand, wrist to the knuckles
Incision and drainage, wound care, antibiotics
Cat: finger (proximal or distal interphalangeal) joints · human: young men, fights, knuckle (metacarpophalangeal) joint
Incision and drainage, wound care, antibiotics
Incision and drainage, wound care, antibiotics
Incision and drainage, wound care, antibiotics

blocks.html:
• Kanavel's signs: ① whole finger swollen ② flexed posture ③ tender along the tendon sheath ④ intense pain during extension
  • Rest and elevation for both superficial and deep infections
3. Joint infections beyond staphylococcus and streptococcus

rows: Young, multiple partners, men who have sex with men · female > male
Large-joint monoarthritis (or oligo): knee, wrist, ankle
Blood culture · gonorrhea nucleic acid test (NAAT) or culture of urine, rectum, throat · joint fluid (positive in 50%)
Lyme serology · joint fluid Lyme polymerase chain reaction (PCR) (lower yield)

blocks.html:
• Infectious polyarthritis: bacterial → THINK ENDOCARDITIS · viral → parvovirus B19 (with anemia), chikungunya, Zika, dengue (travel), hepatitis B and C, HIV
  • Reactive arthritis follows a gut or genitourinary infection by several days to weeks (also on the seronegative arthritides chart)
    • mono- or oligoarticular · also dactylitis and enthesitis · a small subset has Reiter syndrome: urethritis, conjunctivitis, arthritis · HLA-B27
    • gut: Campylobacter (especially C. jejuni), Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, C. difficile · genitourinary: Chlamydia trachomatis (also C. pneumoniae, E. coli, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Mycoplasma genitalium)
  • Prosthetic joint infection: high index of suspicion · early vs late · less virulent organisms (coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes) · best managed by the orthopedic surgeon (the one who operated, or a tertiary referral centre) + infectious diseases
4. Osteomyelitis and discitis

• Osteomyelitis = infection of bone
  • Routes: blood-borne (vertebral osteomyelitis, most childhood osteomyelitis) · not blood-borne, usually a contiguous focus (direct inoculation from trauma, after surgery, the diabetic foot)
  • Why it persists: bacteria adhere (fibrinogen, adhesins, biofilm) and hide inside osteoblasts · acute inflammation, edema and small-vessel thrombosis → impaired blood supply → dead bone (sequestrum) in chronic disease
  • Who: adults - diabetic foot · vertebral osteomyelitis in people who inject drugs and middle-aged men · Pott's disease (tuberculosis) · trauma, surgery · sacral wounds · children - under 12, the metaphysis (vascular) · S. aureus always · Salmonella in sickle cell disease · Kingella, other gram-negatives
  • Imaging: X-ray, CT not sensitive enough · MRI most sensitive (and the one for vertebral osteomyelitis) but stays abnormal after cure · don't routinely repeat imaging in a patient improving on treatment · nuclear tagged white cell scan takes 2 days
  • Vertebral osteomyelitis (spondylodiscitis): severe back pain, may be afebrile, check strength, reflexes, sensation, anal tone, saddle anesthesia · blood cultures + MRI spine (± spinal biopsy) · watch for a paravertebral or epidural abscess · IV vancomycin + ceftriaxone, 6 weeks · neurosurgery if the cord is compressed
    • MRI in the lecture case: marrow edema and enhancement in two adjacent bodies (L3, L4), irregular endplates = spondylodiscitis · ask about exposures: tuberculosis, Brucella · Mycobacterium bovis after BCG treatment for bladder cancer
  • Sacral wound osteomyelitis: chronicity? offloading? debridement needed? → culture, plastic surgery, offloading · trauma, clavicle: polymicrobial? tetanus?
  • Cure depends on: vascular supply · chronicity · whether debridement is needed · patient engagement · high antibiotic doses (e.g. ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours) · oral antibiotics did as well as IV in bone and joint infection

blocks.cap: Osteomyelitis progression: focal seeding, then pressure and necrosis, then sequestrum and involucrum in chronic disease

blocks.html: 5. Diabetic foot infection

• Assess: is it truly infected? (a wound is not always infected, and any swab grows bacteria) · chronicity · systemic symptoms · why it happened (new shoes, new job on the feet, not wearing a prescribed boot, diabetic control, vascular disease, Charcot foot, prior ulcers)
  • Exam: location · blood supply? (foot pulses, ankle-brachial index if indicated) · smell · probe to bone? · neuropathy: 10 g monofilament + one more (128 Hz tuning fork vibration, pinprick, ankle reflexes or vibration threshold) · skin, deformity (claw toes, Charcot), footwear, gait
  • Grade: mild - skin and subcutaneous tissue (likely staphylococcus or streptococcus) · moderate - erythema over 2 cm or deeper structures · severe - moderate + systemic inflammatory response
    • infected = at least 2 of: swelling or induration, redness, tenderness, warmth, pus · mild redness 0.5-2 cm around the ulcer · systemic inflammatory response = 2 or more of temperature over 38 °C or under 36 °C, heart rate over 90, breathing over 20 a minute, white count over 12 000 or under 4000
  • Investigations: blood count, electrolytes, creatinine, C-reactive protein · swab only if it looks infected and a good (deep) specimen can be had · X-ray first, MRI most sensitive, tagged white cell scan 2 days
  • Treatment: vascular supply (revascularization?), debridement, offloading, patient engagement - antibiotics alone will not save you · involve orthopedics, plastic or vascular surgery
    • monomicrobial (staphylococcus, streptococcus) → cefazolin (or oral cephalexin, doxycycline, amoxicillin-clavulanate)
    • polymicrobial (chronic ulcer, gram-negatives ± Pseudomonas) → amoxicillin-clavulanate; severe → IV ceftriaxone + metronidazole · Pseudomonas on the swab → piperacillin-tazobactam
    • severe: exclude necrotizing fasciitis · blood cultures · call orthopedics (or vascular) · piperacillin-tazobactam ± vancomycin (MRSA history or risk)
    • IV choices at a glance: cefazolin (S. aureus) · ceftriaxone + metronidazole (polymicrobial) · piperacillin-tazobactam (Pseudomonas) · ± vancomycin (MRSA colonization)

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html: • Osteomyelitis is the main complication of a diabetic foot infection; it is hard to treat

lectures.name: Osteoarthritis
lectures.title: Osteoarthritis
lectures.framing: A chronic single joint that hurts with use is osteoarthritis (OA) until a red flag says otherwise. It is a clinical diagnosis: the X-ray stages it, it does not make it. Then ask the four questions: what stage? which biomechanical factors can be fixed? is there a role for medicines? do they need surgery? No treatment yet preserves the joint; every one aims to improve life with it.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Osteoarthritis is a clinical diagnosis - activity-related pain, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, a cool joint, no red flags - and the X-ray only stages it. A warm joint is not OA. OA is not wear and tear: it is a whole "sick joint" that fails to heal. Only active, exercise-based therapy works; passive therapies do not. No drug preserves the joint. Joint replacement is for end-stage disease only; arthroscopy is not recommended.

blocks.html: 1. Chronic monoarthritis: the differential

• 1. Osteoarthritis · 2. osteoarthritis · 3. osteoarthritis · 4. chronic crystal arthritis (gout, pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate deposition, CPPD), basic calcium phosphate)
  • First tell it apart from mechanical or sports causes of chronic knee pain (no arthritis)
  • Less commonly: inflammatory (autoimmune) arthritis (rheumatoid, seronegative, juvenile idiopathic arthritis) · neuropathic (Charcot) joint (diabetes, syphilis) · chronic infection (atypical mycobacteria, with immunosuppression) · neoplasm (pigmented villonodular synovitis, synovial chondromatosis) · avascular necrosis or spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee
2. Diagnosis and staging

• Presentation of chronic OA monoarthritis
    • one joint: knee >> hip; ankle; shoulder >> big toe (1st metatarsophalangeal joint) · thumb base and hand joints usually come with a polyarthritis
    • pain, aching or stiffness brought on or worsened by activity · not chronic widespread pain (think something else)
    • morning stiffness under 30 minutes (usually under 5)
    • exam: joint tenderness · cool or similar-temperature effusion (not warm or hot) · joint thickening · crepitus
  • Diagnosis = must have + must not have
    • must have: joint pain, stiffness or aching on most days, chronic (over 6 weeks), worse with activity
    • must not have (red flags): infection · autoimmune disease (rheumatoid, seronegative spondyloarthritis) · malignancy · injury (fracture) · avascular necrosis · or crystal disease, tendinopathy
  • X-ray: changes alone do NOT diagnose OA, but they are specific → use it to stage (early, established, late or end-stage) · also the classification criteria for OA research studies
    • what it shows: joint space narrowing and osteophytes · end stage: severe joint space narrowing, bone on bone
  • ⚠ MRI or bone scan: almost never - expensive; only to rule out other problems when the diagnosis of OA is in doubt

blocks.cap: Kellgren-Lawrence grades on knee X-rays: grades 1-2 early OA, grades 3-4 late to end-stage OA

blocks.html: • Kellgren-Lawrence (K/L) grade: 1-2 = early OA · 3-4 = late to end-stage OA
3. OA as a disease

• Epidemiology: 1 in 7 Canadian adults over age 20 · the most common joint disorder worldwide · symptomatic hip and knee OA is the 11th-leading cause of disability worldwide · most symptomatic knee OA starts at 35-55
    • disability = loss of mobility = poor quality of life
    • symptomatic knee OA prevalence rises exponentially in the 4th and 5th decades
  • Primary OA (the majority): risk factors but no clear cause - obesity and metabolic syndrome · ageing and senescence (cartilage thins, making the tissues more susceptible; age raises the risk but does not cause OA) · mechanical factors: joint trauma, alignment · polygenic genetic risk (family history) · female sex 1.4× · muscle weakness · occupation
  • Secondary OA: caused by an underlying disease or injury - post-traumatic (after an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) or meniscus tear) · metabolic or endocrine (acromegaly, hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis) · rare monogenic (Stickler, Marshall syndromes, skeletal and chondral dysplasias) · joints damaged by inflammatory autoimmune arthritis (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis)
    • post-traumatic OA is never "too young": anterior cruciate ligament tear at 23 → knee OA by 36 · over 50% risk of needing a knee replacement by 55, likely higher without goal-directed, evidence-based management
  • Pathophysiology: a "sick joint" - every joint tissue is affected · OA is NOT caused by wear and tear or age; risk factors make the tissues susceptible · chronic metabolic and physiologic stress → inflammation, pain, breakdown · joint failure (like heart failure) = failure of the tissues to heal → remove what impairs healing (obesity, inactivity)
4. Treatment

• The approach, four questions
    • what stage? early · late · end-stage
    • which biomechanical factors can be treated? alignment · overuse or repetitive injury · weakness · gait disturbance
    • is there a role for medical treatment? to improve pain, function, quality of life
    • do they need surgery (joint replacement)? only end-stage disease with unacceptable symptoms and impact on quality of life
  • Goals: non-drug and drug treatments improve symptoms (less pain, better function, less disability, better quality of life) · limited by cost, time and access
  • Non-drug (hip and knee): lose 5% of body weight · 150 minutes of activity a week (walk, swim, bike) · neuromuscular control (Tai-Chi, GLA:D) · walking aids, insoles, shoes, unloader brace · joint protection education · cognitive behavioural therapy · topical heat
    • physiotherapy means ACTIVE therapy: it must involve exercise, preferably neuromuscular for balance and strength · ✘ passive therapies (ultrasound, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), laser, acupuncture) are not recommended
    • education, usually by occupational therapy: protect the joint from what aggravates it · avoid risky movements
  • Drugs (hip and knee): topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) (diclofenac two or three times daily) · acetaminophen (clinically meaningful effect?) · oral NSAIDs if no contraindications · duloxetine (a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, SNRI) · intra-articular corticosteroid for short-term relief
    • inconclusive: herbal remedies, glucosamine, topical NSAIDs for the hip, injected hyaluronic acid, platelet-rich plasma, stem cells
    • opioids: generally avoid · tramadol is the one listed (other opioids: risks > benefit)
    • ✘ not recommended: opioids, neuropathic pain modulators, capsaicin, chondroitin
  • Stepwise, the lecture's late-stage knee (chronic renal failure): physiotherapy for neuromuscular strength and stability for at least 3 months + occupational therapy on safe movements → topical NSAIDs two or three times daily (avoid oral NSAIDs in chronic renal failure) → corticosteroid injection if still refractory → duloxetine (SNRI) trial for 2-3 months if still refractory → end stage on X-ray (bone on bone) despite all of it → refer to orthopedics for arthroplasty
  • Surgery: joint replacement = a salvage procedure for end-stage disease with unacceptable symptoms - strong evidence of benefit · ✘ knee arthroscopy (± meniscectomy or repair) has strong evidence of no meaningful benefit
    • goal: improve symptoms with a prosthesis that replaces the painful joint tissues · limited by cost, time and access

lectures.name: Approach to Polyarthritis
lectures.title: Approach to polyarthritis
lectures.framing: Several sore joints: is it inflammatory or degenerative, acute or chronic, and which joints in what pattern? Every inflammatory arthritis is a clinical diagnosis: the history (timing, pattern, risk factors) and the extra-articular clues get you there; tests narrow it down. Don't reflexively order an antinuclear antibody (ANA) and rheumatoid factor (RF) on every patient with joint pain - consider your differential first.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Symmetric small + large joint polyarthritis sparing the DIPs is rheumatoid arthritis; asymmetric with DIPs, dactylitis and psoriasis is psoriatic; axial with large peripheral joints is a spondyloarthropathy; symmetric weight-bearing is OA. Acute is 6 weeks or less. Red joint → aspirate. A negative ANA rules out connective tissue disease; a positive one rules nothing in. RF and anti-CCP are for diagnosis and prognosis, never for follow-up; anti-CCP is the specific one. Lupus and Sjögren's do not erode. Gout crystals are negative needles; pseudogout crystals are positive rhomboids.

blocks.html: 1. Classifying arthritis

• Type: inflammatory (an immune response attacks the joint: autoimmune · infectious · crystalline) vs non-inflammatory (degenerative = primary osteoarthritis (OA), or secondary OA, e.g. after inflammatory arthritis · cartilage breakdown from recurrent structural trauma · trauma · avascular necrosis · neuropathic (Charcot) · recurrent hemarthrosis · hemochromatosis)
  • Duration: acute 6 weeks or less · chronic over 6 weeks · Number: mono 1 joint · oligo 2-3 · poly 4 or more
  • Synovitis (inflamed synovium) = more fluid (swelling) · warmth · pain · stiffness · redness only with infection or crystals
2. Causes of inflammatory polyarthritis

rows: Polyarticular gout · infectious and post-infectious, including viral · rheumatic fever · drug reaction (serum sickness) · early rheumatoid, connective tissue disease, vasculitis or seronegative arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis · connective tissue disease (lupus, myositis, Sjögren's, scleroderma, mixed) · reactive arthritis · seronegative spondyloarthropathy (psoriatic, enteropathic) · palindromic rheumatism · systemic vasculitis · polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis · adult-onset Still's · sarcoidosis · drug reactions

blocks.html:
• Many acute polyarthritides become chronic if the basis is autoimmune
  • Acute differential: mainly inflammatory (infectious · early autoimmune · crystalline) · chronic: mainly established seropositive and seronegative autoimmune disease
  • Viral arthritis: during or weeks after the infection · self-limited, supportive care; if severe, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and a short prednisone course (the viruses: see 05 - MSK Infections)
3. History: timing, pattern, risk factors

• Onset: acute (hours to days) → crystal, infectious · insidious (weeks to months) → rheumatoid, connective tissue disease, degenerative
  • Course: episodic (comes and goes, usually acute, lasting days) → crystal · migratory → palindromic rheumatism, rheumatic fever, early gonococcal arthritis · progressive and additive → rheumatoid, connective tissue disease, degenerative
  • Pattern (small: metacarpophalangeal (MCP), proximal and distal interphalangeal (PIP, DIP), metatarsophalangeal (MTP), interphalangeal (IP) · medium/large: shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee, ankle · axial: spine, sacroiliac)

rows: Rheumatoid arthritis (other symmetric: lupus, connective tissue disease)
Primarily axial, with peripheral large joints

blocks.html:
• Joint clues: axial → ankylosing spondylitis · 1st carpometacarpal (thumb base) → OA · 1st MTP → gout, OA · DIPs → OA, psoriatic arthritis; spared in rheumatoid and other connective tissue diseases · MCPs → rheumatoid, calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) · wrists, shoulders, elbows, ankles → rheumatoid, CPPD, psoriatic
  • Other musculoskeletal findings: synovitis · tenosynovitis · dactylitis (sausage digit) · enthesitis (tendon insertion) · bursitis · deformities (nodules, Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes, swan-neck, boutonnière, ulnar deviation, MCP subluxation)
  • Risk factors: age, sex, ethnicity · family history (autoimmune disease · psoriasis · inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)) · triggers (infection, medication, injury, diet for gout) · comorbidities (psoriasis, IBD, chronic kidney disease)
  • Age: degenerative rare to start young, rises with age · inflammatory: rheumatoid arthritis and most connective tissue diseases peak around age 40, a second, later peak = elderly-onset rheumatoid arthritis

blocks.cap: Rheumatoid arthritis: symmetric small joints of the hands and feet plus large joints, with the distal interphalangeal joints spared
Osteoarthritis: distal and proximal interphalangeal joints, thumb base, big toe, and the weight-bearing hips, knees and spine

blocks.html: 4. Extra-articular manifestations

rows: Ulnar deviation and MCP subluxation · rheumatoid nodules · pulmonary nodules · episcleritis
Skin psoriasis · nail pitting, nail psoriasis · enthesitis · dactylitis · uveitis
<mark class="lo">Conjunctivitis · urethritis · arthritis ("can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree")</mark> · vesicopustular skin lesions
Malar rash · discoid lupus · oral ulcers · subacute lupus rash
Heliotrope · Gottron's sign and papules · shawl, V and holster signs · mechanic's hands

blocks.html: • By organ system: eyes (uveitis, scleritis, episcleritis, dry eyes (sicca)) · mouth (aphthous ulcers) · skin (malar rash, diffuse photosensitive rash, Gottron's, vasculitic rash, erythema nodosum, livedo reticularis, Raynaud's, tophi, nodules, keratoderma blenorrhagicum, skin thickening, sclerodactyly, calcinosis, digital ulcers) · nails (psoriasis, pitting, psoriatic nail dystrophy) · lungs (interstitial lung disease (ILD), pleural effusions, nodules) · heart (pericarditis, myocarditis) · kidney (glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis) · gut (esophageal dysmotility, IBD) · genitourinary (urethritis, genital ulcers) · blood (hemolytic anemia, low platelets, low lymphocytes) · constitutional (enlarged lymph nodes, fevers)
5. Investigations

• Routine: blood count (low hemoglobin = anemia of chronic disease · high platelets = inflammation · low platelets or white cells = autoimmune cytopenia) · creatinine · liver enzymes · C-reactive protein (CRP), the most used; erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) not routine
    • Creatinine: acute kidney injury in glomerulonephritis or vasculitis · drug clearance (NSAIDs, some disease-modifying drugs) · liver enzymes: drug clearance · autoimmune hepatitis goes with connective tissue disease · ESR is nonspecific, falsely raised by many things
  • Special: gout → uric acid · viral → serologies · ankylosing spondylitis → HLA-B27 (human leukocyte antigen B27) · CPPD → underlying causes (hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypothyroidism)
  • Rheumatoid factor (RF): IgM against IgG · rheumatoid arthritis (RA) 70-80% but also healthy people (5-20%, more with age), Sjögren's, lupus, myositis, mixed connective tissue disease, hepatitis B and C, tuberculosis, syphilis, endocarditis, chronic lung disease (idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, silicosis, sarcoidosis), lymphoma → neither sensitive nor specific · anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) 95% specific, may precede arthritis by years · order only when RA is suspected, never to monitor · seropositive = more aggressive
    • When to order: initial diagnosis only, e.g. true swollen joints plus raised inflammatory markers · titres do not predict flares or response to therapy · seropositive = more joints, erosions and X-ray progression, extra-articular disease
  • Antinuclear antibody (ANA): up to 30% of healthy people → a positive ANA does not rule in connective tissue disease; a negative one typically rules it out (the specific antibodies: 02 - Rheumatology Investigations)
    • Positive ANA also in: rheumatoid arthritis · ILD · other autoimmune disease (thyroid, autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, IBD, multiple sclerosis) · infection (tuberculosis, hepatitis, HIV, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, parvovirus) · lymphoma, leukemia · vaccinations
  • Extractable nuclear antigens (ENA): anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA), anti-Sm → lupus · anti-SSA/Ro, anti-SSB/La → Sjögren's · anti-centromere, anti-Scl70, anti-RNA polymerase 3 → scleroderma · anti-Jo1 → dermatomyositis · anti-ribonucleoprotein (anti-RNP) → mixed connective tissue disease · anti-histone → drug-induced lupus
  • Lupus activity: in a flare anti-dsDNA rises, complement C3 and C4 fall (consumed in the complement cascade) = seroconcordant · markers that do not move as expected = serodiscordant
  • Joint aspiration: inflammatory vs not, rule out infection and crystals; diagnostic ± therapeutic - fluid interpretation in 02 - Rheumatology Investigations
    • Fluid white cells: normal under 200 · non-inflammatory under 2000 · inflammatory over 2000, over 50% neutrophils, crystals possible · infectious over 2000, over 75% neutrophils, Gram stain and culture positive
    • Crystals: urate (gout) = needles, negatively birefringent (yellow) · calcium pyrophosphate (CPPD) = rhomboid or rods, positively birefringent (blue)
  • X-rays: little help in acute polyarthritis (damage takes years) · inflammatory: periarticular osteopenia, soft-tissue swelling, symmetric narrowing, erosions (RA, psoriatic and other spondyloarthritis, gout, septic - not lupus or Sjögren's) · degenerative: osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts, asymmetric narrowing
    • Also inflammatory: periostitis · deformities (subluxation, deviation) · degenerative: erosions only in erosive OA · deviation from extra bone growth · joint distribution matters
    • Useful for: inflammatory vs degenerative in longstanding symptoms · telling inflammatory types apart · baseline before treatment · progressive damage despite treatment
6. Management, briefly

• Non-drug: gentle physiotherapy · muscle strengthening · cool or warm compresses · rest
  • Drugs: acetaminophen, NSAIDs · corticosteroids (prednisone, intramuscular Depo-Medrol, joint injection) · disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs): conventional (methotrexate), targeted (tofacitinib), biologic (adalimumab) · gout: colchicine, NSAIDs, steroids, allopurinol, febuxostat · pseudogout: colchicine, NSAIDs, steroids
  • Detail in the disease lectures and 03 - Rheumatology Treatments

blocks.html:
• RA: warm, swollen, not red; > 60 minutes of morning stiffness; palindromic onset possible; x-ray unhelpful early
  • Crystalline polyarthritis: gout = small joints of the foot, CPPD = knee; acute, red

lectures.name: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis
lectures.title: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
lectures.framing: A child with a joint swollen for more than 6 weeks and no other cause: which of the seven subtypes is it? The subtype, set by fever and rash, or how many joints in the first 6 months, decides the uveitis screening and the treatment. What makes children different from adults is growth and silent uveitis.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A young ANA-positive girl with oligoarticular JIA has the highest risk of silent uveitis, so she needs slit lamp screening every 3 months whatever her joints are doing. Oligoarticular = 4 or fewer joints, a painless limp, almost never the hip. Systemic = daily spiking fever + salmon rash, mistaken for infection or leukemia, risk of macrophage activation syndrome, interleukin-1 or -6 blockers. Enthesitis-related = boys over 10, HLA-B27, painful red eye, 30% become ankylosing spondylitis. ANA prognosticates, it does not diagnose.

blocks.html: 1. Definition and presentation

• Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA): onset under 16 · 1 or more joints · lasting over 6 weeks · other causes excluded (a diagnosis of exclusion)
    • the diagnosis is clinical: bloodwork and imaging are adjuncts
  • The most common chronic rheumatic disease of childhood (about 1 in 1000 Canadian children), rarer than adult inflammatory arthritis (1%) · most subtypes more common in girls · rare before 6 months
  • Presents as: joint pain with inflammatory features: morning stiffness, better with movement, responds to NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) · usually subacute or chronic · altered weight-bearing, functional loss parents notice · may have extra-articular features
  • Red flags (think of something else): constitutional symptoms · acute onset · severe pain · can't walk · night pain waking the child · severe tenderness or redness of the joint
2. The seven subtypes

rows: 4 or fewer joints, 1-2 at first: knee, ankle, wrist, elbow · warm, swollen, not very tender → "painless limp" · almost never the hip
5 or more joints in the first 6 months, slow onset · fewer joints, asymmetric · stiff 60+ min after inactivity · fatigue

Spiking fevers ≥ 39 °C once or twice daily, late afternoon, well between · evanescent salmon rash with the fever · aches without swelling early, effusions later · unwell during the fever, better when it settles · big liver and spleen, nodes, serositis · lethargy, weight loss, growth disturbance · often thought to be infection or leukemia
White cells and platelets high, anemia · the most serious subtype
Enthesitis · sacroiliitis · dactylitis · may have peripheral joints · family history of ankylosing spondylitis, bowel disease, psoriasis, uveitis, reactive arthritis
HLA-B27 in 50% · uveitis symptomatic (pain, photophobia, decreased vision), often recurrent, may be both eyes · often a good prognosis, but 30% develop ankylosing spondylitis
Family history of psoriasis · nail pitting, onycholysis (nail lifting) · dactylitis
Fits none of the categories, or 2 or more (e.g. oligoarthritis + family history of psoriasis + HLA-B27)

blocks.html:
• Oligoarticular prognosis is usually good, in thirds: ⅓ no other joints, may remit for good · ⅓ 1-2 more joints but 4 or fewer in total · ⅓ extend to many joints ("extended course")
  • The "twins" (enthesitis-related and psoriatic) are the childhood forms of the adult seronegative spondyloarthropathies
3. Complications: a growing skeleton

• Untreated synovitis over time → muscle atrophy · joint contracture · joint damage and deformity · leg length discrepancy
  • Growth: general growth slows during active disease · local: shortening or lengthening of a limb · micrognathia (small jaw)
    • the inflamed joint first shows advanced maturation (early ossification: carpal bones, patella), then growth arrest
    • early epiphyseal closure → short limb or small mandible · inflamed during adolescence → delayed closure → long limb
  • X-ray: soft tissue swelling, effusion, periarticular osteopenia · joint space loss and erosion uncommon · ankylosis of the neck and wrist possible
  • Morbidity: uveitis → blindness · functional disability · rarely joint replacement · growth disturbance · lower rates of finishing school and reaching work goals · macrophage activation syndrome in systemic JIA
  • A big impact on growth and development and on the physical, social and emotional functioning of the child and family · early detection and referral prevent morbidity

blocks.cap: Accelerated ossification: more carpal bones have appeared in the inflamed right wrist than the left in a 2-year-old

blocks.html: 4. Uveitis

• Anterior uveitis is the most common extra-articular feature · mostly in the first 4 years of JIA
  • Typically asymptomatic (except in enthesitis-related) and does not track the arthritis, so regular slit lamp screening · untreated → synechiae, glaucoma, cataract, band keratopathy, cystoid macular edema, blindness
  • Risk factors: ANA positive · girl · young · recent onset
  • Screening interval by subtype, age at onset, disease duration and ANA
    • ANA-positive oligo- or polyarticular, onset at 6 or under → every 3 months for the first 4 years, then 6 months for the next 3
    • every other oligo- or polyarticular child → every 6 months (7 years if onset at 6 or under · 4 years if onset over 6)
    • then yearly · systemic → yearly throughout
  • Treatment: steroid drops → oral steroids → methotrexate → biologics (infliximab, adalimumab) · uveitis can drive treatment on its own

blocks.cap: Anterior, intermediate and posterior uveitis; JIA mostly causes the anterior form

blocks.html: 5. Exam and investigations

• Pediatric gait, arms, legs and spine screen (pGALS) for: a child with muscle, joint or bone pain · an unwell child with fever, constitutional symptoms or rash · a limp · delayed or lost motor milestones · a chronic disease with known musculoskeletal (MSK) involvement
    • watch standing (posture, rashes such as psoriasis, deformity: leg length, knee or ankle valgus or varus, scoliosis, swelling, muscle wasting, flat feet) and walking
    • arms: hands out straight · turn hands over and make a fist · pinch index finger and thumb · touch the fingertips · squeeze the metacarpophalangeal joints · hands behind the neck
    • legs and spine: knee effusion (patella tap or cross-fluctuation: a small one can be missed by the tap alone) · knees bend and straighten, feel for crepitus · hip flexion and internal rotation, knee at 90° · ear to shoulder (neck) · bend forward and touch the toes (spine, scoliosis)
    • the extras over adult GALS (gait, arms, legs, spine): walk on heels · walk on tiptoes · palms together, backs together · reach up "touch the sky" and look at the ceiling · open wide, three of the child's own fingers in the mouth (temporomandibular joints)
  • Bloods support and exclude, they do not diagnose
    • complete blood count: white cells and platelets high in systemic JIA · anemia (normocytic or microcytic)
    • erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP): normal or raised
    • ANA predicts uveitis risk, it does NOT diagnose JIA · RF classifies and prognosticates polyarticular JIA · HLA-B27 for enthesitis-related
  • X-ray: rule out other causes (tumour), especially with one joint · compare the other side
6. Treatment

• Goals: short term: relieve discomfort, preserve function, prevent deformity, control inflammation · long term: limit side effects, normal growth and development, rehabilitation, school and psychosocial support
  • Team: pediatric rheumatologist · physiotherapist · occupational therapist · nurse · ophthalmologist · family doctor or pediatrician · social worker · psychologist · teacher
  • Non-drug, for everyone: education and psychological support · physiotherapy (range of motion, fitness) · occupational therapy (aids) · nutrition
  • First steps for a new child: preliminary investigations · start an NSAID · refer to rheumatology AND optometry or ophthalmology · family doctors should be able to do the pGALS screen

rows: NSAIDs and/or steroid joint injection · NSAIDs: naproxen, indomethacin, piroxicam, meloxicam, diclofenac, celecoxib
Not improving or extended → treat as polyarticular
NSAIDs · steroid injection or oral steroid bridge
Shared decision with the family: etanercept, adalimumab, tocilizumab, abatacept
Fever persists → anakinra (interleukin-1 blocker) or tocilizumab (interleukin-6 blocker)
No fever → treat as oligo- or polyarticular
Axial → anti-TNF (tumour necrosis factor blockers) · topical steroids for uveitis

lectures.name: Connective Tissue Disorders
lectures.title: Connective tissue disorders
lectures.framing: Connective tissue is in every organ, so these autoimmune diseases are multi-system, more common in women, usually antinuclear antibody (ANA) positive, often with Raynaud's. The lecture's five: SLE, Sjögren's, systemic sclerosis, inflammatory myositis and mixed connective tissue disease. Tell them apart by the signature feature and the specific antibody, then treat by which organ is involved and how badly.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A negative ANA makes lupus highly unlikely; a positive ANA proves nothing, so order anti-DNA only when the ANA is positive. Hydroxychloroquine is the anchor drug for every lupus patient. The malar rash spares the nasolabial folds; the discoid rash scars. Anti-DNA and anti-Smith point to lupus, anti-Ro/La to Sjögren's, anti-Jo-1 to myositis with lung disease, anticentromere to limited and anti-Scl-70 to diffuse scleroderma. Dermatomyositis in an older adult can be paraneoplastic. Scleroderma renal crisis → ACE inhibitor. APS with fetal loss → ASA + heparin, not warfarin.

blocks.html: 1. Telling them apart

rows: 1 in 1000 · women 9:1, young (the most common)
Half of cases with SLE · in 10-20% of SLE
Rash in the sun · oral ulcers · non-erosive arthritis · serositis · kidney · counts down
Recurrent clots (arteries or veins) or recurrent pregnancy loss · livedo reticularis · low platelets
Dry eyes + dry mouth (sicca) · parotid swelling · dental caries
Proximal weakness (shoulders, hips, neck), high creatine kinase (CK) · dermato: heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules, mechanic's hands · poly: no rash
Tight skin (sclerodactyly) · Raynaud's in nearly all · dysphagia, reflux · fingertip ulcers
Anticardiolipin · lupus anticoagulant · false-positive Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) syphilis test · must be persistent
ANA over 95% · limited: anticentromere · diffuse: anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I; lung fibrosis), anti-nucleolar, anti-RNA polymerase (renal crisis)
Kidney · brain (seizure, psychosis) · cardiovascular events from early atherosclerosis · infection
Cancer (dermatomyositis, older adults) · swallowing and aspiration · heart rhythm · interstitial lung disease
Highest mortality of all: lung fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, heart, renal crisis
Hydroxychloroquine for everyone + steroids by severity

blocks.html:
• Choose the best disease (the lecture's own drill): proximal weakness + high CK → polymyositis · the same + new Raynaud's + rash over the knuckles → dermatomyositis · dry eyes and mouth → Sjögren's · rash in the sun + oral ulcers → SLE · dysphagia, Raynaud's, fingertip ulcers, sclerodactyly → systemic sclerosis · repeated clots + livedo → APS · not specific: interstitial lung disease, Raynaud's, a positive ANA
    • the lecture's cases: sun rash, mouth and nose sores, ANA + anti-DNA, blood and protein in the urine → SLE · dry eyes and mouth with new repeated cavities, parotid swelling, anti-Ro, anti-La, purpura on the shins → Sjögren's · retrosternal dysphagia, tight skin of hands, arms and face, crackles at the lung bases, nucleolar ANA, anti-Scl-70 → systemic sclerosis
2. Lupus: what to look for

• Classification criteria, not diagnostic criteria (made to standardise research groups)
    • 1982 American College of Rheumatology (ACR): at least 4 of 11, for over 6 weeks (below) · many still use it · a second set from the SLE International Co-operating Clinics (SLICC)
    • 2019 EULAR/ACR (European and American rheumatology bodies): ANA ≥ 1:80 required + 10 or more points, at least one clinical domain, highest item per domain, "ever had" counts, nothing with another explanation
  • Lupus can be systemic (SLE) or skin only (cutaneous) · subacute cutaneous lupus: widespread, non-scarring, photosensitive rash (upper back, shoulders, arms, neck; face often spared), usually anti-Ro positive, in either form
  • Lupus loves rashes: besides the three in the criteria, livedo reticularis and vasculitis (small vessel = leukocytoclastic · larger vessel = the digital arteries)

rows: Fixed redness over the cheeks and nose, spares the nasolabial folds · photosensitive · presenting feature in under ⅓ · not rosacea, which has dilated vessels, isn't autoimmune and doesn't spare the folds
Raised patches with adherent scale and follicular plugging · head, neck, arms, hands · heals with scarring
Often several, sometimes painless, witnessed, no other cause
Pleuritis (worse breathing in, effusion) · pericarditis (worse lying down, effusion, ECG changes)

Glomerulonephritis: protein + blood in urine, a rising creatinine is bad · World Health Organization classes: 1 normal or minimal change · 2 mesangial · 3 focal proliferative · 4 diffuse proliferative (the worst) · 5 membranous
Seizures or psychosis with no drug or metabolic cause (uremia, ketoacidosis, electrolytes)

Hemolytic anemia (Coombs positive, reticulocytes, large mean corpuscular volume) · white cells under 4.0 or lymphocytes under 1.55, on 2 or more occasions · platelets under 100,000 with no offending drug · antibodies break the cells apart
Screening test: over 95% of SLE positive, so negative makes SLE highly unlikely; never rules in (many healthy people are positive; the commonest cause of a positive ANA is no obvious cause)
Anti-double-stranded DNA · anti-Smith · antiphospholipid (anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, false-positive VDRL because the test uses a phospholipid membrane) · lupus loves to make antibodies

blocks.cap: Lupus hand: ulnar deviation without erosions - the deformity is ligamentous and reducible

blocks.html: 3. Lupus: tests, cause, treatment

• Tests serve three jobs: diagnosis, prognosis, treatment safety: complete blood count · ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) · creatinine and urinalysis · ANA · maybe the extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) panel and complement (C3, C4, CH50) · pregnancy test
    • don't order anti-DNA unless the ANA is positive (it cannot be positive with a negative ANA) · test interpretation is in 02 - Rheumatology Investigations
    • the lecture's case: 22-year-old with malar rash, rash in the sun, morning stiffness and swollen knuckles, Raynaud's, hair loss, fatigue, weight loss · white cells 2.8, hemoglobin 111, platelets 43, urine clear · ANA 1:320 speckled, anti-Smith positive, anti-DNA negative, C3 and C4 low → SLE (at least 5 criteria)
  • Cause: genes (polygenic; interleukin-6, X chromosome, human leukocyte antigen (HLA) DR2 and DR3, complement pathway) + environment (smoking, infection, ultraviolet light, silica, hormones, drugs) · B cells overactive, T cells talk more with fewer suppressors · type I interferon and the nuclear factor kappa B pathway · more nuclear "garbage" (apoptosis), cleared slowly · rarely drug-induced (milder: joints, skin, serositis)
  • Non-drug: education · rest · sun avoidance (sun worsens the rash and can activate systemic disease), sun protection factor (SPF) 30+ · physiotherapy and occupational therapy · rheumatology follow-up · cardiovascular risk (smoking, blood pressure, lipids, diabetes) · clotting risk
  • Drugs, by organ and severity (minor = skin, joints, mucositis; major = internal organs)
    • hydroxychloroquine for every patient unless contraindicated: the anchor drug, may protect against major flares, especially helps skin and joints · an antimalarial, like chloroquine
    • minor: non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for joints · topical steroid for rash · low-dose prednisone for mild-moderate arthritis
    • major: high-dose steroids + mycophenolate or azathioprine · cyclophosphamide only for serious major organ disease (tacrolimus, cyclosporine less often) · methotrexate sometimes for skin and joints · biologic belimumab (less B-cell signalling)
    • the European treatment chart: hydroxychloroquine at every severity · rituximab for severe refractory disease · adjuncts: sun protection, vaccinations, exercise, no smoking, weight, blood pressure, lipids, glucose, antiplatelets or anticoagulants if antiphospholipid positive · target: remission, or low disease activity on prednisone 7.5 mg a day or less
  • Prognosis: worse with major organ disease · die from cardiovascular events (50× more), infection, SLE, drug complications (avascular necrosis, osteoporosis)
4. Antiphospholipid syndrome

• Antibodies attack phospholipids on cells and vessel linings → recurrent arterial or venous clots, or recurrent pregnancy loss, with the antibodies persistently present
  • Primary (no other autoimmune disease, may be autosomal dominant) or secondary (with SLE)
  • Antibodies: anticardiolipin · lupus anticoagulant (falsely prolongs the partial thromboplastin time) · false-positive VDRL · abnormal Russell viper venom time
  • Livedo reticularis: lacy red or purple mottling with distinct borders, not raised, no symptoms, comes and goes · with low platelets

rows: Intravenous (IV) heparin + IV steroids ± plasmapheresis or IV immunoglobulin

blocks.html: 5. Sjögren's and myositis

• Sjögren's: lymphocytes infiltrate exocrine glands → gritty dry eyes worse through the day · dry mouth (dry food hard to swallow, taste change, cavities, bad breath) · parotid swelling
    • beyond the glands: Raynaud's · leg purpura (small-vessel vasculitis) · arthritis · neuropathy · rarely interstitial lung disease · higher risk of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma
    • labs: anemia of chronic disease · low white cells · raised immunoglobulins → very high ESR
  • Inflammatory myositis: proximal weakness (shoulders, hips, neck; trouble getting out of bed)
    • rule out the other causes of proximal weakness first: drugs (steroids, colchicine, hydroxychloroquine, cyclosporine, statins) · toxins (alcohol) · endocrine (thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal) · electrolytes (potassium high or low, low phosphate, low magnesium) · infiltrative (sarcoidosis) · infection · inflammatory · malignancy-related
    • dermatomyositis: peaks in children and older adults; in older adults may be paraneoplastic (adenocarcinoma: ovary, stomach, lung, cervix) · polymyositis: any age · no rash · usually not cancer-linked
    • dermatomyositis skin: dilated nailbed capillaries · heliotrope rash (purple or pink around the eyes) · Gottron's papules (raised, over the knuckles; Gottron's sign when flat) · photosensitive V-neck or cape rash · mechanic's hands · livedo reticularis · calcinosis · rashes often match specific antibodies
    • antisynthetase syndrome: antibodies against aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases → myositis, arthralgia, Raynaud's, mechanic's hands, interstitial lung disease
    • investigations: creatine kinase raised · ESR up in half · ANA 80% · anti-Jo-1 (interstitial lung disease, bad prognosis) · PM/Scl: scleroderma-polymyositis overlap · watch swallowing (aspiration), heart (arrhythmia), lungs (interstitial disease or a weak diaphragm)
    • treatment: high-dose steroids → steroid-sparing (azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, IV immunoglobulin, rituximab) · prevent steroid osteoporosis · lung disease needs aggressive treatment
6. Systemic sclerosis

• Scleroderma is non-systemic (linear, morphea) or systemic (systemic sclerosis) · 2013 ACR/EULAR classification criteria
  • Fibrosis + vascular instability (intimal proliferation, Raynaud's) + autoimmunity · skin tightening of the fingers (sclerodactyly), tendons tight too

rows: Distal to elbows and knees (fingers, face)
ANA over 95% · anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I, 30%), nucleolar ANA (50%), anti-RNA polymerase (renal crisis)
Pulmonary arterial hypertension, late and in older patients
Interstitial lung disease (fibrosis) · may get pulmonary hypertension

blocks.html:
• 15% rule: nearly all have Raynaud's and reflux; many dysphagia; half ever have digital ulcers; 15% each have a current ulcer, significant lung disease, pulmonary hypertension, arthritis, Sjögren's, myositis · 15% of ulcers are complicated · 15% of diffuse get renal crisis
  • Causes of death: lung fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, heart · renal crisis less now, thanks to ACE inhibitors
  • ⚠ Scleroderma renal crisis: high blood pressure + hemolysis + failing kidneys · over 80% die if not recognised · rapid blood pressure control with ACE inhibitors (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, e.g. captopril, enalapril) cut the death rate · highest risk in early diffuse disease · may be the first presentation · some need dialysis
  • Raynaud's: primary (no disease, often no drug) vs secondary (over 95% of scleroderma) · treat with cold avoidance, stopping smoking, nifedipine (calcium channel blocker, the main drug); others: phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE5) inhibitors, topical nitrates, IV prostacyclin (iloprost), other vasodilators
    • reversible colour change of the digits: pallor, then red and/or blue · 3% of everyone, 25-98% in connective tissue diseases, most severe in systemic sclerosis
  • ⚠ Raynaud's + dilated nailfold capillaries + anticentromere → ⅓ develop scleroderma within 5 years
  • Management: treat the organs involved · methotrexate softens skin early in diffuse disease · tocilizumab (anti-interleukin-6), rituximab (B-cell depletion) may help skin and lung, more trials needed · autologous stem cell transplant for severe early diffuse disease with high predicted mortality

blocks.html: • Limited systemic sclerosis is the old CREST: calcinosis, Raynaud's, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia

lectures.name: Seronegative Arthridites
lectures.title: Seronegative arthritides
lectures.framing: A family of inflammatory arthritides that are rheumatoid factor negative and HLA-B27 linked: spine and sacroiliac joints, entheses, sausage digits and uveitis. Ankylosing spondylitis is the prototype; the others are told apart by what comes with the joints: psoriasis, a recent infection, or bowel disease.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Back pain that starts under 40, creeps in over months, stiffens for over an hour in the morning, wakes them at night and gets better with exercise is inflammatory: think ankylosing spondylitis and image the sacroiliac joints. Seronegative = rheumatoid factor negative, HLA-B27 linked. Psoriatic arthritis: asymmetric, distal interphalangeal joints, dactylitis, nail changes; avoid hydroxychloroquine. Reactive arthritis: young man, gut or genital infection 1-3 weeks before, can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree. Conventional DMARDs don't help spinal disease; TNF and IL-17 inhibitors do.

blocks.html: 1. The family

• Spondyloarthritis (SpA) = inflammation of the spine and spinal joints, but it can be purely peripheral with no back symptoms
  • Enthesitis = inflammation where a ligament, tendon or joint capsule inserts into bone, ending in new bone or fibrosis
  • "Seronegative" because rheumatoid factor is absent · linked to HLA-B27 (human leukocyte antigen B27)
  • Members: ankylosing spondylitis (the prototype) · psoriatic arthritis · reactive arthritis · arthritis with Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis · acute anterior uveitis · undifferentiated · juvenile (enthesitis-related)
  • What points to SpA
    • symptoms: inflammatory back pain · peripheral arthritis · enthesitis (heel) · anterior uveitis
    • imaging: sacroiliitis on X-ray or MRI
    • labs: raised ESR and CRP (erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein) · HLA-B27 · family history
    • predisposing diseases: infection (Chlamydia) · psoriasis · Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis
    • history: good response to NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs)
2. Inflammatory vs mechanical back pain

rows: Sacroiliac tenderness · lost mobility in all planes · reduced chest expansion
No sacroiliac tenderness · abnormal flexion · normal chest expansion

blocks.html: 3. Comparing the three main diseases

rows: 5-7% of people with psoriasis (psoriasis: 1.2% of people) · first-degree relatives 50× more likely to get arthritis
Young men, 20-40 · formerly "Reiter's syndrome", a name not to use
Psoriasis first in ⅔, arthritis first or together in ⅓
Gut or genitourinary infection 1-3 weeks earlier (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter; Chlamydia and other sexually transmitted infections) · not an infected joint
Starts at the sacroiliac joints (both sides, symmetric) and climbs → new bone fuses it into a rigid column ("bamboo spine")
Axial in 20-40%: asymmetric sacroiliitis, large non-marginal "jug-handle" syndesmophytes
Usually a lower-limb oligoarthritis; can come before the back pain
Asymmetric oligoarthritis (over 50%) · rheumatoid-like (15-25%) · distal interphalangeal joints (5-10%) · arthritis mutilans (5%)
Anterior uveitis (25-30%) · aortitis, aortic insufficiency, conduction problems · upper-lobe lung fibrosis
Nail changes (80%, vs 30% in psoriasis alone) · dactylitis (sausage digit) · conjunctivitis 20%, uveitis 7% (uveitis more with axial disease)
"Can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree": conjunctivitis or uveitis + urethritis or cervicitis + arthritis · keratoderma blennorrhagicum · circinate balanitis
Over 90% of white patients (50-80% others) · but 8% of the white general population carries it · 50-100× the risk
Self-limiting, chronic or progressive · chronic arthritis or sacroiliitis in 15-30%

Physiotherapy for all (posture, chest expansion, fewer deformities) · NSAIDs (indomethacin best): mild-moderate symptoms, watch for gut side effects · conventional DMARDs don't work in the spine (peripheral disease only) · TNF or IL-17 inhibitors (symptoms, range of motion, fatigue)

Methotrexate (skin + joints), sulfasalazine, leflunomide · apremilast · TNF inhibitors (skin, joints, spine, nails) · IL-12/23 (not the spine), IL-17, IL-23, JAK inhibitors · avoid hydroxychloroquine (psoriasis flares) · conventional DMARDs: little proof they stop X-ray progression · apremilast = phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) inhibitor, skin + joints, slows X-ray progression, weaker than biologics · TNF inhibitors also treat enthesitis and dactylitis and slow X-ray progression · IL-17: skin, spine and joints

blocks.html: • DMARDs = disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs · TNF = tumour necrosis factor · IL = interleukin · JAK = Janus kinase

blocks.cap: Ankylosing spondylitis: bony bridges fuse the vertebrae into a "bamboo spine"

blocks.html: 4. Ankylosing spondylitis in more detail

• Genetics: twins 60% concordant if identical, 20-25% if non-identical and HLA-B27 positive
  • Sacroiliitis on a pelvic X-ray: usually bilateral and symmetric, the synovial-lined lower ⅔ first · earliest erosion on the iliac side (thinner cartilage; "pseudowidening") → sclerosis → complete fusion
  • Classification: modified New York criteria (radiographic sacroiliitis, grade 2 or more on both sides or grade 3-4 on one, + at least 1 clinical criterion) · ASAS (Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society) axial SpA: ≥ 3 months of back pain, onset under 45, then sacroiliitis on imaging + at least 1 SpA feature, or HLA-B27 + at least 2 other features · imaging = active inflammation on MRI or definite sacroiliitis on X-ray
  • Non-radiographic axial SpA: no diagnostic sacroiliac change on X-ray but diagnostic MRI · active inflammation = bone marrow edema, dark on T1 and bright on STIR (short tau inversion recovery) · fat beside the joint on T1 = chronic change
  • Enthesitis sites: sacroiliac joints, discs, manubriosternal joint, pubic symphysis, iliac crests, trochanters, kneecaps, clavicles, heels (Achilles, plantar fascia)
  • Spinal mobility exam (best of two tries each): modified Schober test (standing, a line joining the posterior superior iliac spines near the dimples of Venus, a mark 10 cm above it; measure the increase on full forward bending, to 0.1 cm) · chest expansion at the 4th intercostal space, hands on or behind the head: full breath in minus full breath out, in cm · occiput-to-wall and tragus-to-wall distance (heels and back on the wall, chin level; tragus = mean of left and right)
  • Beyond the spine (A-N-K-S-P-O-N-D): Aortic insufficiency, aortitis, conduction, pericarditis · Neurologic (atlantoaxial subluxation, cauda equina) · Kidney (amyloidosis, chronic prostatitis) · Spine (neck fracture, stenosis, osteoporosis) · Pulmonary (upper-lobe fibrosis, restrictive changes) · Ocular (anterior uveitis, 25-30%) · Nephropathy (immunoglobulin A (IgA)) · Discitis or spondylodiscitis · also microscopic colitis in the terminal ileum and colon (30-60%)
5. Psoriatic vs rheumatoid arthritis

rows: Asymmetric "ray" pattern · distal interphalangeal joints in 30-50% · whole digit (dactylitis)
Symmetric "row" pattern · distal interphalangeal joints uncommon
Dactylitis · enthesitis · skin and nail changes · periarticular redness
Nodules · dry eyes and mouth · vasculitis
Erosions at the distal interphalangeal joints · periostitis, bony proliferation

blocks.html:
• Look for "hidden" psoriasis: navel, scalp, behind the ears, perianal area, nails
  • Nail changes: pitting · transverse ridging · onycholysis (nail lifting) · hyperkeratosis · yellow "oil spots" · splinter hemorrhages · red spots in the lunula
  • Psoriatic arthritis can be peripheral, axial or both · axial disease = typically asymmetric sacroiliitis with large non-marginal "jug-handle" syndesmophytes

blocks.cap: Psoriatic arthritis: asymmetric, including the distal interphalangeal joints, whole digits and the spine
Reactive arthritis: mostly lower-limb large joints, heels and feet, plus the spine

blocks.html: • Ankylosing spondylitis: order X-ray of the sacroiliac joints, CRP/ESR and HLA-B27

lectures.name: Body Pain
lectures.title: Body pain
lectures.framing: Pain all over without swollen joints: what kind of pain is it, and is it inflammatory? An older patient with stiff shoulders and hips and raised inflammatory markers has polymyalgia rheumatica, which melts on low-dose prednisone. Diffuse, migratory pain with fatigue, poor sleep and fog is central pain - fibromyalgia - and that is a positive diagnosis, not a leftover.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Polymyalgia rheumatica = over 50, shoulder and hip girdle stiffness, raised ESR/CRP, no weakness, and a dramatic response to low-dose prednisone within days - no response means the wrong diagnosis. Fibromyalgia has normal inflammatory markers, is a positive diagnosis (2010 criteria), and often sits alongside another disease. Myositis is weakness with a high creatine kinase; PMR is pain without weakness. Fibromyalgia: exercise and education first; duloxetine, pregabalin or low-dose amitriptyline; never opioids. Prednisone over 7.5 mg for over 3 months needs bone protection.

blocks.html: 1. The approach
• ESR = erythrocyte sedimentation rate · CRP = C-reactive protein · PMR = polymyalgia rheumatica
2. Three kinds of pain

rows: Inflammation or mechanical damage in the tissue
Faulty pain processing in the brain and cord → hyperalgesia (pain "turned up")
Diffuse or multifocal, waxes and wanes, migrates · can sound neuropathic · touch and tight clothing hurt
Fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, jaw (temporomandibular) pain, tension headache

blocks.html: • Any mix can coexist - fibromyalgia alongside rheumatoid arthritis or diabetic neuropathy - and treating the peripheral pain can ease the central pain
3. Pain pathways

• Ascending (facilitatory) pathway: carries pain up · glutamate on N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors (plus substance P) · turned up in central pain
  • Descending (inhibitory) pathway: damps the signal · norepinephrine, serotonin, endogenous opioids · turned down in central pain → hypersensitivity
  • In fibromyalgia both are abnormal: less norepinephrine and serotonin breakdown products in spinal fluid, more substance P and glutamate · so any drug that raises norepinephrine and serotonin helps

blocks.cap: Ascending pain pathway (red) carrying pain up the spinothalamic tract; descending modulation (blue) from the periaqueductal grey and brainstem nuclei

blocks.html: 4. Fibromyalgia

• Definition: widespread pain for 3 months or more with other somatic symptoms, not explained by anything else · about 1 in 100, mostly women · can follow emotional or physical trauma
  • What patients say
    • central pain: "I hurt everywhere" · "it hurts to be hugged" · light, noise, smells bother them
    • severity: exhausted, cut back work and family · "fog", forgetful · unrefreshed after 8 hours' sleep · boom-and-bust days
    • somatic, often seen by other specialists first: headaches · jaw pain the dentist can't explain · abdominal pain (irritable bowel) · always feels like a bladder infection (overactive bladder) · non-cardiac chest pain · "stiff hands but the rheumatologist says my joints aren't swollen"
  • 2010 Fibromyalgia Classification Criteria - all three
    • ① widespread pain index 7+ and symptom severity 5+, or pain index 3-6 and severity 9+
    • ② symptoms at a similar level for 3 months or more
    • ③ no other disorder explains the pain
    • the 1990 version (3+ painful regions, 11 of 18 tender points) has been replaced - nice to know
  • ⚠ Not a diagnosis of exclusion: it is common to diagnose fibromyalgia plus something else · risk is higher with any rheumatologic or psychiatric disease, IBD (inflammatory bowel disease), multiple sclerosis, hepatitis B and C, Lyme, HIV, Epstein-Barr virus · treating the other disease alone won't fix the fibromyalgia
  • Targeted tests only: muscle pain → creatine kinase · neuropathic symptoms → diabetes workup · joint complaints → examine for swelling · fatigue → complete blood count, ferritin or iron studies, TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), CRP, liver enzymes, creatinine, albumin, sleep study
  • Mostly diagnosed and managed by family doctors

rows: Family doctor, group programs, the Arthritis Society
Best evidence · weight-bearing or not · Tai Chi, yoga, warm pool · graded, explained, ideally physiotherapy-guided
Nociceptive pain (physio for mechanical back pain, joint injections for osteoarthritis) · sleep apnea · psychiatric illness · rheumatoid arthritis, IBD, endometriosis
duloxetine (best evidence), venlafaxine · work with or without depression · ✘ don't help sleep
pregabalin, gabapentin · act on the facilitatory pathway · ✔ help sleep
amitriptyline, nortriptyline, cyclobenzaprine · help pain, fatigue and sleep · ✘ no effect on mood
Do not use - no better for pain, and sleep, disability and pain interference are better without them

blocks.html: • Prescribing: emphasise non-drug therapy (as effective as drugs) · one drug, lowest dose, titrate slowly · see them regularly · combine if needed · set expectations: half of patients get a 30% improvement
5. Polymyalgia rheumatica

• Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) = insidious pain and stiffness of the neck, shoulders, upper arms and hips · profound morning stiffness · fatigue · weight loss · mild fever, night sweats
  • Who: over 50 · women, Northern European descent · linked to giant cell arteritis
  • A misnomer: the muscles are normal - no weakness, normal biopsy · the inflammation is in joints and the tissues around them (bursae, tendons, capsules) · exam is normal apart from pain
  • Labs: raised ESR and CRP · anemia · high platelets

rows: Normal inflammatory markers · stiffness everywhere, not just proximal
Distal joints · reduced active and passive range of motion
Asymmetric · other symptoms · infection: warm, swollen joint

blocks.html:
• None of them improve as fast or as dramatically on steroids as PMR
  • Treatment
    • ⚠ never treat raised inflammatory markers alone - exclude other causes (cancer) first
    • prednisone 15-20 mg a day → most improve within 48 hours · ⚠ no dramatic response after 3 days → rethink the diagnosis (sources differ: the medwiki note starts at 10-20 mg - check the slides)
    • hold until well and markers normal (1-2 months), then taper slowly, e.g. 15 → 12.5 → 10 mg a month each, then down 1 mg a month (16-18 months in all) · average about 2 years on steroids, some for life · relapses are common
    • bone protection for anyone expected on over 7.5 mg prednisone for over 3 months: calcium 1500 mg/day · vitamin D 1000-2000 IU/day · an antiresorptive (e.g. a bisphosphonate)
