lectures.name: Vasculitis
lectures.title: Vasculitis
lectures.framing: Vasculitis is inflammation of the blood vessel wall, and the patient feels sick all over. The lecture asks two things: when to suspect it in a vague multi-system illness, and how to tell the types apart by the size of vessel they hit, with giant cell arteritis as the emergency you cannot miss.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Suspected giant cell arteritis (over 50, new headache, jaw claudication, raised ESR and CRP) → draw the blood, then prednisone 1 mg/kg (max 60 mg) now; biopsy after. Rule out infection before immunosuppressing. Normal ESR and CRP make giant cell arteritis highly unlikely; a negative temporal artery biopsy does not rule it out. Large = giant cell and Takayasu, medium = polyarteritis nodosa and Kawasaki, small = the ANCA trio, cutaneous leukocytoclastic and Henoch-Schönlein purpura. Order ANCA only when small vessel vasculitis is suspected; a negative one does not rule it out.

blocks.html: 1. What inflamed vessels do

• Mechanism: immune cells infiltrate the vessel wall
    • wall thickens → less blood downstream → can block completely → ischemia and clots
    • damaged wall can balloon out → aneurysm
  • Presents as: systemically unwell (fevers, weight loss, fatigue, fast pulse, diffuse aches) · almost any organ, so examine head to toe · some types are uniformly fatal if untreated

blocks.alt: artery damage in vasculitis - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: A normal artery, then narrowing from inflammation, total occlusion, and an aneurysm with clot

blocks.html: 2. Primary vs secondary

• Primary = no known cause, over 20 disorders, sorted by vessel size
  • Secondary = an identifiable cause, so look for it first:
    • infection: hepatitis B and C, HIV, other viral, bacterial, fungal
    • toxins and drugs: allergic reaction, cocaine
    • cancer: blood cancers, paraneoplastic
    • connective tissue disease: lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjogren's syndrome
  • Infection matters most to exclude: rule it out before making a diagnosis, because steroids make an infection worse
3. Classification by vessel size

rows: giant cell arteritis · Takayasu arteritis
Giant cell arteritis is the most common vasculitis
Classic polyarteritis nodosa · Kawasaki disease · Behcet's disease
Kawasaki disease: one of the two most common in children
granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA, formerly Wegener's) · microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) · eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, formerly Churg-Strauss)
The most common systemic small vessel vasculitides
Cryoglobulinemia · cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis · Henoch-Schönlein purpura

Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis can stand alone or be part of another type (the lecture's case: painful non-blanching purpura on the legs, ankle pain and swelling, unwell for 6 weeks · differential: coagulopathy or vasculitis) · Henoch-Schönlein purpura: the other most common in children

blocks.html: 4. When to suspect it, and the workup

• Suspect primary vasculitis in someone: chronically unwell with fevers, chills or weight loss · several organ systems · purpura · very sick with multi-organ failure · lung hemorrhage plus renal dysfunction · and no infection or cancer found
  • Diagnosis is hard: rare, many types, variable and vague symptoms that can take years, many organs, mimics common diseases, can be caused by other diseases · yet diagnose it in time to prevent complications
  • History and exam are critical; tests confirm. Biopsy of an involved tissue clinches it, but is not always possible
  • Every patient: head-to-toe history and exam · rule out infection · age-appropriate cancer screening up to date · complete blood count, creatinine, liver enzymes, ESR and CRP (erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein), urinalysis · chest X-ray · urgent rheumatology referral, other services by organ
    • inflammation (non-specific): normocytic anemia · reactive thrombocytosis · high ESR and CRP · low albumin (chronic)
    • silent organ damage: kidneys and lungs may give no symptoms → creatinine · blood and protein in the urine · chest X-ray (nodules in GPA)
    • rule out infection: white cells · blood, urine, sputum cultures (fungal, acid-fast) · liver enzymes · hepatitis B and C (cryoglobulins, low complement) · HIV · syphilis (VDRL)
    • rule out cancer: age-appropriate screening · serum protein electrophoresis

blocks.alt: organ involvement in vasculitis - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: What vasculitis can do to each organ, from stroke and vision loss to purpura and glomerulonephritis

blocks.html: 5. Giant cell arteritis

• Who: only over 50 (most over 70) · lifetime risk 1% women, 0.5% men · Northern European descent
  • Which vessels: a large vessel vasculitis with a predilection for cranial arteries, especially the temporal artery (temporal arteritis)
  • Presents as: new headache · temporal and scalp tenderness · jaw claudication · tongue claudication · diplopia · vision loss · stroke · plus fatigue, fever, weight loss, limb claudication, Raynaud's, chest pain, arthritis · polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms (limb girdle pain and stiffness, worse in the morning): see 11 - Body Pain
  • Exam: tender temples · swollen, rope-like temporal artery · optic disc swelling · pulselessness, bruits, blood pressure difference
  • Vision loss in 15-20%: may be transient (amaurosis fugax); untreated, total loss follows in the same and the other eye within days to months · acute painless loss is permanent
  • Differential of the cranial picture: sinusitis · cranial neuropathy · dental infection · intracranial tumour · temporomandibular arthritis · severe hypertension · acute angle-closure glaucoma · migraine or cluster headache · meningitis or encephalitis · neck pain
  • Investigations
    • ESR and CRP immediately: if neither is raised, GCA is highly unlikely (under 2% are negative for both)
    • temporal artery biopsy within 1-2 weeks: transmural inflammation + giant cells is 100% specific, but 50-70% are negative (skip lesions), so a negative biopsy cannot rule it out
    • temporal artery Doppler ultrasound in specialised centres: halo sign (wall edema), specificity over 85%, absent in ~30%, unreliable outside specialty centres
  • Management
    • draw ESR and CRP, then start prednisone 1 mg/kg (max 60 mg daily) at once; if blood cannot be drawn, start anyway and do not wait for results
    • protect against steroid side effects: proton pump inhibitor · calcium and vitamin D · bisphosphonate
    • vision loss or stroke symptoms → emergency department (urgent ophthalmology or neurology) · arrange the biopsy or ultrasound · refer to rheumatology
    • the lecture's patient felt 100% better after 5 days of prednisone
6. ANCA-associated vasculitis

• Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) target granules inside neutrophils · rare (20-30 per million) · fatal untreated · even when treated, mortality and morbidity are high and relapses are common
  • Presents as (described in every organ)
    • sinonasal: bloody crusty discharge, sinus pain · eye: mass behind the eye → diplopia
    • lungs: dyspnea (nodules, severe adult-onset asthma, pulmonary embolism) · lung hemorrhage
    • kidneys: high creatinine, protein and blood in the urine
    • inflammatory arthritis · mononeuritis multiplex (paresthesias, weakness) · skin: purpura, urticarial vasculitis, ulcers
  • ANCA test: only if small vessel vasculitis is suspected (usually by specialists; primary care may order it if no timely specialist) · details in 02 - Rheumatology Investigations
    • immunofluorescence: cytoplasmic (c-ANCA) → GPA, perinuclear (p-ANCA) → MPA or EGPA · ELISA (one antibody, more specific): anti-proteinase 3 (PR3), anti-myeloperoxidase (MPO)
    • false positives: infection (endocarditis), cancer, medications, cocaine · negative in up to 30% of GPA and 50-60% of MPA/EGPA
  • Biopsy: first-line in single-organ disease · in multi-organ disease, a specialist decides whether one is needed · purpura or urticarial vasculitis → punch biopsy in primary care (sent for histopathology, immunofluorescence and cultures) · ulcers → deep excisional biopsy by a surgeon · other tissues (orbit, sinonasal mass, lung nodule, lymph node, kidney if active urine sediment, sural nerve if neuropathy on EMG) → refer
  • Where to send them
    • unstable vitals, lung hemorrhage, significant dyspnea or renal failure → admit to hospital
    • active urine sediment with a normal creatinine → urgent nephrology and close monitoring
    • everyone else → urgent rheumatology and other specialists by organ
7. Treating cutaneous vasculitis

• Acetaminophen does not treat it · no evidence for cannabinoids
  • First line for non-severe skin disease: a topical corticosteroid
  • NSAIDs if no contraindication · colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily (adjust for kidney function; main side effect diarrhea) for skin and joints
  • Oral steroids work very well but carry side effects: only if other agents fail, infection is excluded and skin disease is severe (prednisone 30 mg for a week, then down 5 mg every 5 days)
  • Methotrexate is too slow for acute symptoms; for non-resolving, scarring or severe skin disease
  • With hepatitis C, treat the infection with antivirals first

lectures.name: Rheumatology Investigations
lectures.title: Rheumatology investigations
lectures.framing: No rheumatic disease is diagnosed by a blood test alone - there must be clinical features too (the one exception is gout, proven by uric acid crystals in joint fluid). For a suspected connective tissue disease (CTD) the antinuclear antibody (ANA) is the screen and comes first; anti-DNA only follows a positive ANA, the extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) panel names the antibody, and complement is a specialist's test.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Order the ANA only when you suspect a connective tissue disease - a positive rules nothing in, a negative makes most CTDs less likely - and never follow a negative one with anti-DNA, or repeat it · anti-DNA is very specific but only ~50% sensitive, and tracks renal lupus · anti-Sm is the fairly specific ENA; Ro goes with photosensitive lupus and congenital heart block · complement is a specialist's test · rheumatoid factor is non-specific; anti-CCP is the specific one · ANCA only when vasculitis is suspected.

blocks.html: 1. ANA: what it is and when to order it

• What it is: autoantibodies that bind to antigens in the nucleus of cells - the immune system should make antibodies to foreign proteins, not human ones
  • Order it only when you suspect an autoimmune connective tissue disease - otherwise it is a waste of money
    • about 1 in 3 women are ANA positive, but lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus, SLE) is 1 in 1,000 → many false positives
    • yes: weight loss, a new rash in the sun, high creatine kinase and new weakness · new oral ulcers, hair loss, low white cells and platelets · new glomerulonephritis of unknown cause (yes/maybe)
    • no: a low white count explained by myelodysplastic syndrome with no lupus features · fatigue and widespread pain (fibromyalgia)
  • Reading it: a titre - the stronger the positive, the larger the dilution: 1/1280 is a strong positive · the pattern can change with the dilution (1/80 speckled and homogeneous, 1/640 homogeneous)
  • Do not repeat it: not a negative from a year ago with no new symptoms, and no utility in following the titre - a positive at any time can count in the criteria for SLE
  • A positive ANA does not rule in disease; a negative ANA makes most CTDs less likely
  • CTDs are heterogeneous · many have characteristic clinical and lab features that make the diagnosis · treatment depends on the organ involved and the severity, and should involve a specialist
2. Anti-DNA

• An autoantibody against the DNA in the nucleus → the ANA should be positive
  • Order only with a positive ANA, when you are expecting SLE - a young woman with low white cells, low platelets, a malar rash and hair loss gets the ANA first, not anti-DNA
  • Very specific for SLE but very insensitive: positive in only about 50%
  • Correlates with renal SLE and disease activity - high in active disease, may turn negative after treatment
  • Pitfall: outside labs often use a kit that also detects single-stranded DNA, which is neither sensitive nor specific
3. ENA panel
• The lab screens positive or negative, then runs more assays for which antibody

rows: SLE with photosensitivity and rash · babies of positive mothers: congenital heart block, neonatal lupus
Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) and SLE
Scleroderma, especially with interstitial lung disease

blocks.html: 4. Complement (C3, C4)

• Low in active lupus, especially lupus nephritis - complement is used up when antibodies bind healthy tissue · or an inherent deficiency of one or more alleles
  • Specialist test - a waste of money for a family physician to order
5. Other rheumatology blood tests

• Pick the test from the clinical picture: acute hot single joint → aspirate (cell count, culture, crystals) · symmetric small-joint polyarthritis → rheumatoid factor + anti-CCP + ESR and CRP · inflammatory back pain, enthesitis, uveitis → HLA-B27 + ESR and CRP + sacroiliac imaging · suspected vasculitis → ANCA
  • Abbreviations: erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) · C-reactive protein (CRP) · anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) · human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27) · anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)
  • Many tests are also done for safety - which organs are involved, and is it safe to start a drug (blood count, creatinine, liver enzymes, hepatitis B and C)

rows: Antibody (usually IgM) against the Fc end of IgG
Poor: 5-20% of healthy people · Sjögren's, lupus, myositis, MCTD · hepatitis B and C, tuberculosis, syphilis, endocarditis · lung fibrosis, sarcoidosis · lymphoma
High (95%) - separates rheumatoid arthritis from other causes of a positive rheumatoid factor
Prognosis: positive → more severe disease (erosions, extra-articular features)
Can appear years before arthritis · not covered by the Ontario Health Insurance Plan (OHIP) - only if rheumatoid arthritis is suspected; better to refer

blocks.html:
• ESR and CRP: non-specific - raised in any inflammation, never diagnostic · very high in giant cell arteritis and polymyalgia rheumatica
  • HLA-B27: in over 90% of white people with ankylosing spondylitis, but 8% of the general white population carry it → a gene is not a disease · order when the picture fits (inflammatory back pain, enthesitis, uveitis)
  • ANCA: only if you suspect systemic vasculitis - not covered by OHIP
    • c-ANCA (anti-proteinase 3) → granulomatosis with polyangiitis · more likely to mean real vasculitis
    • p-ANCA (anti-myeloperoxidase) → microscopic polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis · more false positives
    • both positive → think cocaine cut with levamisole · levels follow disease activity only loosely

blocks.alt: c-ANCA vs p-ANCA staining patterns - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: c-ANCA stains granules across the neutrophil's cytoplasm; p-ANCA stains around the nucleus

lectures.name: Rheumatology Treatments
lectures.title: Rheumatology treatments
lectures.framing: Two kinds of drug: ones that relieve symptoms fast (steroids, NSAIDs, acetaminophen) and ones that change the disease (DMARDs, then biologics). In rheumatoid arthritis joint damage happens early, so start a disease-modifying drug early and aggressively, and use prednisone short term, as a bridge.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Methotrexate (weekly, teratogenic, liver, marrow and lung toxicity, monthly bloodwork, folic acid) is the first DMARD, started within 3 months - and triple therapy beats one drug · NSAIDs and steroids relieve symptoms but do not stop joint damage · high-dose prednisone only for organ- or life-threatening disease; gout and polymyalgia rheumatica need medium doses · hydroxychloroquine: yearly eye exam, no bloodwork, safe in pregnancy · leflunomide → hypertension · no TNF inhibitor with infection, heart failure class III-IV, cancer or multiple sclerosis · aspirate an acute hot joint before anything is injected.

blocks.cap: The four drug groups: steroids by dose and route, NSAIDs and analgesics, conventional DMARDs and biologics, each with when to choose it, what to avoid and what to watch

blocks.html: 1. Steroids

• Prednisone: non-specific - blocks pro-inflammatory proteins, ↓ neutrophil migration, inhibits cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α), ↓ prostaglandins and leukotrienes · most useful in the ACUTE setting because it works rapidly · ↓ pain, swelling, stiffness and physical disability · good short term, not long term: used short term or as a bridge until steroid-sparing drugs start
  • Dose depends on the condition
    • High (~1 mg/kg of ideal body weight) - life- or organ-threatening: ANCA-associated vasculitis · lupus nephritis · inflammatory myositis · giant cell arteritis · intravenous (IV) methylprednisolone 1 g daily × 3 days ("pulse") in an emergency, to jumpstart it before high-dose oral prednisone, e.g. giant cell arteritis with vision involvement
    • Medium - flares without major organ involvement: rheumatoid arthritis flare 20-40 mg, tapered as the DMARD starts · polymyalgia rheumatica 15-20 mg daily × 4 weeks, a quick taper to 10 mg daily, then down 1 mg every 4 weeks until off · self-limited, lasts 6 months to 2 years · with giant cell arteritis (~15%) → high dose, to lower the risk of blindness · acute gout 25-30 mg × 3 days, then down 5 mg every 3 days (NSAIDs or colchicine work too) · self-limited, so no high dose · lower doses with relative contraindications such as diabetes or cardiovascular disease
    • Low (5 mg or less) - chronic use when nothing else works or is tolerated (the adrenals make the equivalent of ~7 mg a day)
  • Routes: by mouth (easy to taper) · intramuscular (lasts 3-4 weeks; poor adherence) · intravenous (rapid, then switch to oral) · intra-articular when only a few joints or weight-bearing joints are involved, with fewer systemic effects · for inflammatory arthritis, osteoarthritis, rotator cuff tendinitis
  • Side effects of chronic use: appetite and weight gain · gastritis · mood change, psychosis · infection · Cushing's syndrome · acne · osteoporosis · avascular necrosis · hypertension · hyperglycemia · cataracts and glaucoma · proximal myopathy · slow wound healing · thin skin
  • Relative contraindications → a steroid-sparing drug: diabetes · cardiovascular disease · osteoporosis · recurrent infections · glaucoma or cataract
2. NSAIDs, acetaminophen, opioids

rows: Ibuprofen 600-800 mg three times daily · naproxen 500 mg twice daily · meloxicam 15 mg daily · diclofenac 75 mg twice daily · indomethacin 50 mg three times daily
Up to 3 g a day in divided doses (e.g. 2 extra strength tablets three times a day)
Reversibly block COX-1 and COX-2 → ↓ prostaglandins
Block COX-2 only → spare the stomach-protecting prostaglandins
Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout, pseudogout · efficacy similar, try another if one fails
Osteoarthritis, mechanical back pain, regional pain
Hardly ever used - the goal is to treat the inflammation, which eases the pain · a possible role in chronic pain, but other options preferred (misuse)

Hypertension, myocardial infarction, stroke · gastritis, peptic ulcer · renal insufficiency · caution in cardiovascular, GI and renal disease · interactions (anticoagulants) · 3rd trimester: premature closure of the ductus arteriosus · screening CBC, ALT, creatinine
Minimal: no stomach, constipation, blood pressure or cognitive effects · liver disease: max 2 g a day
Impaired cognition, constipation, dependence and withdrawal

blocks.html:
• NSAIDs are NOT disease-modifying: they ease pain and swelling in new rheumatoid arthritis or flares but do not prevent disease activity or delay erosions
  • Abbreviations: non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) · cyclooxygenase (COX) · gastrointestinal (GI) · complete blood count (CBC) · alanine aminotransferase (ALT) · erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) · C-reactive protein (CRP)

blocks.alt: COX pathway and NSAIDs - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Arachidonic acid feeds COX-1 (stomach, kidney, platelets) and COX-2 (inflammation, pain, fever); non-selective NSAIDs block both, coxibs only COX-2

blocks.html: 3. Conventional DMARDs

• Why early: joint damage is early - 90% of the joints are affected in the first year, erosions in >90% within 2 years (X-ray progression fastest in the first 2 years), disability is early and half are work-disabled at 10 years, and severe disease raises mortality → a window of opportunity before any erosions
  • Principles: treat early (within 3 months of symptoms) · treat aggressively (triple therapy beats one drug in early rheumatoid arthritis) · treat to target (remission: no swollen or tender joints) · adjust every 3-6 months if the target is not met
  • Starting: discuss side effects, interactions, contraindications · baseline bloodwork · most need monthly bloodwork

rows: 20-25 mg weekly, by mouth or subcutaneous · 6-8 weeks
Fatigue, GI upset, mouth ulcers · liver toxicity, myelosuppression, infection · acute pneumonitis
Baseline hepatitis B and C ± chest x-ray · monthly CBC, ALT, creatinine, ESR, CRP
Teratogenic · folic acid 5 mg weekly · avoid alcohol and sulfa antibiotics · dose by kidney function
200-400 mg daily (6.5 mg/kg/day of ideal body weight) · 6-12 weeks
Retinal toxicity (rare, ~1/5,000; bull's eye maculopathy) · ↓ visual acuity (accommodation) · GI upset, rash, sun sensitivity, headache · no myelosuppression
Baseline and yearly eye exam (visual acuity, colour vision, visual fields) · no lab monitoring
500-1,000 mg daily, up weekly to 2 g a day in divided doses (max 3 g) · 6-8 weeks
Headache (33%), lightheadedness, GI upset, rash (photosensitivity) · liver toxicity, aplastic anemia, infection · reversible low sperm count (33%)
Screen glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency · baseline hepatitis B and C · monthly CBC, ALT, creatinine, ESR, CRP
Safe in pregnancy · not with a sulfa allergy
10-20 mg daily (optional loading dose 100 mg × 3 days) · 6-8 weeks
GI upset, weight loss, hypertension · liver, low white cells, infection · peripheral neuropathy · hair loss (10-15%) · pneumonitis (less than methotrexate)
Blood pressure at baseline · baseline hepatitis B and C · monthly bloodwork
Teratogenic · cholestyramine washout (8 g three times daily × 11 days) · avoid alcohol

blocks.html:
• Shared toxicities of methotrexate, sulfasalazine and leflunomide: GI upset, hepatotoxicity, myelosuppression, infection (G H M I) · lung toxicity: methotrexate and leflunomide
  • Strategy: start triple therapy for 3-6 months · optimize dose and route · incomplete response: methotrexate by mouth → subcutaneous (better absorbed) · add leflunomide · add a biologic
  • Less used: gold, azathioprine, cyclosporine, cyclophosphamide
4. Biologics

• Like DMARDs they suppress inflammation and prevent joint damage, but they TARGET specific molecules and cells (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6) - remission is now possible · expensive (~$10-20,000 a year) → usually after other DMARDs have failed
  • Why TNF: excess TNF-α in the blood and joints → more IL-1, IL-6, IL-8 → these act on chondrocytes and osteoclasts → bone and cartilage erosion
  • TNF inhibitors: adalimumab · etanercept (a decoy receptor) · infliximab (intravenous; the other four subcutaneous) · golimumab · certolizumab pegol · onset 2 weeks to 3 months (infliximab can be faster)
    • Adverse effects: injection or infusion reactions · infections including tuberculosis and opportunistic ones · demyelination (multiple sclerosis) · worse heart failure · skin cancer (<1%), possibly lymphoma · drug-induced lupus
    • Do not use with: active, recent or recurrent infection · heart failure class III-IV · active cancer · multiple sclerosis or a family history of it
    • Stop or hold if fever, infection, antibiotics, or upcoming surgery (delayed wound healing)
  • Other targets: tocilizumab (IL-6) · abatacept (T-cell co-stimulation blockade) · rituximab (B-cell depletion) · newer: small molecules (JAK-STAT inhibitors such as tofacitinib) and biosimilars
  • Abbreviations: tumour necrosis factor (TNF) · interleukin (IL)
5. Joint aspiration and injection

• Informed consent for every procedure: benefits, complications, and a competent patient (or substitute decision maker)
    • complications: infection (septic joint, very low risk) · bleeding · fat atrophy or skin depigmentation if too superficial · tendon rupture (very small) · some systemic absorption (worse sugar or blood pressure control) · post-injection flare (uncommon, settles)
  • Diagnostic aspiration: always aspirate a first acute monoarthritis to rule out infection · send for only 3 things - cell count, crystals, culture and Gram stain (C3G: lavender top for count and crystals, sterile container for culture)
    • diagnoses septic arthritis, crystal arthritis, and inflammatory vs non-inflammatory · cloudier fluid = more cells
    • cell count: < 2,000 non-inflammatory · > 2,000 inflammatory · > 50,000 with many neutrophils → suspect a septic joint, consult orthopedic surgery
  • Therapeutic: draining fluid eases pain and swelling · steroid (e.g. triamcinolone) for inflammatory synovitis or osteoarthritis pain · hyaluronic acid for osteoarthritis pain
  • Relative contraindications to a steroid injection: septic joint or suspicion of one · overlying cellulitis or skin infection · psoriatic plaques over the site · prosthetic joint · severe thrombocytopenia or bleeding disorder · allergy to the topical anesthetic
    • ⚠ suspect infection? get the fluid, but wait until the culture is negative before injecting steroid

lectures.name: Pediatric Orthopedics
lectures.title: Pediatric orthopedics
lectures.framing: Children's bones are not small adult bones: they bend, they have a growth plate that breaks first, and they remodel. The lecture is an approach to pediatric musculoskeletal (MSK) problems in two halves: injuries (fracture patterns, growth plate, apophysis) and the developmental problems you screen for (hip dysplasia, clubfoot, leg shape, scoliosis). The limping child has its own chart: 09 - Child with a Limp.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ A child's growth plate fails before the ligament - a "sprain" in a child may be a Salter-Harris I fracture, and every growth plate injury needs follow-up for 1-2 years · type II is the most common · Barlow pushes out, Ortolani slips in, both useless after 3-6 months · Pavlik harness up to 6 months · Ponseti casting then boots and bar for clubfoot · bow legs normal to 2, knock knees 3-7 · scoliosis rarely hurts, and surgery aims to stop progression.

blocks.html: 1. How children's bones differ

• More porous and pliable → different fracture patterns
  • Periosteum (outer bone-forming layer) is thicker and more active → adds width and drives healing
  • Physis (growth plate) = cartilage at the ends of long bones
    • a site of relative weakness: the growth plate is more likely to fail than a ligament, so children fracture rather than sprain or dislocate
    • injury can cause growth arrest
  • Long bones grow by endochondral ossification: a hyaline cartilage model is replaced by bone at primary (diaphysis) and secondary (epiphysis) ossification centres; the physis is replaced last
  • Apophyses = tendon insertion sites: where avulsions and overuse injuries happen
2. Pediatric fractures

• Mechanisms: falls from low height · sport · pedestrian struck · vehicle operator · non-accidental injury in infants and toddlers
  • Most are single-limb and minor

rows: Cortex buckles on itself under compression - the most common
Distal radius metaphysis after a fall on an outstretched hand
Bone bends and breaks on one side only
Bone bows with no visible fracture line
A burst of muscle contraction pulls the apophysis off a fast-growing bone · any apophysis
Pelvis (the lecture's case: a 14-year-old boy with sudden anterior hip pain and an antalgic limp in a 100 m dash) · 5th metatarsal · medial epicondyle · treatment often non-surgical

blocks.alt: pediatric fracture types - buckle, greenstick, plastic deformation - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Three fractures only children get: buckle, greenstick and plastic deformation

blocks.html:
• Healing is seldom the problem - getting the alignment right early is ("as long as the two bone ends are in the same room they will heal together") · alignment criteria depend on the child's age
  • Remodelling (the skeleton restoring its own alignment)
    • helps: at least 2 years of growth left · metaphyseal fracture · defect in the plane of the joint
    • does not help: displaced intra-articular fractures · mid-shaft fractures with significant angulation or rotation · defect out of the joint's plane
  • Closed reduction: get everything ready first · hematoma block or conscious sedation (most control) → splint or cast (duration by site and type) → always post-reduction and post-casting films to check the reduction → timely follow-up
    • casting is an active treatment that takes skill and experience
    • reductions fail when not pre-planned on the X-ray and the deformed arm · when details are missed (direction and size of the force, translation AND angulation, hand position while moulding) · or the cast has excess padding or is too short
3. Growth plate injuries: Salter-Harris

rows: Often misdiagnosed as a sprain (sprains are rare in kids) · excellent prognosis · stable with closed reduction
Through the physis and up into the metaphysis
Most common · distal radius · prognosis usually good · usually stable with closed reduction
Through the physis and down into the epiphysis
Intra-articular · needs an anatomic reduction · prognosis usually good
Intra-articular · danger of a bony bridge between metaphysis and epiphysis · lateral condyle of the humerus, distal tibia · needs anatomic reduction
Often missed · diagnosed late, by the growth arrest · refer to orthopedics for follow-up

blocks.html:
• Major complication: growth arrest → leg length discrepancy or angular deformity · about 10% develop a growth disturbance
    • risk factors: age · severity · type (IV and V) · method of reduction · vascularity of the growth plate · open versus closed injury
    • treatment depends on the growth remaining
  • Every growth plate injury is serious, whatever the type or site: follow at least 1 year (preferably 2) and warn the family about complications

blocks.cap: Salter-Harris types I to V: through the physis, into the metaphysis, into the epiphysis, through all three, and a compression

blocks.html: 4. Elbow and overuse injuries

• The elbow is a confusing area of pediatric trauma: ossification centres vary in appearance, the very young have none at all, and the exam is often limited
  • Elbow ossification centres should appear in this order and by these ages, CRITOE, at about 1 · 3 · 5 · 7 · 9 · 11 years: capitellum · radial head · internal (medial) epicondyle · trochlea · olecranon · external (lateral) epicondyle
  • Swelling = suspect a more serious bony injury. Call pediatric orthopedics for: a significantly swollen elbow (especially before ossification) · instability · a displaced fracture · an incongruously reduced dislocation
  • Apophysitis = overuse traction injury at a tendon insertion, in adolescents
    • Osgood-Schlatter disease (tibial tuberosity: microavulsions from repeated traction partly separate it; girls 8-14, boys 10-15; localized pain, swelling, tenderness, usually gradual) · Sinding-Larsen disease (distal patella) · Sever's disease (calcaneus)
    • clinical diagnosis · benign and self-limiting, settles within 2 years, excellent prognosis · RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation) when acute · activity as tolerated (often modified) · anti-inflammatories as needed
  • Overuse injuries in general: adolescents, activity-related · apophysitis (knee, foot, hip, pelvis) · stress fractures · osteochondritis dissecans (loss of blood flow to the bone under the cartilage; a piece may soften or come loose)
5. Developmental dysplasia of the hip

• What: a spectrum from a shallow (dysplastic) acetabulum to perinatal subluxation or dislocation · 1-6 per 1,000 births, left more often · picture and treatment depend on age and severity
  • Risk factors: first-born · female · breech · family history · oligohydramnios · race (more common in Caucasian and North American Indigenous, less in Black and Asian populations) · other MSK problems (torticollis, calcaneovalgus foot, clubfoot, scoliosis)
  • Exam: look for other MSK problems and dysmorphic features · hip range of motion · leg length · instability · gait
    • Barlow test - "sign of exit": supine, hips and knees at right angles, adduct and push back → a reduced hip slips out · if positive, reduce it
    • Ortolani test - "sign of entry": finger on the greater trochanter, lift and abduct → a dislocated hip slips back in
    • both unreliable after 3-6 months → limited abduction · Galeazzi test (leg length discrepancy) · waddling gait, painless limp
  • Treatment by age: diagnose early to prevent long-term disability · up to 6 months → Pavlik harness · older → closed reduction and spica cast, or open reduction ± osteotomy
6. Clubfoot

• Ankle in plantarflexion, heel and forefoot in varus · genetic component · associated with spina bifida and other syndromes · untreated: progressive deformity and stiffness, much less walking and activity, footwear a problem
  • Ponseti method, started in the first weeks:
    • ① weekly manipulation and casting for 4-6 weeks
    • ② percutaneous Achilles tendon lengthening
    • ③ cast for 3 weeks
    • ④ abduction brace ("boots and bar"): full-time 3 months, then nights for 2-3 years
  • Posteromedial release surgery only for Ponseti-resistant or recurrent feet (extensive dissection)
7. Rotation and angulation: normal variants

• In-toeing and out-toeing, knock knees and bow legs, flat feet - extremely common complaints, variation in normal, rarely a problem for function or appearance · avoid overtreating normal variants
  • Bow legs (genu varum) normal from birth to 2 · knock knees (genu valgum) normal from 3 to 7 → reassure
  • Warning signs: excessive or asymmetric · short stature · progressive bowing · persisting beyond 7-8 · suspected underlying disease (nutritional deficiency, metabolic bone disease, skeletal dysplasia, previous trauma)
  • A limp: causes differ by age - missed hip dysplasia · clubfoot · hip disease (transient synovitis, Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis) · overuse · trauma, accidental and non-accidental · neuromuscular or inflammatory disease · warning signs in any abnormal gait: asymmetry · progressive · leg length difference · pain · deformity · a suspected associated condition
8. Scoliosis

• Structural lateral curvature plus rotational deformity of the spine
  • Types: idiopathic (most common - adolescent, F > M) · neuromuscular (cerebral palsy, spina bifida, neurofibromatosis) · congenital (skeletal anomaly) · other secondary (post-traumatic)
  • History: rarely painful · noticed incidentally · a rib hump · neurological review of systems · rule out a neuromuscular disorder (cerebral palsy, neurofibromatosis, spinal muscular atrophy) and congenital scoliosis · family and past history
  • Exam: dressed for it · gait · curve severity and flexibility · skin over the spine (dimple, hairy patch, lipoma, hemangioma) · Adam's forward bend test - rib prominence on the convex side (absent in postural scoliosis) · thorough neurological exam
  • X-ray: location, levels, direction, magnitude in degrees (e.g. right thoracic, T7-T12, 45°) · rule out congenital anomalies, trauma, tumour
  • Progression risk: girls · young, pre-menarchal · larger curve · double curve · thoracic
  • Treatment: education (natural history, risk of progression, monitoring plan) · brace (thoracic lumbar sacral orthosis, "Boston") · no medication · surgical fusion to stop progression, by curve size and progression risk: fusion over the involved levels, instrumentation to correct and stabilise while it fuses · modern pedicle screws correct more and fix more stably than the old rods, but cost more and take longer

lectures.name: Fracture Radiology
lectures.title: Fracture radiology
lectures.framing: Describe every fracture x-ray in the same order, so the person on the phone can picture it without seeing it. Detect it first (trace the cortex, look for secondary signs), then describe it systematically: views → location → type → descriptors → joint surface → other findings → bone quality, then what healing looks like. More than one descriptor for each fracture. Mnemonic OLD ACIDS: Open or closed · Location · Degree (complete or incomplete) · Articular surface · Comminution and type · Intrinsic bone quality · Displacement · Soft tissue injury.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Trace the cortex and look for secondary signs: a fat-fluid level or effusion means an intra-articular fracture even when no line is seen · an oblique fracture shows on one view, a spiral needs several · describe the distal fragment relative to the proximal (not for the clavicle) · intra-articular reductions must be anatomic · a transverse fracture with trivial trauma suggests pathological bone · the line widens at 10-14 days because it is healing · delayed union is twice the expected time, non-union no healing in 6-9 months.

blocks.html: 1. Get the right films

• Standard views: anteroposterior (AP, front-to-back) · lateral · oblique · the body is described in anatomic position
  • Special views for particular sites:
    • mortise view - ankle (shown beside the AP in the lecture)
    • scaphoid views - wrist in ulnar deviation, and the clenched-fist view
    • Y-view - shoulder
  • More than one view: an oblique fracture shows on one view, a spiral needs multiple views
2. Location

• Right or left · which bone · which part:
    • epiphysis (end) · physis (growth plate - immature skeleton only) · metaphysis · diaphysis (shaft) · apophysis (non-articular bump where muscles or tendons attach, under traction)
  • A growth plate fracture is a Salter-Harris injury: see 04 - Pediatric Orthopedics
3. Type
• Complete (all the way through) or incomplete (bowing, buckle, greenstick, Salter-Harris - immature skeleton) · others: avulsion, open

rows: Straight across, perpendicular to the shaft
Check a second view to tell from spiral
Twisting injury · needs multiple views · can resemble oblique, with a butterfly fragment

blocks.alt: fracture patterns on x-ray - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: Transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted and butterfly-fragment fractures on x-ray

blocks.html: 4. Descriptors (displacement)

• Describe the distal fragment relative to the proximal one - except the clavicle, where the proximal fragment is described relative to the distal (neck muscles pull it up)
  • Four components: angulation · translation · rotation · distraction
  • Translation (displacement) - movement of the ends away from each other, loss of alignment along the long axis, in shaft widths · more than a full width = "off-ended"
  • Angulation - by the direction of the apex: varus = apex lateral (distal fragment directed laterally, as the slide puts it) · valgus = apex medial (distal fragment pointing medially)
  • Rotation - distal fragment turned internally or externally; hard to read, so look at the joints above and below
  • Length: distraction (pulled apart) · impaction (driven in, "telescoped") · override (fragments overlap) - both of the last two foreshorten

blocks.cap: Translation is measured in shaft widths: half-shaft width versus off-ended

blocks.html: 5. Joint surface involvement

• Extra-articular: joint spared · reduction can be relatively anatomic · the bone remodels, particularly with weight-bearing
  • Intra-articular: risk of secondary osteoarthritis · reduction must be anatomic · longer to heal
    • step-off or depression - an abrupt break in the joint's cortical line; trace the cortex
    • fracture not appreciable? look for the secondary signs: hemarthrosis (effusion) and a fat-fluid level (lipohemarthrosis)
    • subluxation or dislocation

blocks.cap: Extra-articular fracture spares the joint surface; intra-articular runs into it

blocks.html: 6. Other findings

• Open (compound) - through the skin (the lecture's case: upper and mid third of the tibia and fibula)
  • Foreign body or hardware · periprosthetic fracture around an implant
  • Avulsion - a tendon or ligament pulls off a fragment (e.g. an intra-articular, dorsally displaced triangular fragment at the extensor tendon attachment on the distal phalanx)
  • Diastasis - a widened or incongruent joint with or without fracture: pubic symphysis, acromioclavicular joint
  • Amputation
7. Bone quality
• Weakened bone → pathological (fragility) fracture: usually transverse, spontaneous or with trivial trauma
8. Healing on x-ray

• Mostly secondary (spontaneous) healing: inflammatory, then reparative (callus), then remodelling phases; complete remodelling takes years · primary (contact) healing when the bone surfaces are directly apposed, as in internal fixation: no callus (Kirschner wires (K-wires) in the lecture)
  • Healing is a clinical diagnosis: no tenderness, no motion at the fracture site, weight-bearing possible
  • On x-ray: the fracture line widens at 10-14 days (resorption, not displacement) · callus at 2 weeks · union = mature bridging callus with the medullary space restored
  • Upper limb 3-10 weeks (distal humerus longest, 8-10) · lower limb 6-12 weeks (femoral neck and shaft longest)
  • Delayed union = healing takes twice as long as expected · non-union = no healing in 6-9 months · malunion = non-anatomic healing · management: see 07 - Fracture Management

lectures.name: MSK Oncology
lectures.title: MSK oncology: the soft tissue mass
lectures.framing: Almost every lump is benign, but the one that is a sarcoma must not be shelled out like a lipoma. The lecture turns on which features make a mass suspicious, and what to do before anyone cuts: image and core biopsy, not excise.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Over 5 cm, deep, fixed, growing or painful → image (MRI) and core biopsy before anyone excises it - under 5 cm with no suspicious feature can be excised · no fine needle aspiration for primary diagnosis · sarcomas are usually painless and spread to the lung (stage with CT chest) · wide resection plus mostly pre-operative radiation · adjuvant chemotherapy is not standard.

blocks.html: 1. Soft tissue and its tumours

• Soft tissue = non-epithelial, extraskeletal tissue (muscle, fat, fibrous tissue, vessels, nerves), excluding the reticuloendothelial system, glia and the supporting tissue of organs · from mesoderm ("mesenchymal")
  • Benign tumours are about 100× more common than malignant (about 300 vs 2 per 100,000) · sarcoma = a malignant tumour of soft tissue or bone · rare
  • Incidence rises with age, except the pediatric sarcomas: neuroblastoma · rhabdomyosarcoma · Ewing sarcoma · equal distribution around the world

blocks.cap: Soft tissues under the microscope: skeletal muscle, vessels, nerve, smooth muscle, fat and fibrous tissue

blocks.html: 2. Causes and classification

• About 99% have no known cause · trauma: myositis ossificans
  • Known links
    • environmental: asbestos → mesothelioma · vinyl chloride → angiosarcoma · herbicides, dioxin, radiation, foreign material → undifferentiated sarcoma
    • virus: human herpesvirus 8 → Kaposi sarcoma
    • immunodeficiency: chronic lymphedema → angiosarcoma (Stewart-Treves)
    • genetic: Li–Fraumeni syndrome (p53) · retinoblastoma (Rb) · neurofibromatosis (neurofibromin)
  • Named by the adult tissue they resemble:

• Behaviour: benign - limited growth, may recur, no spread · intermediate - locally aggressive, no or rare (5-10%) metastasis · malignant - locally aggressive, metastasises often
    • well-differentiated liposarcoma (atypical lipomatous tumour) recurs locally but does not spread · it can progress to dedifferentiated liposarcoma, which recurs and metastasises
  • Diagnosis is histological: routine histology first (it sets the differential and picks the extra tests), then histochemistry, immunohistochemistry, cytogenetics, molecular tests, electron microscopy
3. History and exam

• History - pin the timeline down:
    • when first noticed, how big then and now (compare to fruit or nuts) → has it grown?
    • trauma · pain or numbness (sarcomas are usually painless; significant symptoms → think metastases, and document them before you do anything) · recurrence (what was it called before?) · other lumps (multiple lipomas are common) · family history of lumps (lipomas and sarcomas can run in families)
  • Exam: location, size, skin changes · consistency · superficial (subcutaneous) or deep (muscle) · mobile, tethered or fixed · regional nodes (uncommonly involved)
4. What to do next

• Under 5 cm, no suspicious features → excise
  • Over 5 cm, or under 5 cm with any suspicious feature → imaging (MRI preferred, CT, rarely ultrasound) or a surgical expert BEFORE biopsy
  • Why not just cut it out? The common presentation: a lump thought benign, sarcoma never on the differential, excised with little or no margin, and the pathology says sarcoma ("whoops") · errors in biopsy or excision can reduce the chance of cure and lead to amputation
  • Biopsy, by a physician experienced in sarcoma, disturbing the mass as little as possible
    • core needle - the best compromise: less invasive, adequate tissue, good diagnosis · incisional - more tissue, more invasive · excisional - not ideal if it is a sarcoma
    • fine needle aspiration is cheap, easy, fast and atraumatic but not used for primary diagnosis: poor cell yield, hard to tell tumour types apart, too little tissue for extra tests
    • then expert pathology review with ancillary tests
  • Lipoma or well-differentiated liposarcoma? Immunohistochemistry: MDM2 negative and CD34 positive → lipoma
5. Treatment and prognosis

• Staging first (CT chest) · all possible sarcomas go to a multidisciplinary team
  • Surgery: wide resection (a cuff of normal tissue) is preferred · marginal resection is the "whoops" · a wide resection with a 1-2 cm margin is rare; one with a positive or close margin is common, hence the radiation
  • Radiation: added to surgery it cuts local recurrence from 30% to 10% · mostly pre-operative: better long-term function, because only the tumour is radiated and the surgery removes most of the radiated tissue · in the lecture's cases: 6 weeks of radiation, then surgery 6-8 weeks later
  • Chemotherapy: uncommon (select subtypes, trials) · adjuvant chemotherapy is not standard (no survival benefit) · very curable with chemotherapy plus radiation or surgery: osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma in young adults
  • Leiomyosarcoma and liposarcoma: often curable with surgery plus radiation
  • Not curable → palliative care can still greatly improve quality of life
  • Follow-up (the lecture's case 2): clinic at 6 months, chest X-ray yearly, discharged with no recurrence at 5 years
  • Prognosis tools: nomograms such as Memorial Sloan Kettering's

lectures.name: Fracture Management
lectures.title: Fracture management
lectures.framing: Every fracture follows the same sequence: resuscitate → reduce → hold the reduction → check it on x-ray → rehabilitate. The lecture then covers the two situations that change the plan - open fractures and the complications, of which compartment syndrome is the emergency.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch = compartment syndrome, a clinical diagnosis - remove the cast, call orthopedics, fasciotomy; do not wait for the pulse to go · any fracture with a wound is open: early antibiotics, tetanus, early debridement and stabilisation · non-union = not healed in twice the expected time; hypertrophic means not enough stability · femoral head, talus and scaphoid are the avascular necrosis sites · heterotopic ossification hides from x-ray early.

blocks.html: 1. Goals and steps

• Goals: restore anatomy (length, alignment, rotation, translation) · allow early motion · avoid complications of immobility and of poor healing · improve function
  • ① Resuscitate - bones bleed, and sharp edges can injure vessels
  • ② Reduce (not needed if non-displaced) - choice depends on fracture type and site, displacement, open or closed, and whether the patient can have surgery (other injuries may be more life-threatening)
    • closed (no direct view): analgesia and sedation → longitudinal traction, exaggerating the deformity → keeping traction, reverse it
    • open: in the operating room under anesthesia, seeing the fragments
  • ③ Maintain the reduction
    • cast or splint
    • external fixation - screws held by an external fixator
    • internal fixation - plates, screws, pins, nails · with open reduction = open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF)
  • ④ Post-reduction x-ray - is the reduction adequate (orthopedics has criteria), and is the chosen fixation maintaining it?
  • ⑤ Rehabilitation - as much movement as is safe, as early as possible · protect weight-bearing as directed · physiotherapy and occupational therapy for basic and functional mobility · prevent contractures
2. Open fractures

• Fractured bone or hematoma exposed through a traumatic break in soft tissue and skin · any fracture with a wound, even distant, is open until proven otherwise
  • More complications: infection, non-union and delayed union, incomplete recovery - worse with more energy (contamination, soft tissue trauma, dead bone)
  • Goal: turn an unstable, contaminated wound into a stable, clean one that lets the fracture heal
  • The lecture's case: open, spiral fracture of the distal third of the tibial shaft · mildly displaced: shortened, posterior translation, apex lateral angulation
    • early antibiotics (the lecture's case: 2 g intravenous cefazolin) · tetanus prophylaxis (given in the emergency department) · closed reduction and splint while waiting for orthopedics
    • early surgery: remove all dead tissue including bone fragments · gently irrigate with sterile saline · stabilise (the case: intramedullary nail)
    • early closure of the soft tissue: minimal contamination and little tissue removed → direct closure at the open reduction and internal fixation · a worse injury may need a plastic surgery flap
3. Compartment syndrome

• Pressure in a closed fascio-osseous space rises beyond what the structures inside can tolerate · lower leg (tibial fracture) and forearm most often
  • Muscle and nerve are metabolically active → injury within 2 hours of ischemia → cell death → leaky capillaries → more swelling → more pressure
  • Causes: external - tight cast, direct pressure, circumferential burn eschar · internal - hematoma, fluid leak (extensive burns, reperfusion after a vascular repair, crush)
  • A clinical diagnosis - urgent call to orthopedics
    • pain out of proportion to the injury · pain on passive stretch of the compartment's muscles (a tibial fracture with rising narcotic needs, terrible pain, and pain on dorsiflexion for the anterior compartment or plantarflexion for the posterior)
    • paresthesia (midterm) → paralysis (very late)
    • pulselessness is not typical - by then it has been missed
  • No test is needed when the clinical picture is there · measure pressure only when the patient cannot communicate (uncooperative, sedated, child): diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure under 20 mmHg, or compartment pressure over 30 mmHg
  • Management: call orthopedics · remove casts and compressive dressings · elevate · cool · monitor · definitive: fasciotomy
4. Other complications

rows: Clots from Virchow's triad: endothelial injury, stasis, hypercoagulability

Describes most orthopedic trauma patients · higher risk: multiple injuries · spinal cord or head injury · lower limb or pelvic fracture · older age · long surgery or long wait · prevent mechanically (intermittent pneumatic compression; an inferior vena cava filter stops emboli, not clot) or with drugs (acetylsalicylic acid, low-molecular-weight heparin), chosen for the patient (e.g. polytrauma with a bleed in the head)
Not healed in twice the expected time

Atrophic - no significant bone, impaired healing · hypertrophic - lots of bone but not stable enough · infected · fix with stabilisation (especially if hypertrophic), biology (nutrition, metabolic, stop smoking, bone graft), clearing infection (irrigation, debridement, antibiotics), reconstruction
Assess every plane: shortening, angulation, rotation, translation · osteotomy (a surgical break, ± removing bone, to realign and stabilise) if it affects comfort or function now or later
Bone cell death from lost blood supply
Femoral head, talus, scaphoid - all have a retrograde blood supply · pain · surgical
Uncommon in hip and knee, over 50% after ankle fractures · pain on weight-bearing, less motion · managed like osteoarthritis: pain control, physiotherapy to keep mobility, surgery if all else fails
Excessive ectopic bone, often after trauma

Polytrauma (around fracture sites), head injury, burns (over 30% of body surface) · hip, knee, elbow · stiffness up to ankylosis · early: redness, swelling, tenderness · x-ray and CT negative early (not yet calcified) - bone scan · control inflammation and pain · excise once mature if it causes pain, skin breakdown or lost motion

lectures.name: Physical Activity Prescription
lectures.title: Physical activity prescription
lectures.framing: Physical activity works like a drug, so prescribe it like one: check it is safe, then write a dose with F.I.T.T., then tailor it. The biggest gain comes from getting inactive people to do some, and a doctor's advice alone raises activity.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ 150 minutes a week of moderate-to-vigorous activity plus strength training twice a week - and the biggest gain is from none to some · talk test: sing = light, talk = moderate, no conversation = vigorous · blood pressure over 180/100 is an absolute contraindication until controlled · raised blood pressure without symptoms → start at low to moderate intensity · F.I.T.T. = 5 times a week, moderate, 30 minutes, aerobic · beta-blockers blunt heart rate, so cap intensity.

blocks.html: 1. Why prescribe it

• Low fitness is an independent risk factor for all-cause mortality, as important as smoking, hypertension and high cholesterol → helping patients move more matters as much as helping them stop smoking or lower blood pressure and cholesterol
  • Risk reductions: all-cause mortality 30% · cognitive decline 40% · type 2 diabetes 35% · hypertension 33% · depression 48% · bone fractures 66% · breast cancer 20% · coronary heart disease and stroke 25% · colorectal cancer 19%
  • Bones and muscles: regular activity cuts hip fractures 55%, through fewer falls (strength, proprioception, coordination, gait, reaction time) · small rise in bone density (1-3%) with regular high-impact training (strengthening, jogging)
  • Heart and blood: ↑ oxygen uptake and use · ↑ endothelial function · ↑ plasma volume, ↓ viscosity · ↑ contractility, coronary flow and stroke volume · ↓ oxygen demand, heart rate and blood pressure
  • In coronary heart disease, stroke and heart disease, exercise compares with drug treatment for mortality
  • Evidence as "medicine" in over 30 conditions, among them depression, anxiety, dementia, type 1 and 2 diabetes, hypertension, lipids, obesity, osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, rheumatoid arthritis, chronic back pain, cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, stroke

blocks.alt: health benefits of physical activity - upper-year notes.jpg
blocks.cap: How much regular physical activity cuts the risk of eight conditions and of death overall

blocks.html: 2. How much: the guidelines and the talk test

• At least 150 minutes a week of moderate-to-vigorous aerobic activity (Canadian guidelines, adults 18-64: in bouts of 10 minutes or more) plus muscle and bone strengthening at least 2 days a week · vigorous only: 75 minutes a week · build strength, sit less, improve balance
  • More is better (dose-response), but the largest benefit is going from none to some → target the sedentary · even 5 minutes has real benefits

rows: ↑ breathing and heart rate, warmer, may sweat if hot or humid
Brisk walking, stairs, cycling, dancing, swimming
Heavy enough that only 10-15 repetitions are possible
Standing from sitting, stairs, heavy gardening or shopping, weights, bands, push-ups, sit-ups

blocks.html: 3. Is it safe? Screening and risk

• Death during vigorous exercise is rare (about 47 per 100,000 a year, vs 190 for motorcycle accidents and 260 for cancer) → sedentary patients start low, go slow
  • Any patient with unstable or uncontrolled symptoms must be reviewed before starting
  • Absolute contraindications: new or uncontrolled arrhythmia · resting or uncontrolled tachycardia · resting blood pressure over 180/100 · symptomatic hypotension · unstable or crescendo angina · acute or unstable heart failure · unstable diabetes · acute febrile illness

rows: Asymptomatic, low risk but significant risk factors (e.g. ↑ blood pressure)
Begin with low to moderate intensity
<mark class="lo">Supervision at first, or referral to an exercise specialist</mark>

blocks.html:
• Pre-participation screening (American College of Sports Medicine): regular exerciser? → signs or symptoms? → known disease? · symptoms → medical clearance (a regular exerciser stops) · known disease without symptoms → clearance if inactive, moderate intensity if already active · none → light-to-moderate if inactive, moderate-to-vigorous if active
    • signs and symptoms: chest, neck, jaw or arm pain · breathless at rest or mild exertion · dizziness or syncope · orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea · ankle edema · palpitations · claudication · known murmur · unusual fatigue · stop and evaluate if any occur during exercise
4. Writing the prescription

• History: current activity · intentions · past activity and enjoyment (school, job, leisure, everyday) · preferences (alone, team, group, indoors or out) and barriers · is it safe (symptoms, past history)
  • Goals are personal - playing with grandchildren, less breathless on stairs, lower disease risk (often after an event such as a myocardial infarction or cancer), looking good (not everyone is moved by health)
  • The lecture's case: a 68-year-old woman, sedentary (used to walk her dog on trails), worried about falling · new, untreated hypertension (140/85) · father died after a myocardial infarction at 70, mother broke a hip at 73
  • The 3 A's: Ask (current activity, do they know the benefits) · Advise (on the benefits) · Act (signpost on to help and support)

rows: Moderate - can talk but not sing
Aerobic: walking, cycling, dancing, swimming, jogging

blocks.html: • Adjust if there is severe pain during exercise, pain that does not settle afterwards, more night pain, or more joint swelling
5. Hypertension and its medications

• Hypertension: control blood pressure over 180/100 with medication first · warm-up 15 min and cool-down 10 min · keep the feet moving · protect joints if obese or inactive · one rest day a week
    • avoid: very strenuous resistance training (left ventricular pressure can exceed 300 mmHg) · vigorous exercise with left ventricular hypertrophy · lying-down exercise (postural hypotension) · isometric and overhead exercise
  • Antihypertensives are not a contraindication to exercise
    • ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) - minimal problems, recommended
    • calcium channel blockers - small risk of postural hypotension, extend the warm-down, recommended
    • diuretics - dehydration risk, accessible toilets
    • beta-blockers - ↓ maximum heart rate and performance → bad for high-intensity exercise; avoid in athletes (an ACE inhibitor first line) · but good for limiting the hypertensive response to exercise
  • Abbreviation: angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)
6. The doctor's role

• Prescribing activity is cost-effective: only 25% of physicians counsel it, yet 92% of patients say they would follow a doctor's advice · a prescription raises activity by about 10% (could save $2 billion a year in Canada)
  • In hospital too: most inpatients barely walk · activity can be written on the medication chart (sit up in a chair, get dressed, walk on the ward)
  • Tips: know why it works · ask about history and preferences · focus on behaviour change · shared decisions · signpost to evidence-based resources (social determinants of health) · follow up

lectures.name: Child with a Limp
lectures.title: The child with a limp
lectures.framing: A limping child's age narrows the list, and one question comes first: is this a septic joint? After infection is ruled out, three hip conditions own the lecture - transient synovitis (young, after a virus, settles), Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (school-age, the femoral head dies), and slipped capital femoral epiphysis (overweight teenager, an emergency).
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ An overweight teenager with a limp and knee pain has a slipped capital femoral epiphysis until the hip x-ray says otherwise - stop weight-bearing and call orthopedics · fever, high markers and refusal to bear weight point to a septic joint, not transient synovitis · transient synovitis: 3-10, after a virus, afebrile, normal tests, gone in 7-10 days · Perthes: 4-8, painless limp, avascular femoral head, keep the motion.

blocks.html: 1. Approach

• Abbreviations: erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) · juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) · slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) · non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID)
  • Kocher criteria (septic arthritis vs transient synovitis of the hip): temperature over 38.5 °C · white cell count over 12 × 10⁹/L · ESR over 40 mm/h · cannot walk on it · (C-reactive protein was added later)
  • Uncommon but serious at every age: leukemia · tumours (neuroblastoma metastases and eosinophilic granuloma under 4; Ewing sarcoma 4-16; osteoid osteoma and osteosarcoma in teens)
  • Other causes: missed developmental dysplasia of the hip (painless waddle, leg length difference) · clubfoot · overuse injury · trauma · neuromuscular disease · inflammatory arthritis
  • Warning signs in any abnormal gait: asymmetry · getting worse · leg length difference · pain · deformity · an associated condition
2. The three hip conditions

rows: Non-infectious inflammation of the hip lining after a viral infection
Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Fracture through the growth plate: the head ends up posterior and inferior on the neck - really the neck moves up and rotates outward while the head stays in the socket
Ages 3-10, boys 2:1 · most common cause of hip pain under 10
Ages 4-8, boys 5:1 · family history, low birth weight, second-hand smoke · most common childhood hip disorder
Ages 8-15 (girls about 12, boys about 14) · obesity is the #1 risk factor · growth spurt, endocrine disease, radiation, family history · left more often, 1 in 5 both hips
Sudden, 7-10 days after a cold or sore throat
Gradual, painless limp first, then pain over weeks to months
Hip, referred to thigh or knee · better through the day
Mild, hip or referred to the knee · worse with activity, better with rest
Hip, thigh or knee pain - knee pain in a teenager can be a hip problem
Afebrile or low fever (under 38) · looks well · hip held flexed, abducted, externally rotated · less internal rotation and abduction
Looks well · less abduction and internal rotation · apparent leg length difference (adductor tightness)
Antalgic gait, may not bear weight · hip rolls into external rotation when flexed (Drehmann sign) · less internal rotation and abduction · thigh wasting
Usually normal: blood count, ESR and CRP (may be slightly up), x-ray and ultrasound - done to rule out septic arthritis
X-ray AP pelvis and frog-leg lateral (flattening, fragmentation) · bone scan, MRI
X-ray AP and frog-leg: earliest sign a wide, irregular physis · Klein's line along the top of the neck misses the head (Trethowan sign) · MRI if unclear

Refer orthopedics · keep range of motion with physiotherapy (better motion, better outcome) · take weight off (crutches, brace, swimming, cycling) · NSAIDs, acetaminophen · surgery (osteotomy) for some
Stop weight-bearing at once · emergency orthopedics · pin it where it lies (do not force a reduction): stable → one screw in situ · unstable → open reduction and internal fixation
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head (about 25%) · arthritis · the fixed physis stops growing (little growth left)
